Engineering, physics, computer science and economics all ask for it, and employers read it as proof that you can think clearly. It is also a subject where habits beat talent: a student who solves a few problems every day beats one who crams. This chapter is your map. ::: ## What A Level Mathematics contains The course has three strands. - **Pure mathematics** is the language and the toolkit: algebra, functions, graphs, trigonometry, sequences, calculus, vectors and, for Cambridge, complex numbers. It carries 60% of a full A Level, and everything else depends on it. - **Mechanics** uses mathematics to explain how forces make things move: forces, motion, momentum, energy and power. - **Probability and statistics** deals with data, counting, chance and the distributions used to model real situations. The course comes in two halves. **AS Level** is the first half, normally one year, and **A2** is the second. You can stop after the AS or carry on to the full A Level. Cambridge assumes IGCSE or O Level Mathematics; the five foundation chapters fill any gaps. ## The Cambridge 9709 papers Cambridge International AS & A Level Mathematics has syllabus code **9709**. It is assessed by six written papers. You sit only some of them, and you answer every question on each paper. | Paper | Name | Time | Marks | AS weight | A Level weight | |---|---|---|---|---|---| | P1 | Pure Mathematics 1 | 1 h 50 | 75 | 60% | 30% | | P2 | Pure Mathematics 2 | 1 h 15 | 50 | 40% | not used | | P3 | Pure Mathematics 3 | 1 h 50 | 75 | not used | 30% | | P4 | Mechanics | 1 h 15 | 50 | 40% | 20% | | P5 | Probability & Statistics 1 | 1 h 15 | 50 | 40% | 20% | | P6 | Probability & Statistics 2 | 1 h 15 | 50 | not used | 20% | ### Choosing a route | Qualification | Papers you sit | |---|---| | AS Level (choose one) | P1 + P2, or P1 + P4, or P1 + P5 | | A Level, route 1 | P1 + P3 + P4 + P5 | | A Level, route 2 | P1 + P3 + P5 + P6 | :::html ::: :::warn Check the route before you commit **P1 + P2 is an AS-only route.** P2 belongs to no A Level combination, so a student who may want the full A Level should take P1 + P4 or P1 + P5 at AS. Also, **P4 and P6 cannot be combined**: route 2 has no Mechanics, and an AS that includes P4 can only continue by route 1. ::: Paper 3 includes every topic of Paper 2. You can take the A Level in stages (AS first, the rest a year later) or all at the end; [Exam boards and how the exams work](#start.boards) explains sittings. ## Which chapter covers what | Paper | Chapters in this guide | |---|---| | Foundations (all papers) | [Numbers and fractions](#math.f.numbers); [Algebra from scratch](#math.f.algebra); [Powers and surds](#math.f.powers); [Straight lines](#math.f.graphs); [Geometry and trigonometry](#math.f.geometry) | | P1 Pure 1 | [Quadratics](#math.p1.quadratics); [Functions](#math.p1.functions); [Coordinate geometry](#math.p1.coord); [Circular measure](#math.p1.circular); [Trigonometry](#math.p1.trig); [Series](#math.p1.series); [Differentiation](#math.p1.diff); [Integration](#math.p1.integ) | | P2 and P3 | [Modulus, polynomials and partial fractions](#math.p3.algebra); [Logarithms and exponentials](#math.p3.logs); [Further trigonometry](#math.p3.trig); [Further differentiation](#math.p3.diff); [Kinematics](#math.m.kinematics); [Newton's laws](#math.m.newton); [Momentum](#math.m.momentum); [Work, energy and power](#math.m.energy) | | P5 Statistics 1 | [Data](#math.s1.data); [Permutations and combinations](#math.s1.perms); [Probability](#math.s1.prob); [Discrete random variables](#math.s1.drv); [The normal distribution](#math.s1.normal) | | P6 Statistics 2 | [Poisson distribution](#math.s2.poisson); [Linear combinations](#math.s2.linear); [Continuous random variables](#math.s2.crv); [Sampling and estimation](#math.s2.sampling); [Hypothesis testing](#math.s2.hypothesis) | | UK boards only | [Correlation and regression](#math.s.regression); [Projectiles and moments](#math.m.projectiles) | | After A Level | [Further Mathematics](#math.further) | Paper 2 has only the simplest integration, such as \(e^{2x+1}\) and \(\sin 3x\). Partial fractions, integration by substitution and by parts, vectors, differential equations and complex numbers are Paper 3 only. ## The formula booklet Every 9709 paper comes with the booklet **MF19**, the List of Formulae and Tables of the Normal Distribution. It gives results such as trigonometric identities, standard derivatives and integrals, the binomial expansion and the normal distribution table, but never says when to use them. Read it once early, then learn everything it leaves out. The [Maths formula sheet](#tools.f.math) collects the key results of this course. :::board **Edexcel International A Level (IAL)** has six units, sat in January, May/June or October: four Pure (P1 to P4) and two applied units from options such as M1 (Mechanics 1), S1 (Statistics 1) and D1 (Decision Mathematics 1). The pure content is close to Cambridge P1 and P3, but complex numbers belong to Further Mathematics, and Decision Mathematics is not in 9709. Edexcel mechanics uses \(g = 9.8\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}\); Cambridge uses \(g = 10\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}\). **AQA 7357, Edexcel 9MA0 and OCR H240** (the UK A Levels) have three 2-hour papers, each worth one third of the grade, with pure, statistics and mechanics mixed through all three. Everyone studies all strands, and the statistics questions use a **large data set** that you explore in advance. There is no Poisson distribution or complex numbers, but the UK courses add proof, regression, projectiles and moments. ::: ## Recommended order and pace Follow the pure chapters in sidebar order, because each uses the one before. These weeks assume 7 to 8 hours of study a week. | Stage | What to do | Weeks | |---|---|---| | 1 | Foundations: try each "Try it yourself" first and study only your gaps | 2 to 4 | | 2 | P1: Quadratics to Integration, in order | 14 to 16 | | 3 | First applied paper (Mechanics or Statistics 1) | 8 to 10 | | 4 | AS revision and past papers | 3 to 4 | | 5 | P3 chapters, which include all of P2 | 14 to 16 | | 6 | Second applied paper | 8 to 10 | | 7 | Whole-course revision and timed papers | 8 to 10 | :::tip A week that works Three 90-minute sessions on new material (read, redo each worked example without looking, then try the questions), one 90-minute mixed-practice session, and one hour redoing last week's mistakes. [Build your personal study plan](#road.planner) turns your exam date into a timetable. ::: ## Calculators All 9709 papers allow a calculator, and a scientific one is enough. Check your board's current rules before buying, because calculators that do algebra, store text or connect to a network are not allowed. A calculator never replaces working: when a question says "show that" or "exact", you must show the algebra. ## How to reach an A* 1. **Treat Pure Mathematics as the core.** It carries 60% of the marks, and every applied topic uses its algebra and calculus. 2. **Practise, do not only read.** After each chapter do every "Try it yourself" question, then past-paper questions on the topic, then full timed papers in the final months. [Past papers and mark schemes](#road.pastpapers) shows how. 3. **Keep an error log.** For each lost mark, note the cause: knowledge, method, arithmetic or misreading. Redo the question a week later. 4. **Show every step and obey the accuracy rule.** Give 3 significant figures (angles to 1 decimal place) unless the question asks for an exact answer, and work to at least 4 so that the last digit is right. 5. **Learn the language of mark schemes.** Method marks (M) reward the right approach even after a slip; accuracy marks (A) depend on the method. [Exam technique](#road.technique) has more. 6. **Aim above the line.** Thresholds change every session ([how the A* is awarded](#start.grades)), so a score near 85% in timed practice leaves a safe margin. Start with the official syllabus and past papers; [The best resources by subject](#road.resources) lists good free extras. :::recap - Mathematics has three strands: Pure (60% of an A Level), Mechanics, and Probability & Statistics. - AS routes: P1 + P2, P1 + P4 or P1 + P5. A Level routes: P1, P3, P4, P5 or P1, P3, P5, P6. - P1 + P2 cannot lead to the A Level, and P4 and P6 cannot be combined. - Learn what MF19 leaves out. Edexcel IAL has units P1 to P4 plus two applied units; the UK boards have three mixed 2-hour papers. - Follow the chapters in order, study 7 to 8 hours a week, and keep an error log. ::: Next: start with [Numbers, fractions and percentages](#math.f.numbers), or go straight to [Quadratics](#math.p1.quadratics) if the foundations feel secure. If you love the subject, [Further Mathematics: a guided tour](#math.further) shows what comes after. @chapter math.f.numbers @title Numbers, fractions and percentages @level pre @paper Prior knowledge for CAIE 9709 · Edexcel IAL · AQA/OCR/Edexcel (GCSE or IGCSE Number) @time 4–6 hours @summary The arithmetic that every A Level assumes: types of number, negatives, the order of operations, fractions, decimals, percentages and multipliers, ratio and proportion, rounding, estimation, primes, HCF and LCM. :::why Every A Level question uses arithmetic. Calculators are allowed in Cambridge 9709, but a calculator cannot repair a wrong idea. A student who is unsure about fractions, negatives or percentages loses marks in algebra, statistics and mechanics too, and cannot tell when an answer is absurd. A few hours here make every later chapter easier. ::: You need nothing except basic school arithmetic. If a section feels easy, try its questions in the box at the end and move on. The next chapter, [Algebra from scratch](#math.f.algebra), turns these rules into letters. ## Types of number Numbers come in families, and each family sits inside a bigger one. :::def Integer A whole number, positive, negative or zero: \(\ldots, -2, -1, 0, 1, 2, \ldots\) ::: :::def Rational number A number that can be written as a fraction \(\dfrac{a}{b}\) with \(a\) and \(b\) integers and \(b \neq 0\). Its decimal form stops (such as \(0.25\)) or repeats for ever (such as \(0.333\ldots\)). ::: :::def Irrational number A number that cannot be written as a fraction of two integers. Its decimal form never stops and never repeats, for example \(\sqrt{2}\), \(\pi\) and \(e\). ::: Together, rational and irrational numbers make up the **real numbers**: every point on the number line. The **natural numbers** are the counting numbers \(1, 2, 3, \ldots\) The symbols \(\mathbb{N}\), \(\mathbb{Z}\), \(\mathbb{Q}\) and \(\mathbb{R}\) are shorthand you will meet in function questions, such as "\(x \in \mathbb{R}\)", which means "\(x\) is a real number". :::html ::: ## Negative numbers Picture a number line: adding moves you right, subtracting moves you left. The signs follow four rules. | Situation | Rule | Example | |---|---|---| | Subtracting a negative | Same as adding | \(5 - (-3) = 8\) | | Adding a negative | Same as subtracting | \(5 + (-3) = 2\) | | Multiplying or dividing, same signs | Positive answer | \((-4) \times (-6) = 24\) | | Multiplying or dividing, different signs | Negative answer | \(12 \div (-3) = -4\) | :::warn Squaring a negative number \(-3^2\) means \(-(3^2) = -9\), because the power acts before the minus sign. \((-3)^2 = (-3) \times (-3) = 9\). This slip causes many errors in the quadratic formula, so use brackets every time you square a negative number. ::: ## The order of operations Calculations are done in a fixed order, remembered as **BIDMAS**: Brackets, Indices (powers and roots), Division and Multiplication, then Addition and Subtraction. Division and multiplication share the same rank, so work left to right. Addition and subtraction also share a rank. A fraction line and a root sign act like brackets. :::eg Work out \(3 + 4 \times 2^2 - 10 \div 5\) Indices first: \(2^2 = 4\). Then multiplication and division, left to right: \(4 \times 4 = 16\) and \(10 \div 5 = 2\). Finally \(3 + 16 - 2 = 17\). ::: :::eg Work out \(12 - (3 - 7)^2 \div 2\) Brackets: \(3 - 7 = -4\). Indices: \((-4)^2 = 16\). Division: \(16 \div 2 = 8\). Subtraction: \(12 - 8 = 4\). ::: :::tip Brackets on the calculator To work out \(\dfrac{5 + 7}{2 \times 3}\), type \((5 + 7) \div (2 \times 3)\) and get \(2\). Without the brackets the calculator computes \(5 + 7 \div 2 \times 3 = 15.5\). ::: ## Fractions A fraction \(\dfrac{a}{b}\) has a **numerator** \(a\) on top and a **denominator** \(b\) below. Fractions such as \(\tfrac24\) and \(\tfrac36\) are **equivalent** to \(\tfrac12\): multiply or divide top and bottom by the same number. To **simplify** a fraction, divide both parts by their highest common factor (explained at the end of this chapter). :::steps 1. **Add or subtract:** write both fractions over a common denominator, then add or subtract the numerators only. 2. **Multiply:** multiply the numerators and multiply the denominators. Cancel common factors first to keep the numbers small. 3. **Divide:** turn the second fraction upside down (its **reciprocal**) and multiply. 4. **Mixed numbers:** change \(2\tfrac13\) to the improper fraction \(\tfrac73\) before doing anything else. ::: :::eg Work out \(\dfrac34 + \dfrac56\) and \(3\tfrac14 - 1\tfrac56\) The lowest common denominator of 4 and 6 is 12: \[\frac34 + \frac56 = \frac{9}{12} + \frac{10}{12} = \frac{19}{12} = 1\tfrac{7}{12}\] Change to improper fractions: \(3\tfrac14 = \tfrac{13}{4}\) and \(1\tfrac56 = \tfrac{11}{6}\). Then \[\frac{13}{4} - \frac{11}{6} = \frac{39}{12} - \frac{22}{12} = \frac{17}{12} = 1\tfrac{5}{12}\] ::: :::eg Work out \(2\tfrac13 \times 1\tfrac12\) and \(\dfrac58 \div \dfrac{15}{16}\) \[2\tfrac13 \times 1\tfrac12 = \frac{7}{3} \times \frac{3}{2} = \frac{7}{2} = 3\tfrac12\] (the 3s cancel). For the division, flip the second fraction and cancel: \[\frac58 \div \frac{15}{16} = \frac58 \times \frac{16}{15} = \frac{1 \times 2}{1 \times 3} = \frac23\] ::: :::warn Never add fractions straight across \(\tfrac12 + \tfrac13\) is not \(\tfrac25\). The answer must be bigger than \(\tfrac12\), and \(\tfrac25\) is smaller. The correct answer is \(\tfrac36 + \tfrac26 = \tfrac56\). The same rules work for fractions that contain letters. ::: ## Decimals and recurring decimals Each place to the right of the decimal point is ten times smaller: tenths, hundredths, thousandths. To change a fraction to a decimal, divide the top by the bottom: \(\tfrac38 = 3 \div 8 = 0.375\). To go back, write the decimal over a power of 10 and simplify: \(0.35 = \tfrac{35}{100} = \tfrac{7}{20}\). Some fractions never terminate. \(\tfrac13 = 0.333\ldots\) is written \(0.\dot{3}\), where the dot marks the repeating digit. For a block of digits, a dot goes over the first and last digit, so \(0.272727\ldots = 0.\dot{2}\dot{7}\). Every recurring decimal is a rational number, and there is a method to find its fraction. :::eg Write \(0.\dot{2}\dot{7}\) as a fraction in its simplest form. Let \(x = 0.272727\ldots\) Two digits repeat, so multiply by 100: \(100x = 27.272727\ldots\) Subtract the first line from the second so the repeating part disappears: \[99x = 27 \quad\Rightarrow\quad x = \frac{27}{99} = \frac{3}{11}\] Check: \(3 \div 11 = 0.2727\ldots\) The same idea sums geometric series in [Series](#math.p1.series). ::: ## Percentages :::def Percentage A fraction with denominator 100. "Per cent" means "out of 100", so \(45\% = \dfrac{45}{100} = 0.45\). ::: To change a percentage to a decimal, divide by 100. To find a percentage of an amount, multiply by the decimal: \(35\%\) of \(80 = 0.35 \times 80 = 28\). To find a **percentage change**, always compare with the **original** value: \[\text{percentage change} = \frac{\text{change}}{\text{original}} \times 100\%\] The most useful tool is the **multiplier**. :::key Percentage multipliers - Increase by \(p\%\): multiply by \(1 + \dfrac{p}{100}\). So \(+15\%\) is \(\times 1.15\). - Decrease by \(p\%\): multiply by \(1 - \dfrac{p}{100}\). So \(-20\%\) is \(\times 0.8\). - Repeat a change \(n\) times: multiply by the multiplier to the power \(n\). - Undo a change: **divide** by the multiplier. ::: :::eg A phone falls in price from $250 to $210. Find the percentage decrease. \[\frac{250 - 210}{250} \times 100\% = \frac{40}{250} \times 100\% = 16\%\] ::: :::eg After a 20% discount a jacket costs $64. What was the original price? The sale price is \(80\%\) of the original, so \(\text{original} \times 0.8 = 64\) and \[\text{original} = \frac{64}{0.8} = 80\] Check: \(20\%\) of \(80\) is \(16\), and \(80 - 16 = 64\). Taking \(20\%\) off \(64\), or multiplying it by \(1.2\), would be wrong, because the \(20\%\) was taken from the original price, not from \(64\). ::: :::eg $5000 is invested at 4% compound interest a year. How much is it worth after 3 years? Each year the amount is multiplied by \(1.04\): \[5000 \times 1.04^3 = 5624.32\] The investment is worth $5624.32. ::: ## Ratio and proportion A **ratio** compares quantities. Simplify it by dividing every part by their highest common factor: \(18 : 24 : 30 = 3 : 4 : 5\). To share an amount in a ratio, add the parts, find the value of one part, then multiply. :::eg Share $240 in the ratio 3 : 5. There are \(3 + 5 = 8\) parts, and \(240 \div 8 = 30\) per part. The shares are $90 and $150 (that is \(3 \times 30\) and \(5 \times 30\)). Check: \(90 + 150 = 240\). ::: Two quantities are in **direct proportion** if doubling one doubles the other (\(y = kx\)). Find the value of one unit first. They are in **inverse proportion** if doubling one halves the other (\(y = \dfrac{k}{x}\)): the product stays constant. :::eg 12 biscuits need 250 g of flour. How much flour for 30 biscuits? Five workers take 12 days to build a wall; how long would 8 workers take? Flour: \(250 \div 12\) g per biscuit, so \(250 \div 12 \times 30 = 625\) g. Workers: more workers means fewer days, so use inverse proportion. The job is \(5 \times 12 = 60\) worker-days, so 8 workers take \(60 \div 8 = 7.5\) days. ::: ## Rounding, significant figures and estimation :::def Significant figures The digits of a number counted from the first non-zero digit on the left. Zeros at the start are not significant: \(0.00397\) has 3 significant figures. Zeros that come after another digit are significant if they show accuracy: \(2.10\) has 3. ::: To round to a given place, look at the digit **after** it. If it is 5 or more, round up; otherwise leave the digit as it is. Then fill any gap before the decimal point with zeros. | Number | 2 decimal places | 3 significant figures | |---|---|---| | \(47.8564\) | \(47.86\) | \(47.9\) | | \(0.003972\) | \(0.00\) | \(0.00397\) | | \(58\,762.4\) | \(58\,762.40\) | \(58\,800\) | | \(2.0996\) | \(2.10\) | \(2.10\) | The second row shows why significant figures matter for small numbers: two decimal places destroy all the information. In the last row the zero must be written, because \(2.1\) would claim only 2 significant figures. :::exam Accuracy rules in Cambridge papers Unless the question says otherwise, give non-exact answers to **3 significant figures**, and angles in degrees to **1 decimal place**. Money is normally given to 2 decimal places. "Exact" means leave fractions, surds and \(\pi\) in the answer. Never round in the middle of a calculation: keep the full value on your calculator, use the answer key, and round only the final answer. Early rounding can cost the accuracy mark. ::: **Estimation** checks that an answer is sensible. Round each number to 1 significant figure and calculate. :::eg Estimate \(\dfrac{6.82 \times 29.4}{0.48}\), then use a calculator. \(\dfrac{7 \times 30}{0.5} = \dfrac{210}{0.5} = 420\). A calculator gives \(417.725\ldots\), which is \(418\) to 3 significant figures. The two answers agree, so a slip such as a misplaced decimal point is unlikely. ::: ## Primes, factors and multiples :::def Prime number A whole number greater than 1 whose only factors are 1 and itself. The first primes are \(2, 3, 5, 7, 11, 13, \ldots\) The number 2 is the only even prime. ::: Every whole number greater than 1 is a product of primes in exactly one way, apart from the order. To find it, divide repeatedly by the smallest prime that fits: \(84 = 2 \times 42 = 2 \times 2 \times 21 = 2^2 \times 3 \times 7\). To test whether \(n\) is prime, try the primes up to \(\sqrt{n}\). For 91, \(\sqrt{91} \approx 9.5\), and \(7 \times 13 = 91\), so 91 is not prime. :::def Highest common factor (HCF) The largest whole number that divides exactly into each of the given numbers. ::: :::def Lowest common multiple (LCM) The smallest positive whole number that each of the given numbers divides into exactly. ::: :::eg Find the HCF and LCM of 84 and 90. \(84 = 2^2 \times 3 \times 7\) and \(90 = 2 \times 3^2 \times 5\). **HCF:** take the primes common to both, each to its **lowest** power: \(2 \times 3 = 6\). **LCM:** take every prime that appears, each to its **highest** power: \(2^2 \times 3^2 \times 5 \times 7 = 1260\). Check: \(\text{HCF} \times \text{LCM} = 6 \times 1260 = 7560 = 84 \times 90\). This check works for any two numbers. ::: The HCF simplifies fractions (\(\tfrac{84}{90} = \tfrac{14}{15}\)) and the LCM gives common denominators. It also solves timing problems: two lights that flash every 12 seconds and every 18 seconds flash together every \(\text{LCM}(12, 18) = 36\) seconds. :::try Start easy, finish at exam standard Q: Work out \(8 - 2 \times (5 - 9)^2 + 12 \div 4\). A: Brackets: \(5 - 9 = -4\). Indices: \((-4)^2 = 16\). Multiplication and division: \(2 \times 16 = 32\) and \(12 \div 4 = 3\). So \(8 - 32 + 3 = -21\). Q: Work out (a) \(\dfrac23 + \dfrac35\), (b) \(3\tfrac12 \div 1\tfrac34\), (c) \(\dfrac56 \times \dfrac{9}{10}\). A: (a) \(\dfrac{10}{15} + \dfrac{9}{15} = \dfrac{19}{15} = 1\tfrac{4}{15}\). (b) \(\dfrac72 \div \dfrac74 = \dfrac72 \times \dfrac47 = \dfrac{4}{2} = 2\). (c) \(\dfrac{5 \times 9}{6 \times 10} = \dfrac{45}{60} = \dfrac34\). Q: Show that \(0.7\dot{2} = \dfrac{13}{18}\). A: Let \(x = 0.7222\ldots\) Then \(100x = 72.222\ldots\) and \(10x = 7.222\ldots\) Subtracting, \(90x = 65\), so \(x = \dfrac{65}{90} = \dfrac{13}{18}\). Q: (a) Increase 340 by 12.5%. (b) A laptop costs $480 after a 20% reduction. Find its original price. A: (a) \(340 \times 1.125 = 382.5\). (b) \(480 \div 0.8 = 600\). The original price was $600. Q: A car costs $18 000 new and loses 15% of its value each year. Find its value after 3 years, to the nearest dollar. A: The multiplier is \(0.85\). Value \(= 18\,000 \times 0.85^3 = 11\,054.25\), so the value is $11 054 to the nearest dollar. Q: (a) Share 360 in the ratio 2 : 3 : 7. (b) Six pumps empty a tank in 10 hours. How long do 4 pumps take? A: (a) There are 12 parts and \(360 \div 12 = 30\), so the shares are 60, 90 and 210. (b) Inverse proportion: \(6 \times 10 = 60\) pump-hours, and \(60 \div 4 = 15\) hours. Q: (a) Round 0.0486 to 2 significant figures. (b) Round 6382.5 to 3 significant figures. (c) Estimate \(\dfrac{38.7 \times 4.92}{0.0987}\) by rounding each number to 1 significant figure. A: (a) \(0.049\). (b) \(6380\). (c) \(\dfrac{40 \times 5}{0.1} = 2000\) (the exact value is about \(1930\)). Q: (Exam style) (a) Find the HCF and the LCM of 72 and 108. (b) Hence write \(\dfrac{17}{72} + \dfrac{11}{108}\) as a single fraction. A: (a) \(72 = 2^3 \times 3^2\) and \(108 = 2^2 \times 3^3\). HCF \(= 2^2 \times 3^2 = 36\). [M1 A1] LCM \(= 2^3 \times 3^3 = 216\). [A1] (b) The common denominator is the LCM, 216: \(\dfrac{17}{72} = \dfrac{51}{216}\) and \(\dfrac{11}{108} = \dfrac{22}{216}\). [M1] The sum is \(\dfrac{73}{216}\). [A1] ::: :::quiz ? Which of these numbers is irrational? - \(\dfrac{22}{7}\) - \(\sqrt{16}\) - \(0.\dot{3}\) + \(\sqrt{7}\) > \(\tfrac{22}{7}\) is a fraction, so it is rational (it is only close to \(\pi\)). \(\sqrt{16} = 4\) and \(0.\dot{3} = \tfrac13\) are rational. \(\sqrt{7}\) is not a whole number or a fraction, so it is irrational. ? What is the value of \(-4^2\) by the rules of BIDMAS? - \(16\) + \(-16\) - \(8\) - \(-8\) > The power acts first: \(4^2 = 16\), and then the minus sign applies, giving \(-16\). To get \(16\) you must write \((-4)^2\). ? After an 8% increase a price is $135. What was the price before the increase? - $124.20 + $125 - $145.80 - $127 > The multiplier is \(1.08\), so you undo it by dividing: \(135 \div 1.08 = 125\). Taking 8% off \(135\) gives \(124.20\), which is a common wrong answer. ? Round \(0.0070684\) to 3 significant figures. - \(0.007\) - \(0.0071\) + \(0.00707\) - \(0.01\) > The first significant figure is the 7 after the leading zeros. Three significant figures are \(7, 0, 6\), and the next digit is 8, so the 6 rounds up to 7, giving \(0.00707\). ::: :::recap - Natural numbers sit inside integers, integers inside rational numbers, and rational plus irrational numbers make the real numbers. - Follow BIDMAS. Square negative numbers with brackets: \(-3^2 = -9\) but \((-3)^2 = 9\). - Fractions: add with a common denominator, multiply straight across, divide by flipping the second fraction. Change mixed numbers to improper fractions first. - Percentage change is the change divided by the **original**. Use multipliers: \(\times 1.15\) for \(+15\%\), \(\times 0.8\) for \(-20\%\), and divide to reverse. - Ratio and proportion: find the value of one part or one unit first. - Round to 3 significant figures unless told otherwise; round only at the end; estimate to check. - HCF uses the lowest powers of common primes; LCM uses the highest powers of all primes. ::: Next: [Algebra from scratch](#math.f.algebra).

@group Welcome @chapter start.what @title What are A Levels? @level start @time 20 minutes @summary A Levels are two-year qualifications in single subjects, usually taken at 16–18 after GCSE, IGCSE or O Level, and used for university entry around the world. This chapter explains how they work, how they compare with other systems, and what studying them is really like. :::why Before you open a textbook, it helps to know the rules of the game. Students lose time and money because nobody explained the basics: which exam board they are entered for, whether their first-year exams count, or which subjects their chosen degree requires. The next twenty minutes will save you months later. ::: ## A Levels in plain English **A Level** is short for **Advanced Level**. An A Level is a qualification in **one subject**, such as Mathematics, Chemistry or Business. Most students study three of them at the same time, over two years, between the ages of 16 and 18. At the end you receive one grade for each subject, from A* (the highest) down to E. :::def A Level An Advanced Level qualification in a single subject, normally studied over two years after GCSE, IGCSE or O Level and graded A* to E. It is the main qualification for university entry in England, Wales and Northern Ireland, and schools in many other countries offer it too. ::: A Levels follow the exams most students take at about 16: **GCSE** (General Certificate of Secondary Education) in England, Wales and Northern Ireland, **IGCSE** (International GCSE) in international schools, or **O Level** (Ordinary Level), still offered by Cambridge in some countries. In England, the two A Level years are **Year 12** and **Year 13**, together called the **sixth form**. In Turkey they match the ages of Grades 11 and 12 of *lise*. Scotland has its own system (Highers and Advanced Highers), so A Levels are less common there. ## Two halves: AS and A2 An A Level course splits naturally into two halves of about one year each. :::def AS Level Advanced Subsidiary Level: a qualification covering roughly the first half of an A Level, normally studied in one year. Cambridge International grades it a to e (lower-case letters); UK boards use A to E. There is no A* at AS Level. ::: The second half is usually called **A2**, and this guide labels first-year content "AS" and second-year content "A2". Whether your AS result counts depends on the exam board: | Exam board | Does the AS count towards the full A Level? | |---|---| | Cambridge International | Yes, on the "staged" route: AS first, then the result is carried forward. You can also sit everything at the end. | | Pearson Edexcel International (IAL) | Yes: the first-year units make up half the qualification. | | AQA, OCR, Pearson Edexcel and Eduqas in England | No. The AS is a separate qualification; all A Level exams come at the end of Year 13. | | WJEC (Wales) and CCEA (Northern Ireland) | Yes. The AS is worth 40% of the A Level. | :::html ::: ## How many subjects, and which grades? Most students take **three A Levels**. Students who choose Further Mathematics usually take four, because Further Maths is studied alongside Mathematics, not instead of it. Some schools ask everyone to start four subjects and drop one at the end of the first year, keeping it as an AS. | Qualification | Pass grades, highest first | |---|---| | A Level (all boards) | A*, A, B, C, D, E | | AS Level (Cambridge International) | a, b, c, d, e | | AS Level (UK boards) | A, B, C, D, E | A result below E is recorded as U (ungraded), which is not a pass. Universities usually make offers in grades, such as "AAB", or in UCAS tariff points, which turn grades into numbers. [Grades, marks and UCAS points](#start.grades) explains both. ## How much work is an A Level? :::def Guided learning hours The time a student spends being taught, or doing study directed and supervised by a teacher, for a qualification. Cambridge International plans for about 360 guided learning hours for each A Level and about 180 for each AS Level. Private study comes on top. ::: Two school years have about 36 teaching weeks each, so 360 hours works out at about **5 hours of teaching per subject per week**. Add homework, revision and practice, and a normal A Level week looks like this: | Activity | Hours per subject per week | For three subjects | |---|---|---| | Lessons (or, if you study alone, working through chapters) | 4–5 | 12–15 | | Homework and reviewing notes | 2–3 | 6–9 | | Practice questions, and later past papers | 1–2 | 3–6 | | **Total** | **7–10** | **21–30** | Three A Levels are close to a full-time job. In school, that means lessons in each subject on most days, homework in every subject, and a short test or practical most weeks. If you study alone, you are teacher and student at once: lesson time becomes reading, working through examples and checking answers. :::tip A self-study week that works Give each subject at least three separate sessions a week rather than one long one: short, regular sessions beat a weekend marathon because you forget less in between. Keep one session a week for older topics. [Build your personal study plan](#road.planner) turns your exam date into a week-by-week timetable. ::: ## Why depth matters At IGCSE you probably studied eight to ten subjects. At A Level you study three, and each goes much deeper: A Level Chemistry, for example, explains *why* reactions happen and asks you to predict ones you have never seen. Because of this depth, examiners test understanding more than memory. Only part of the marks are for recalling facts; the rest reward applying ideas to unfamiliar situations, handling data, and analysing or evaluating. :::def Assessment objectives (AOs) The skills an exam is designed to reward, listed with their weightings in every syllabus. Typical AOs are knowledge and understanding, application, and analysis and evaluation; science subjects also have one for experimental skills. ::: :::analogy IGCSE checks that you can follow a recipe. A Level checks whether you can cook a good meal from whatever is in the fridge. You still need to know the recipes, but the marks go to people who understand why each step works. ::: Most students find the first term the hardest: the pace is faster, the ideas are more abstract, and you are expected to work more independently. This is normal, and it is why every chapter in this guide starts from zero and builds up in small steps. The same depth is why universities value A Levels: two years of serious work on a few hard subjects is excellent preparation for a degree. ## Who uses A Levels? A Levels are the standard entry qualification for UK universities, and universities in many other countries accept them too. Each university sets its own requirements, so always check the entry requirements for international students on each course page. Several organisations, called **exam boards**, write and mark A Levels. Schools in the UK use boards such as AQA, OCR, Pearson Edexcel, WJEC/Eduqas and CCEA. International schools mostly use **Cambridge International** (often shortened to CAIE) or **Pearson Edexcel International** (IAL), and OxfordAQA also offers international A Levels. UK universities accept A Levels from all the major boards. This guide follows Cambridge International and points out where the others differ. ## How A Levels compare with other systems | | A Levels | IB Diploma | US Advanced Placement (AP) | National systems (e.g. Turkey) | |---|---|---|---|---| | Length | 2 years | 2 years | Usually 1 year per course | Final years of school, then an entrance exam | | Subjects | Usually 3, in depth | 6 (3 Higher Level, 3 Standard Level) plus a core | Any number of single-subject exams | A broad school curriculum | | Extra parts | Optional Extended Project (EPQ) at UK boards | Theory of Knowledge, Extended Essay, CAS | None | Varies by country | | Grading | A* to E per subject | 1 to 7 per subject, 45 points maximum | 1 to 5 per exam | School grades plus an exam score | | Main use | University entry in the UK and worldwide | University entry worldwide | US college admission and credit | Entry to that country's universities | None of these is "better". The **IB Diploma** suits students who want breadth (CAS stands for creativity, activity, service). **AP** exams are taken alongside an American high school diploma, and UK universities usually ask for several AP scores as well as the diploma. **National systems**, such as Turkey's *lise* diploma plus the **YKS** entrance exam run by ÖSYM, are designed mainly for entry to that country's own universities. A Levels suit students who are ready to specialise. :::note Studying in Turkey? A Levels do not replace the YKS for most places at Turkish universities. Students in Turkey usually take A Levels to apply abroad, and many UK universities ask applicants from Turkey for A Levels, the IB, AP results or a foundation year rather than the national diploma alone. To keep both routes open, check the current rules with ÖSYM and with each university. ::: ## Can anyone take A Levels? Yes. There is no age limit, and you do not need to be at a school. Adults, home-schooled students and school students adding a subject their school does not teach can all enter as a **private candidate**. :::def Private candidate A student who enters for exams through an approved exam centre without being taught there. Private candidates sit the same papers and receive the same grades and certificates as school students. ::: Private candidates register with an exam centre that accepts external students, pay the fees and sit the exams there. In Turkey, the British Council (in Istanbul and Ankara) and some approved schools act as centres. Sciences need care: Cambridge's science A Levels include a laboratory exam that your centre must be able to run, while Edexcel International tests practical skills in written papers, one reason many private candidates choose it. [Studying as a private candidate](#road.private) explains the process. ## Where to go from here :::steps 1. Decide roughly what, and where, you want to study next. 2. Check the subjects that degree needs: [Choosing your subjects](#start.choose). 3. Pick a board and exam series: [Exam boards and how the exams work](#start.boards). 4. Learn how grades and offers work: [Grades, marks and UCAS points](#start.grades). 5. Make a plan and start: [How to use this guide](#start.howto). ::: :::quiz ? Cambridge reports AS grades in lower-case letters, a to e, to tell them apart from full A Level grades. ? A student in England sits AQA AS exams at the end of Year 12. (AS results from WJEC in Wales and CCEA in Northern Ireland do count, at 40%.) ?
