Each subject is graded 1–7, with a maximum of 45 points. ::: :::recap - An A Level is a two-year qualification in one subject, usually taken at 16–18 after GCSE, IGCSE or O Level. - Most students take three A Levels, or four if they add Further Mathematics. - A Level grades are A* to E. AS grades are a to e (Cambridge) or A to E (UK boards), with no A* at AS. - The AS counts towards the A Level at Cambridge (if carried forward), Edexcel International, WJEC and CCEA, but not with the boards in England. - Each A Level is designed for about 360 guided learning hours (about 5 hours of teaching a week), plus your own study. - A Levels reward understanding and application, not just memory, and universities worldwide accept them. - Anyone can take A Levels at any age, including as a private candidate. ::: Next: [Exam boards and how the exams work](#start.boards). @chapter start.boards @title Exam boards and how the exams work @level start @time 25 minutes @summary Who sets A Level exams, how Cambridge International, Pearson Edexcel International and the boards in England organise them, when exams and results happen, and how papers, mark schemes and grade boundaries work. :::why Two students can both be "doing A Level Physics" and sit completely different exams: different papers, different months, different resit rules. Knowing your board and its rules tells you which syllabus to follow, which past papers to practise and when your deadlines fall. ::: ## What an exam board does An exam board writes the syllabus, sets the papers, marks them and awards the grades. All boards teach broadly the same subjects at the same level, but the details differ: the exact topics, the number and style of papers, the exam months and the resit rules. :::def Exam board An organisation that writes the syllabus for a qualification, sets and marks the exams, and awards grades and certificates. Also called an awarding body. ::: :::def Syllabus The official document listing exactly what can be examined in a subject, how the exams are structured and what each assessment objective is worth. Cambridge calls it a syllabus; Pearson and the UK boards call it a specification. ::: ## The main boards | Board | Qualification | Where it is used | |---|---|---| | Cambridge International (CAIE) | Cambridge International AS & A Level | International schools in many countries; private candidates at approved centres | | Pearson Edexcel International | International Advanced Level (IAL) | International schools; widely used by private candidates, including at British Council centres | | AQA | AS and A Level | Schools in England | | OCR | AS and A Level | Schools in England | | Pearson Edexcel (UK) | AS and A Level | Schools in England, and some British schools abroad | | WJEC / Eduqas | AS and A Level | WJEC in Wales; Eduqas is the same organisation's brand in England | Northern Ireland has its own board, CCEA, and OxfordAQA offers international A Levels in some countries. Cambridge International and OCR both belong to Cambridge University Press & Assessment, but they set different qualifications. AQA, OCR, Pearson Edexcel and Eduqas follow the same rules for A Levels in England, set by the regulator Ofqual, so their A Levels share one structure. ## Cambridge International: AS first, or everything at the end A Cambridge A Level is made of several papers, which Cambridge calls **components**. The AS papers make up the AS Level and also half of the full A Level; the A Level adds more papers on second-year content. You can take them in three ways: :::steps 1. **AS Level only.** Sit the AS papers and receive an AS qualification. 2. **Staged route.** Sit the AS papers in one series and the remaining A Level papers in a later one. Your AS result is carried forward and combined with them. 3. **Linear route.** Sit every paper, AS and A Level, in the same series at the end of the course. ::: An AS result can be carried forward to complete the A Level **within 13 months**. In practice, an AS taken in June can be completed in the following June series. :::warn The 13-month rule If you sit AS in June 2026, you must complete the A Level by the June 2027 series for the AS to count. If you wait longer, you would have to sit all the papers, AS ones included, in a single series. ::: A real example is Cambridge International AS & A Level Physics (9702). Chemistry (9701) and Biology (9700) follow the same pattern. | Paper | Type | Time | Marks | Share of A Level | |---|---|---|---|---| | 1 | Multiple choice (AS) | 1 h 15 min | 40 | 15.5% | | 2 | AS structured questions | 1 h 15 min | 60 | 23% | | 3 | Advanced practical skills (laboratory exam) | 2 h | 40 | 11.5% | | 4 | A Level structured questions | 2 h | 100 | 38.5% | | 5 | Planning, analysis and evaluation | 1 h 15 min | 30 | 11.5% | Papers 1–3 form the AS (50% of the A Level); Papers 4 and 5 are the second-year papers. Cambridge runs two main **exam series** each year: **June** (exams from roughly late April to mid-June) and **November** (October and November). A third, March, series is available in India only. June results come out in August (the June 2026 A Level results were released on 11 August 2026), and November results in January. :::def Exam series A period in which a board runs a full set of exams, named after its main month, such as the June series or the November series. ::: ## Pearson Edexcel International: units taken in stages An IAL is **modular**: it is split into **units**, each examined by one paper. IAL sciences have six units, three for the International AS and three more for the full IAL. IAL Mathematics also has six: four Pure units and two applied units (mechanics, statistics or decision mathematics). :::def Modular qualification A qualification split into separately examined units that can be taken at different times, with the results combined at the end. Edexcel International A Levels are modular; A Levels from the boards in England are linear. ::: - There are three sittings a year: **January**, **May/June** and **October/November**. Most units are offered in every sitting. - You can spread units over several sittings, for example Pure 1 in January and Pure 2 in June. - You can **resit** a unit to improve it, and the better result counts. - Each unit's raw mark is converted to a **uniform mark** so that units from different sittings can be added fairly ([how this works](#start.grades)). - When you have all the units you need, your centre claims the qualification (called "cashing in") and your overall grade is calculated. - In the sciences, practical skills are tested in written papers (Units 3 and 6), not in a laboratory exam. ## The boards in England: linear A Levels A Levels from AQA, OCR, Pearson Edexcel and Eduqas are **linear**: - Every exam that counts is sat in May and June at the end of Year 13. - The AS is a separate qualification whose marks never count towards the A Level, so many schools no longer enter students for it. - There is one exam series a year, in the summer. To improve a grade, you resit all the exam papers the following summer; coursework marks can usually be carried forward. - In Biology, Chemistry and Physics you also receive a **Practical Endorsement**, reported separately as Pass or Not classified, based on at least 12 practical activities assessed by your teacher. Many universities expect a Pass. - Some subjects include coursework, officially called **non-exam assessment (NEA)**: typically 20% in History, Geography, English Literature and Computer Science, and more in subjects such as Design and Technology and Art. ## The three systems side by side | | Cambridge International | Edexcel International (IAL) | Boards in England | |---|---|---|---| | Structure | Papers; AS papers form half the A Level | Units; AS units form half the IAL | Linear: all papers at the end | | Does the AS count? | Yes, if carried forward within 13 months | Yes | No | | Exam series | June and November (March in India only) | January, May/June, October/November | Summer only | | Improving a grade | Retake in a later series | Resit single units; the better result counts | Resit all papers the next summer | | Science practicals | Laboratory exam plus a planning paper | Written practical-skills papers | Practical Endorsement plus practical questions in written papers | | Results | August (June series), January (November series) | Roughly two months after each sitting | Mid-August | :::board WJEC A Levels in Wales and CCEA A Levels in Northern Ireland are unitised: the AS counts for 40% of the A Level. Scotland uses its own qualifications (Highers and Advanced Highers). Rules change from time to time, so always check the current syllabus for your board. ::: ## What the papers look like | Paper type | What you do | Common in | |---|---|---| | Multiple choice | Answer 30–40 questions, each with four options | Cambridge sciences, Economics, Accounting | | Structured questions | Answer a question in parts (a), (b), (c): short answers, calculations, explanations | Every subject | | Extended response | Write a long answer, marked by "levels of response" | Business, Economics, English, History | | Data response or case study | Answer questions on unseen data, a text or a business case | Business, Economics, Geography | | Practical exam | Carry out experiments in a laboratory under exam conditions | Cambridge sciences | | Planning and analysis | Plan an experiment and analyse given results, on paper | Cambridge and Edexcel International sciences | | Coursework (NEA) | Complete a project over several weeks, marked by teachers and checked by the board | Some subjects at the boards in England | ## Mark schemes, examiner reports and grade boundaries After each series, boards publish three documents that are gold for revision: - **Mark schemes** show exactly what earned each mark. In Maths they use M (method), A (accuracy) and B (independent) marks; in essay subjects they describe levels of response. - **Examiner reports** explain, question by question, what candidates did well and where they lost marks. - **Grade boundaries** (Cambridge calls them grade thresholds) give the minimum mark for each grade. They are set after marking, for each paper in each series. [Grades, marks and UCAS points](#start.grades) explains why they move. Cambridge puts a selection of past papers, mark schemes and examiner reports on its public website, and schools get more through its School Support Hub. Pearson, AQA and OCR publish theirs on their qualification pages, although the most recent papers are sometimes released to teachers first. :::exam Use mark schemes from day one Do not wait for "past-paper season". After every topic, try two or three past-paper questions on it and mark them yourself with the official scheme. You will quickly learn which words and steps examiners need to see. [Phase 4: Past papers and mark schemes](#road.pastpapers) shows a full method. ::: ## Entries and deadlines You cannot simply turn up on exam day. Your school, or your exam centre if you are a private candidate, must **enter** you for each paper months before the series. For a June series, the deadline usually falls early in the same year, and many centres set their own earlier deadline. Late entries, if accepted at all, cost extra. Fees are set by each centre and vary, so ask for the full price per subject, including any centre charges. :::warn Confirm four things before you start studying Check with your centre: the board, the syllabus code (for example 9702 for Cambridge Physics), the exam series, and the entry deadline. A year spent studying the wrong syllabus is an expensive mistake. ::: :::quiz ? A student sits Cambridge AS Physics in June 2026. By which series must she complete the A Level for her AS result to be carried forward? - November 2027 + June 2027 - June 2028 - There is no time limit > Cambridge lets you carry an AS result forward for 13 months. June 2026 to June 2027 is 12 months; November 2027 would be 17 months. ? Which board offers sittings in January, May/June and October/November and lets you resit individual units? - Cambridge International + Pearson Edexcel International (IAL) - AQA - OCR > IAL is modular, with three sittings a year. Cambridge has June and November series, and the boards in England examine A Levels only in the summer. ? What is the Practical Endorsement? - A Cambridge laboratory exam worth 11.5% of the A Level + A separate Pass or Not classified result for practical work in sciences at the boards in England - Extra UCAS points for practical subjects - A written practical paper at Edexcel International > The Practical Endorsement is reported separately from the A Level grade and is based on practical activities assessed by your teacher. ? When are grade boundaries set? - Before the exam, and they never change + After marking, separately for each paper in each series - Only once, when a new syllabus starts - By your teacher, after your mock exams > Boundaries are set after the papers are marked, so that a harder paper does not unfairly lower grades. They can change from series to series. ::: :::recap - An exam board writes the syllabus, sets and marks the papers and awards grades. Always study the syllabus with the correct code for your exam year. - Cambridge: papers called components; AS papers form half the A Level; take AS only, AS first (carried forward within 13 months), or everything at the end. - Cambridge series: June (results in August) and November (results in January); March in India only. - Edexcel International: modular units, sittings in January, May/June and October/November, single-unit resits, and written practical-skills papers. - Boards in England: linear, all exams in May–June of Year 13, AS does not count, Practical Endorsement in sciences, NEA in some subjects. - Mark schemes, examiner reports and grade boundaries are published after each series: use them throughout the course. - Entries close months before the exams, so confirm your board, syllabus code, series and deadline early. ::: Next: [Grades, marks and UCAS points](#start.grades). @chapter start.grades @title Grades, marks and UCAS points @level start @time 25 minutes @summary How raw marks become grades, why grade boundaries move, how the A* is awarded, and how UCAS tariff points, university offers and predicted grades work. :::why Your grades open university doors, so it pays to know exactly how they are calculated. Understanding grade boundaries also changes how you study: it shows why every single mark matters, and why a hard paper is not a disaster. ::: ## The grades | Qualification | Pass grades, highest first | |---|---| | A Level | A*, A, B, C, D, E | | AS Level | a, b, c, d, e at Cambridge; A, B, C, D, E at UK boards | A result below the lowest pass grade is reported as ungraded (U), and no qualification is awarded in that subject. Your certificate shows a grade for each subject, not a percentage. ## From raw marks to a grade Each paper is marked and you receive a **raw mark**. Your raw marks are combined, using each paper's weighting, and the total is compared with the **grade boundaries** for that series. :::def Raw mark The number of marks you actually score on a paper, before any conversion; for example, 52 out of 75. ::: :::def Grade boundary The minimum mark needed for a particular grade on a paper or qualification in a given exam series. Boundaries are set after marking and can change from series to series. Cambridge calls them grade thresholds. ::: ### Why boundaries move No two papers are equally difficult. If this year's paper is harder than last year's, the same student scores fewer marks. To keep an A worth the same every year, senior examiners study the papers, samples of marked scripts and statistics, and then set the boundaries. A harder paper gets lower boundaries; an easier paper gets higher ones. | Mark needed (out of 100) | Series 1: harder paper | Series 2: easier paper | |---|---|---| | Grade A | 68 | 76 | | Grade C | 47 | 55 | These numbers are invented to show the idea; each board publishes the real boundaries for every series. Three lessons follow: 1. **There is no fixed percentage for an A.** "70% is an A" is a myth. 2. **A hard paper is hard for everyone.** If a paper feels brutal, keep collecting marks: the boundaries will reflect it. 3. **Every mark counts.** Neighbouring grades are often separated by only a handful of marks on each paper, so one extra method mark here and there can lift a whole grade. :::tip Estimating your grade from a past paper Mark the paper with the official mark scheme, then compare your total with the published boundaries for **that same series**, not this year's or an average. Do this for papers from several different years to get a fair picture. ::: ## How the A* is awarded - **Cambridge International** awards A* for the full A Level only, based on your total across all the papers. There is no A* at AS. - **Edexcel International** requires an A overall plus an especially high score on the A2 (second-year) units, so an A* reflects strength in the hardest material. - **The boards in England** set the A* as the top boundary on your total mark, like any other grade. ## Uniform marks at Edexcel International In a modular system, you might sit one unit in a January with a hard paper and another in a June with an easy one. Simply adding the raw marks would be unfair. Pearson solves this with **uniform marks**. :::def Uniform mark A raw unit mark converted onto a fixed scale, so that results from papers of different difficulty, taken in different sittings, can be added fairly. The grade boundaries on the uniform scale stay the same every series. ::: The conversion uses each sitting's grade boundaries: a raw mark exactly on the A boundary always becomes the same uniform mark, however hard the paper was. Your uniform marks from all the units are then added, and the total decides your overall grade. Pearson's results show the uniform mark for each unit, which tells you how close you were to the next grade. :::analogy Uniform marks work like currency exchange. Raw marks from different sittings are like dollars, euros and lira: you cannot add them directly. Converting everything into one currency first lets you add them fairly. ::: ## UCAS tariff points **UCAS** (the Universities and Colleges Admissions Service) handles applications to UK universities. Its **tariff** turns grades into points so that different qualifications can be compared. :::def UCAS tariff points A points system that converts qualifications and grades into numbers so that different qualifications can be compared. Some universities state their entry requirements in tariff points. ::: | Grade | A Level | AS Level | Extended Project (EPQ) | |---|---|---|---| | A* | 56 | no A* | 28 | | A (AS: a) | 48 | 20 | 24 | | B (AS: b) | 40 | 16 | 20 | | C (AS: c) | 32 | 12 | 16 | | D (AS: d) | 24 | 10 | 12 | | E (AS: e) | 16 | 6 | 8 | An EPQ is worth exactly half an A Level at every grade. An AS that you later complete as a full A Level in the same subject does not count separately: only the A Level counts. :::eg Adding up tariff points A student has A Levels in Mathematics (A*), Physics (A) and Chemistry (B), an AS in Further Mathematics (grade b) and an EPQ (grade A). How many UCAS tariff points does she have? A Levels: \(56 + 48 + 40 = 144\) AS Further Mathematics, grade b: \(16\) EPQ, grade A: \(24\) Total: \(144 + 16 + 24 = 184\) points. ::: Try your own combination in the calculator: choose a grade for each qualification and watch the total change. :::html
::: :::warn Points are not everything AAA and A*AB are both worth 144 points, but a course asking for "A*AA including Mathematics" accepts neither. Most selective universities make offers in **grades** and name the subjects. Use points only when a course actually asks for them. ::: ## What offers look like You apply through UCAS to up to five courses (four at most in medicine, dentistry or veterinary science). Each university replies with an offer or a rejection. Typical offers read like this: - **"AAA"**: three A grades, sometimes excluding certain subjects. - **"A*AA, including A* in Mathematics and A in Physics"**: grades plus named subjects, as for many engineering courses. - **"ABB including Biology and Chemistry"**: a common pattern for life sciences. - **"112 UCAS points, including a C in Business"**: a tariff offer, which BBC would meet (\(40 + 40 + 32 = 112\)). - **"AAB, or ABB with an A in the EPQ"**: some universities lower an offer for a strong EPQ. :::def Conditional offer A university place that becomes yours only if you meet stated conditions, usually particular grades. An unconditional offer has no grade conditions, usually because you already have your results. ::: From your offers you choose one **firm** choice and, if you wish, one **insurance** choice with lower grades as a backup. On results day, the university confirms your place if you meet the conditions. If you miss both, **Clearing** matches students without a place to courses that still have vacancies. Some courses also set admissions tests or interviews; see [University applications and admissions tests](#road.university). :::key UCAS deadlines for 2027 entry - **15 October 2026**: Oxford, Cambridge, and most courses in medicine, dentistry and veterinary science. - **13 January 2027**: deadline for equal consideration for most other courses. ::: ## Predicted grades Universities usually decide before your final exams, so they rely on predictions. :::def Predicted grades The grades your teachers expect you to achieve, entered on your UCAS application. Universities make most offers on the basis of predicted grades, because final results arrive after most decisions are made. ::: Teachers predict from evidence: classwork, mock exams, AS results if you have them, and the progress you have shown. A prediction below a course's typical offer usually means no offer, so the evidence you give your teachers matters. Private candidates still need predicted grades and a reference; a tutor, a former teacher or a school can provide them. [Studying as a private candidate](#road.private) explains how. :::exam Earn your predictions Do your mocks properly, under timed conditions, and keep a record of your past-paper scores. A strong AS result, on Cambridge's staged route or at Edexcel International, is the most convincing evidence of all. ::: :::quiz ? How many UCAS tariff points is A*AB at A Level? - 128 - 136 + 144 - 152 > \(56 + 48 + 40 = 144\). 128 is ABB, 136 is AAB and 152 is A*AA. ? Which statement about the A* at Cambridge International is correct? + It is awarded for the full A Level only; there is no A* at AS. - It can be awarded at AS as a*. - It needs at least 90% on every single paper. - It is given to the top 10% of candidates in each country. > Cambridge awards A* on your total across all the A Level papers. AS grades run from a to e. ? Why do grade boundaries change from one series to the next? - Because more students take some exams than others + To keep each grade at the same standard when papers differ in difficulty - Because each examiner sets their own boundaries - To give a fixed number of A* grades each year > A harder paper gets lower boundaries and an easier paper higher ones, so an A means the same standard every year. ? What problem do uniform marks solve at Edexcel International? - They turn grades into UCAS points. + They let units sat in different sittings, with papers of different difficulty, be added fairly. - They replace grade boundaries completely. - They decide which units you are allowed to resit. > Each raw unit mark is converted onto a fixed scale using that sitting's boundaries, and then the uniform marks are added. ::: :::recap - A Level grades run A* to E, AS grades a to e (Cambridge) or A to E (UK boards); U is not a pass. - Raw marks are compared with grade boundaries set after marking. Harder papers get lower boundaries, so there is no fixed percentage for an A. - Cambridge awards A* for the full A Level only. Edexcel International requires an A overall plus a very high score on the A2 units. - Edexcel International converts raw unit marks into uniform marks so that units from different sittings add up fairly. - UCAS tariff: A* 56, A 48, B 40, C 32, D 24, E 16; AS a 20, b 16, c 12, d 10, e 6; EPQ A* 28 down to E 8. - Selective universities mostly make grade offers that name subjects; some use tariff points. - Offers are based on predicted grades, so mocks and past-paper scores matter. For 2027 entry, UCAS deadlines are 15 October 2026 and 13 January 2027. ::: Next: [Choosing your subjects](#start.choose). @chapter start.choose @title Choosing your subjects @level start @time 30 minutes @summary How to choose A Level subjects that fit the degree or career you want: typical requirements for popular courses, how many subjects to take, strong combinations, entry requirements, honest workload notes and the mistakes to avoid. :::why Your A Level subjects decide which degrees you can apply for. At most universities you cannot study medicine without Chemistry, or engineering without Mathematics. An evening of research now protects options you may want in two years' time. ::: ## Work backwards from your goal The safest way to choose is to start at the end: :::steps 1. Write down two or three degree courses you might want to study, even if you are unsure. 2. Look up each course's subject requirements on the websites of a few universities you like. 3. Choose subjects that satisfy all of them, so you keep every option open. 4. Fill any remaining place with a subject you enjoy and can do well in. ::: University websites separate subjects that are required from those that are only preferred, and the difference matters. :::def Required subject An A Level subject that a course insists on; without it, an application is normally rejected. Universities also list "preferred" or "recommended" subjects, which strengthen an application but are not compulsory. ::: ## Typical requirements for popular courses | If you want to study | Usually required | Recommended or useful | Also note | |---|---|---|---| | Medicine | Chemistry, and usually Biology | Maths or Physics | UCAT at most schools; interviews; apply by 15 October | | Dentistry | Chemistry and Biology | Maths or Physics | UCAT at most schools; interviews; apply by 15 October | | Veterinary science | Chemistry and Biology | Maths or Physics | Animal work experience expected; apply by 15 October | | Engineering | Maths, and usually Physics | Further Maths, strongly recommended for top courses; Chemistry for chemical engineering | ESAT at some universities (e.g. Cambridge, Imperial, Oxford) | | Computer science | Maths | Further Maths; Physics or Computer Science | The A Level of the same name is rarely required; TMUA at some universities | | Mathematics or physics | Maths (and Physics for physics) | Further Maths, often expected at top universities | Admissions tests at some universities | | Economics | Maths at most selective universities | Further Maths for the most competitive courses | The A Level of the same name is rarely required; TMUA at some universities | | Business, management, accounting | Usually none | Maths, especially for finance and accounting | A Level Business is not required | | Law | None in the UK | Essay subjects such as History, English Literature or a language | LNAT at several universities | | Architecture | Often none | Art or Design; Maths or Physics | A portfolio of creative work is usually required | | Psychology | Often none | Biology or Maths; some courses want one science | A psychology degree contains a lot of statistics | | Natural sciences | Two or more of Maths, Physics, Chemistry and Biology | Maths for any physical science | Requirements depend on which sciences you plan to take | These are typical UK requirements. Every university sets its own, they change from year to year, and universities in other countries have different rules, so confirm the details on each course page for your year of entry. [University applications and admissions tests](#road.university) explains UCAT, LNAT, TMUA and ESAT. ## How many subjects? **Three** A Levels is the standard, and university offers are almost always based on three. A fourth makes sense mainly when it is Further Mathematics, or when you are strong enough to take it without your other grades suffering. A fourth A Level rarely earns you a lower offer, but a weaker grade in one of your main three can cost you a place. :::tip The "3 + 1" option If you cannot decide between four subjects, start all four. At Cambridge or Edexcel International you can sit the AS in one of them at the end of the first year and stop there, keeping a useful extra qualification. An AS at the boards in England is also possible, but it is a separate exam and many schools no longer offer it. ::: ## Strong combinations and keeping doors open | Combination | Keeps these doors open | |---|---| | Maths, Physics, Chemistry | Engineering, physics, chemistry, natural sciences, computer science | | Maths, Further Maths, Physics | Engineering, mathematics, physics, computer science: the strongest choice for the most competitive courses | | Biology, Chemistry, plus Maths or Physics | Medicine, dentistry, veterinary science, pharmacy, biomedical sciences, and still some physical sciences | | Biology, Chemistry, Psychology | Medicine at universities that accept any third subject, psychology, life sciences | | Maths, Economics, plus History or Further Maths | Economics, finance, management, politics | | English Literature, History, plus a language or Politics | Law, history, politics, languages, journalism | | Maths, Physics, Art | Architecture, design engineering | If you are not sure yet what you want to study, choose subjects that keep the most doors open: - **Mathematics** is the subject most often required or preferred: engineering, physics, computer science, economics and many sciences ask for it, and it helps with the statistics in psychology and biology. - **Chemistry** opens medicine, dentistry, veterinary science, pharmacy, biochemistry and chemical engineering. - **One essay subject** keeps law, the humanities and the social sciences possible. - It is easier to move from sciences to a humanities degree than the other way round, because most humanities degrees do not require particular subjects. ## Entry requirements: are you ready? Exam boards set no formal entry requirements, but schools do, and so does common sense: A Level builds directly on IGCSE. Typical school requirements look like this: | A Level subject | Typical GCSE/IGCSE grade needed | |---|---| | Mathematics | 7 (A), sometimes 6 (B) | | Further Mathematics | 8 or 9 (A*), and a confident start in A Level Maths | | Physics, Chemistry, Biology | 6 or 7 (B or A) in that science, and at least 6 in Maths | | Essay subjects (History, English Literature) | 6 (B) in English and a related subject | | New subjects (Economics, Psychology, Law) | Good grades in English and Maths; no earlier study needed | If you are teaching yourself and never took the IGCSE, read what the syllabus recommends as prior learning, then fill gaps with the foundation chapters: [Algebra from scratch](#math.f.algebra), [Physics from zero](#phys.f.basics), [Chemistry from zero](#chem.f.basics) and [Biology from zero](#bio.f.basics). [Phase 1: Fix your foundations](#road.foundations) gives a checklist. ## Honest workload notes No A Level is easy at A* standard, but subjects are hard in different ways. - **Mathematics** demands fluent algebra and a lot of practice. Answers are right or wrong, so it needs less extended writing, which helps if English is your second language. - **Further Mathematics** roughly doubles your maths load. Take it only if you are strong at Maths and enjoy it; it also makes ordinary Maths feel easier. - **Physics** needs confident Maths and clear explanations of ideas, not just formulas. - **Chemistry** combines a large amount of content with calculations, and later topics build directly on earlier ones, so falling behind early is costly. - **Biology** has a large amount of content and precise vocabulary, with many longer written answers. - **Essay subjects** (History, English Literature, Economics, Business) need wide reading and plenty of writing practice. If English is not your first language, start practising timed writing early; it is entirely possible to reach the top grades. - **Private candidates** should check that their centre can run every part of the course, such as a science laboratory exam or coursework, before choosing. ## Common mistakes :::warn Choosing for the wrong reasons - Picking a subject because your friends take it or because you like one teacher. - Dropping Mathematics without checking: it is required or preferred for engineering, computer science, physics, economics and more. - Assuming you need the A Level of the same name: law, economics, psychology, business and computer science degrees rarely require it. - Taking Further Maths when your Maths is not yet secure. - Taking four or five subjects "to impress" and getting lower grades in all of them. - Choosing two very similar subjects, such as Business and Economics, without checking: some selective universities prefer them not to be two of your three. ::: :::exam Grades matter as much as subjects A university looks at both what you studied and how well you did. A subject you enjoy and can score an A in is usually a better choice than a "prestigious" one in which you would get a C, provided the required subjects for your course are covered. ::: :::quiz ? Which A Level do most UK medical schools require? - Biology + Chemistry - Physics - Psychology > Chemistry is required by most UK medical schools; Biology is usually required or strongly preferred too. ? A student wants to study engineering at a very competitive UK university. Which combination is strongest? + Mathematics, Further Mathematics, Physics - Physics, Chemistry, Biology - Mathematics, Economics, Business - Design and Technology, Art, Physics > Engineering requires Mathematics and usually Physics, and Further Mathematics is strongly recommended for the most competitive courses. ? Which degree usually does not require the A Level of the same name? + Law - Mathematics - Chemistry - Physics > UK law degrees have no required subjects. Mathematics, Chemistry and Physics degrees require those A Levels. ? On how many A Levels are most university offers based? - Two + Three - Four - Five > Offers are almost always based on three A Levels. A fourth is mainly useful when it is Further Mathematics. ::: :::recap - Work backwards: list possible degrees, check their required subjects, then choose subjects that satisfy all of them. - Medicine, dentistry and veterinary science need Chemistry and usually Biology; engineering needs Maths and usually Physics, with Further Maths strongly recommended. - Computer science and economics usually need Maths but rarely the A Level of the same name; law usually needs no particular subject. - Three A Levels is standard; a fourth makes most sense as Further Mathematics. - Maths plus one or two sciences keeps the most options open. - Schools usually expect a 6 or 7 (B or A) at GCSE/IGCSE in a subject, and higher for Further Maths. - Requirements differ between universities and change over time: always check the course page for your entry year. ::: Next: [How to use this guide](#start.howto). @chapter start.howto @title How to use this guide @level start @time 15 minutes @summary How Zero to A* is organised, what each type of box means, how to search, track your progress and use the tools, and a simple learning loop that turns every chapter into exam marks. :::why A guide only helps if you use it actively. Reading a chapter once feels productive, but most of it is forgotten within days. Working through it in the right order, and coming back to it later, is what turns reading into marks. ::: ## How the guide is organised Open the menu (the ☰ button on a phone, or the sidebar on a larger screen) to see every subject: the six main subjects (Mathematics, Physics, Chemistry, Biology, Engineering and Business), Economics and Accounting, short guides to other subjects, the preparation road, the toolbox and practice quizzes. Each subject is split into groups of chapters in a sensible order of study, usually starting with a course map. The top of each chapter shows a level label, a short summary and, for subject chapters, the exams that test it and a realistic study time for a beginner. The level labels mean: | Label | What it means | |---|---| | Foundations | GCSE/IGCSE skills that A Level assumes. Start here if you are rusty. | | AS Level | First-year content. | | A Level (A2) | Second-year content, needed for the full A Level. | | Guide, Reference, Summary | Course maps, the preparation road, formula sheets and short subject summaries. | | Interactive | Tools such as the graph plotter and calculators. | | Beyond A Level | Extension material, such as the tour of Further Mathematics. | Most chapters begin with **Before you start** links to the chapters you need first, and end with a **Next** link. On a wide screen, the **On this page** panel lists the sections and gives an estimated reading time. ## The boxes, and how to use them | Box | What it holds | How to use it | |---|---|---| | Key term | An exact definition in examiner-quality wording | Learn it word for word: definitions are easy marks | | Worked example | A full solution, with marks shown in exam-style ones | Cover the solution and try it first | | Common mistake | An error examiners see every year | Check your own work against it | | Exam technique | What a question wants and where the marks are | Apply it when you practise past papers | | Board differences | Where Edexcel International, AQA or OCR differ from Cambridge | Read the parts for your board | | Tip, Think of it like this | Shortcuts and everyday analogies | Use them to understand, then learn the precise version | | Key facts, Formula | Facts and formulas to memorise | Turn them into flashcards | | Practical skills | Methods, apparatus, safety and errors in experiments | Essential for practical and planning papers | | Try it yourself | Practice questions, each with a hidden full answer | Attempt first; only then press **Show answer** | | Quick check | Multiple-choice questions marked instantly | Read the explanation every time, even when you are right | | Summary | The facts to remember from the chapter | Test yourself on them a week later | Here is what three of them look like. :::def Mark scheme The document examiners use to award marks. It lists the accepted answers and shows exactly where each mark is earned, including method (M), accuracy (A) and independent (B) marks in Mathematics. ::: :::eg A rectangle is \((x + 3)\) cm long and \(x\) cm wide. Its area is \(40\,\mathrm{cm^2}\). Find \(x\). Form the equation: \(x(x + 3) = 40\), so \(x^2 + 3x - 40 = 0\). [B1] Factorise: \((x + 8)(x - 5) = 0\). [M1] So \(x = 5\); reject \(x = -8\), because a length cannot be negative. [A1] **Check:** a rectangle 8 cm long and 5 cm wide has area \(40\,\mathrm{cm^2}\). ::: The mark labels follow the system used in Cambridge and Edexcel mathematics mark schemes: - **M (method)**: for a correct method applied to the problem, even if you then make a slip. - **A (accuracy)**: for a correct answer or step. You can only earn it if you have earned the method mark it depends on. - **B (independent)**: for a correct result or statement that does not depend on a method. So a correct answer with no working may not earn full marks, while a wrong answer with a sound method can still earn some. You will meet problems like this one in [Quadratics](#math.p1.quadratics). :::warn Reading is not the same as doing Following a worked solution feels easy because every step is already there. The real test is whether you can produce it yourself with the page covered. Always try first, then compare. ::: ## Track your progress At the end of every chapter there is a **Mark as learned** button. Press it when you can do the practice questions without help. Learned chapters get a tick in the menu, the progress bar fills up, and the home page shows how many chapters you have learned in each subject, with a link to pick up where you left off. :::warn Progress is saved in this browser only Your ticks, theme and text size are stored on this device, in this browser. They do not move between your phone and your computer, and clearing your browsing data or using a private window removes them. Choose one main device for studying. ::: ## Search, glossary, tools and display - **Search**: press **/** from anywhere (or tap the search box) and type a topic, key term or formula name. Use the arrow keys and Enter to open a result, or Esc to close the list. - **Glossary**: every key-term card in the guide, in one alphabetical list that you can filter by subject: [Glossary](#tools.glossary). - **Tools**: the [graph plotter](#tools.grapher), the [periodic table](#tools.periodic), [calculators](#tools.calc) for UCAS points, formula masses, break-even and more, and formula sheets such as the [maths formula sheet](#tools.f.math). - **Practice**: [Practice quizzes](#practice.quiz) mix questions from every chapter and tell you which chapters to revise. - **Planning**: [Build your personal study plan](#road.planner) turns your exam date into a weekly timetable. - **Display**: the buttons at the top right switch between light and dark mode and cycle the text size from normal to large to extra large. ## The learning loop Use the same six steps for every chapter. :::html ::: :::steps 1. **Read the chapter** with pen and paper. Write each key term in your own words, then compare it with the card. 2. **Study the worked examples.** Cover each solution, attempt it, then compare, noting where the marks are. 3. **Try it yourself** with the chapter closed. Open **Show answer** only after a real attempt, and mark your work honestly. 4. **Take the quick check** and read every explanation. 5. **Mark as learned** only when you can do the practice questions without help. 6. **Revisit after a week.** Redo a few questions and the quick check from memory. Each time you pull an idea back out of memory after a gap, you keep it for longer. ::: :::tip Little and often A main-subject chapter usually takes several sessions, as its study time shows. End each session by writing down three things you learned, and start the next one by recalling them without notes. ::: ## Use the guide with your syllabus, a textbook and past papers | Resource | Use it for | When | |---|---|---| | This guide | Learning each topic from zero, worked examples, practice | Throughout the course | | Official syllabus | The final word on what can be examined | At the start, then as a checklist | | A textbook written for your syllabus | Extra explanations and more questions | Alongside each chapter | | Past papers, mark schemes, examiner reports | Real exam questions and how they are marked | Topic questions from the start; full timed papers in the final months | Download the syllabus for your board and exam year from the board's website and tick off each learning outcome as you finish it. Facts in this guide were checked in October 2026, but if anything here disagrees with your official syllabus, the syllabus wins. For recommended books and websites, see [The best resources by subject](#road.resources); for a past-paper method, see [Phase 4: Past papers and mark schemes](#road.pastpapers). :::try Check you know your way around Q: In a mark scheme, what is the difference between an M mark and an A mark? A: An M mark is for a correct method applied to the problem. An A mark is for an accurate answer or step, and it can only be awarded if the method mark it depends on has been earned. Q: You have just read a chapter and its worked examples. What should you do next, and why? A: Try the practice questions with the chapter closed, and only then check the answers. Recognising a solution is much easier than producing one, and producing answers from memory is what builds lasting understanding. ::: :::quiz ? Which type of mark can be awarded only if the related method mark has been earned? - B mark + A mark - M mark - None: every mark is independent > Accuracy (A) marks depend on the method (M) mark they follow. B marks are independent of method. ? Where is your progress in this guide saved? - In an online account, so it appears on every device + In this browser, on this device only - On your exam board's website - Nowhere: it resets on every visit > Progress is stored in your browser. Clearing browsing data or using a private window removes it. ? When should you press "Mark as learned"? - As soon as you have read the chapter - After reading the worked examples + When you can do the practice questions without help - Only after the final exam > Recognising is not the same as doing. Mark a chapter as learned when you can answer its questions on your own, then revisit it a week later. ::: :::recap - Each subject is split into chapters labelled Foundations, AS Level or A Level (A2), with the exams that test them and a realistic study time. - Key-term cards hold exact definitions; worked examples show marks: M for method, A for accuracy (dependent on M), B for independent results. - Common-mistake, exam-technique and board-difference boxes show where marks are lost and how the boards differ. - Try it yourself hides full answers; quick checks mark you instantly and explain why. - Press / to search.
