@group Pure Mathematics 1 @chapter math.p1.quadratics @title Quadratics @level as @paper CAIE P1 · Edexcel IAL P1 · AQA/OCR/Edexcel Pure @time 6–8 hours @summary A quadratic is any expression whose highest power of \(x\) is \(x^2\). You will learn to solve quadratic equations in three ways, read their graphs, count their solutions without solving, and handle quadratic inequalities and simultaneous equations. :::why Quadratics are the first topic in Paper 1 and they come back everywhere: in coordinate geometry, functions, calculus, mechanics and physics. A ball thrown in the air, the area of a field, the profit of a business at different prices: all of these are modelled by quadratics. If this chapter feels solid, a large part of A Level Pure Mathematics becomes easier. ::: **Before you start**, you should be comfortable with [Algebra from scratch](#math.f.algebra) (expanding brackets, factorising, rearranging) and with [Powers, roots, surds and standard form](#math.f.powers). ## What is a quadratic? Start with an expression you already know, like \(3x + 5\). The highest power of \(x\) is \(x^1\), so we call it **linear**: its graph is a straight line. Now allow an \(x^2\) term, for example \(x^2 - 2x - 3\). The graph is no longer straight. It bends into a symmetrical U-shape called a **parabola**, and the expression is called a **quadratic**. :::def Quadratic expression An expression that can be written in the form \(ax^2 + bx + c\), where \(a\), \(b\) and \(c\) are constants and \(a \neq 0\). ::: The numbers \(a\), \(b\) and \(c\) are called **coefficients**. In \(2x^2 - 7x + 3\) we have \(a = 2\), \(b = -7\) and \(c = 3\). Notice that the sign belongs to the number: \(b\) is \(-7\), not \(7\). Getting this wrong is the most common way to lose marks later in this chapter. :::def Coefficient The number multiplying a power of the variable. In \(ax^2 + bx + c\), \(a\) is the coefficient of \(x^2\), \(b\) is the coefficient of \(x\), and \(c\) is the constant term. ::: A **quadratic equation** sets a quadratic equal to zero, such as \(x^2 - 2x - 3 = 0\). Its solutions are called **roots**. Most quadratic equations have two roots, some have one, and some have no real roots at all. By the end of this chapter you will be able to predict which, before solving anything. :::def Root (of an equation) A value of the variable that makes the equation true. The real roots of \(f(x) = 0\) are the \(x\)-coordinates where the graph of \(y = f(x)\) meets the \(x\)-axis. ::: ## The shape of a quadratic graph Every quadratic graph is a parabola, and four facts let you sketch one quickly. 1. **Which way up?** If \(a > 0\) the graph is ∪-shaped (it has a lowest point). If \(a < 0\) it is ∩-shaped (it has a highest point). 2. **Where does it cross the \(y\)-axis?** Put \(x = 0\): you get \(y = c\). So the \(y\)-intercept is \((0, c)\). 3. **Where does it cross the \(x\)-axis?** At the roots of \(ax^2 + bx + c = 0\), if there are any. 4. **Where is the turning point?** The lowest or highest point is called the **vertex**. The graph is symmetrical about a vertical line through the vertex, called the **line of symmetry**. :::html ::: :::analogy Think of the parabola as a bowl. Water poured into a ∪-shaped bowl collects at the bottom, which is the vertex. The two roots are where the rim of the bowl crosses the table top (the \(x\)-axis). If the whole bowl sits above the table, there are no crossing points, so there are no real roots. ::: Use the sliders below to change \(a\), \(b\) and \(c\) and watch what happens. Make \(a\) negative and the bowl flips. Change \(c\) and the whole graph slides up or down. Notice what happens to the roots as the vertex rises above the \(x\)-axis. :::html
::: ## Method 1: solving by factorising Factorising works because of one simple fact. :::key The zero product rule If \(A \times B = 0\), then \(A = 0\) or \(B = 0\) (or both). ::: So if we can write a quadratic as two brackets multiplied together, each bracket gives us one root. ### When \(a = 1\) To factorise \(x^2 + bx + c\), look for two numbers that **multiply to give \(c\)** and **add to give \(b\)**. :::eg Solve \(x^2 - 5x + 6 = 0\) We need two numbers that multiply to \(+6\) and add to \(-5\). Try the factor pairs of 6: \((1, 6)\), \((2, 3)\), \((-1, -6)\), \((-2, -3)\). Only \(-2\) and \(-3\) add to \(-5\). \[x^2 - 5x + 6 = (x - 2)(x - 3) = 0\] So \(x - 2 = 0\) or \(x - 3 = 0\), giving \(x = 2\) or \(x = 3\). **Check:** \(2^2 - 5(2) + 6 = 4 - 10 + 6 = 0\). It works. ::: ### When \(a \neq 1\): the "ac method" Multiply \(a\) by \(c\). Find two numbers that multiply to \(ac\) and add to \(b\). Use them to split the middle term, then factorise in pairs. :::eg Solve \(2x^2 + 7x - 4 = 0\) Here \(ac = 2 \times (-4) = -8\). Two numbers that multiply to \(-8\) and add to \(7\) are \(8\) and \(-1\). Split the middle term: \(2x^2 + 8x - x - 4 = 0\) Factorise in pairs: \(2x(x + 4) - 1(x + 4) = 0\) Take out the common bracket: \((2x - 1)(x + 4) = 0\) So \(x = \tfrac{1}{2}\) or \(x = -4\). ::: :::warn Never divide by \(x\) To solve \(x^2 = 3x\), it is tempting to divide both sides by \(x\) and get \(x = 3\). But this loses a solution, because \(x\) might be zero (and you cannot divide by zero). Instead, rearrange to \(x^2 - 3x = 0\), factorise to \(x(x - 3) = 0\), and get **both** answers: \(x = 0\) or \(x = 3\). ::: Factorising is the quickest method when it works. It only works neatly when the roots are rational (whole numbers or fractions). If you cannot find the two numbers within about a minute, switch to one of the next two methods. ## Method 2: completing the square Completing the square rewrites a quadratic so you can see its vertex immediately. Exam questions often say "express in the form \(a(x + p)^2 + q\)" or "\((x - p)^2 + q\)". That is a request to complete the square. The idea comes from expanding a squared bracket: \[(x + 3)^2 = x^2 + 6x + 9\] So \(x^2 + 6x\) is "nearly" \((x + 3)^2\). It is just missing the \(9\): \[x^2 + 6x = (x + 3)^2 - 9\] :::key Completing the square (when \(a = 1\)) \[x^2 + bx = \left(x + \frac{b}{2}\right)^2 - \left(\frac{b}{2}\right)^2\] Halve the coefficient of \(x\) to get the number in the bracket, then subtract that number squared. ::: :::eg Write \(x^2 + 6x + 11\) in the form \((x + p)^2 + q\). Hence state the minimum point. Half of \(6\) is \(3\), so \[x^2 + 6x + 11 = (x + 3)^2 - 9 + 11 = (x + 3)^2 + 2\] A square is never negative, so \((x + 3)^2 \geq 0\). The smallest value of the whole expression is \(0 + 2 = 2\), and this happens when \(x + 3 = 0\), that is \(x = -3\). The minimum point of \(y = x^2 + 6x + 11\) is \((-3, 2)\). ::: :::tip Reading the vertex from completed square form For \(y = a(x + p)^2 + q\), the vertex is at \((-p, q)\). Watch the sign: \((x - 4)^2\) gives \(x = +4\), while \((x + 4)^2\) gives \(x = -4\). ::: ### When \(a \neq 1\) Take \(a\) out as a factor of the \(x^2\) and \(x\) terms first, complete the square inside the bracket, then multiply back out. :::eg Express \(2x^2 - 12x + 7\) in the form \(a(x + b)^2 + c\). Hence state the coordinates of the vertex of \(y = 2x^2 - 12x + 7\) and the range of \(f(x) = 2x^2 - 12x + 7\). Factor 2 out of the first two terms: \[2x^2 - 12x + 7 = 2(x^2 - 6x) + 7\] Complete the square inside the bracket: \(x^2 - 6x = (x - 3)^2 - 9\). [M1] \[= 2\big[(x - 3)^2 - 9\big] + 7 = 2(x - 3)^2 - 18 + 7\] \[= 2(x - 3)^2 - 11\] [A1] So \(a = 2\), \(b = -3\), \(c = -11\). The vertex is at \((3, -11)\). [B1] Because \(a = 2 > 0\), this is a minimum, so the range is \(f(x) \geq -11\). [B1] **Check:** put \(x = 0\) into both forms. \(2(0)^2 - 12(0) + 7 = 7\) and \(2(0 - 3)^2 - 11 = 18 - 11 = 7\). They match. ::: You can also solve equations by completing the square: rewrite the equation, then take square roots. Remember that taking a square root gives **two** answers, positive and negative. :::eg Solve \(x^2 + 4x - 1 = 0\), giving exact answers. \[(x + 2)^2 - 4 - 1 = 0 \quad\Rightarrow\quad (x + 2)^2 = 5\] \[x + 2 = \pm\sqrt{5} \quad\Rightarrow\quad x = -2 \pm \sqrt{5}\] "Exact" means leave the surd in. As decimals these are \(0.236\) and \(-4.24\) (3 s.f.). ::: ## Method 3: the quadratic formula If you complete the square on the general quadratic \(ax^2 + bx + c = 0\), you get a formula that solves **every** quadratic equation. :::key The quadratic formula The solutions of \(ax^2 + bx + c = 0\) are \[x = \frac{-b \pm \sqrt{b^2 - 4ac}}{2a}\] ::: :::eg Solve \(3x^2 - 4x - 2 = 0\), giving your answers correct to 3 significant figures. Identify the coefficients carefully, signs included: \(a = 3\), \(b = -4\), \(c = -2\). \[x = \frac{-(-4) \pm \sqrt{(-4)^2 - 4(3)(-2)}}{2(3)} = \frac{4 \pm \sqrt{16 + 24}}{6} = \frac{4 \pm \sqrt{40}}{6}\] [M1] \[x = 1.72 \quad\text{or}\quad x = -0.387\] [A1] ::: :::warn Sign slips in the formula Two errors cost more marks than any others: writing \(-b\) as \(-4\) when \(b = -4\) (it should be \(+4\)), and squaring a negative \(b\) wrongly. \((-4)^2 = 16\), but if you type \(-4^2\) into a calculator you get \(-16\). Always use brackets: \((-4)^2\). ::: :::exam Which method should I use? If the question says **"factorise"**, **"complete the square"** or **"express in the form…"**, you must use that method. Otherwise, try factorising first; if it does not work quickly, use the formula. If the question asks for **exact** answers, keep surds such as \(\sqrt{5}\). If it asks for **3 significant figures**, give exactly three. Cambridge examiners deduct for wrong accuracy. ::: ## The discriminant: how many roots? Look again at the quadratic formula. The part under the square root, \(b^2 - 4ac\), decides everything: - If it is **positive**, \(\pm\sqrt{\phantom{x}}\) gives two different answers, so there are **two distinct real roots**. - If it is **zero**, \(\pm\sqrt{0}\) adds and subtracts nothing, so there is **one repeated root** (often called "equal roots"). - If it is **negative**, there is no real square root, so there are **no real roots**. :::def Discriminant The quantity \(b^2 - 4ac\) for the quadratic \(ax^2 + bx + c\). Its sign tells you how many real roots the equation \(ax^2 + bx + c = 0\) has. ::: :::html ::: :::eg Find the values of \(k\) for which \(x^2 + kx + 9 = 0\) has equal roots. Equal roots means the discriminant is zero: \(a = 1\), \(b = k\), \(c = 9\). \[k^2 - 4(1)(9) = 0 \quad\Rightarrow\quad k^2 = 36 \quad\Rightarrow\quad k = \pm 6\] **Check:** with \(k = 6\), \(x^2 + 6x + 9 = (x + 3)^2\), which does have a repeated root. ::: ### Lines meeting curves A favourite Paper 1 question asks when a straight line **meets**, **touches** (is a **tangent** to), or **misses** a curve. The method is always the same: set the two equations equal, rearrange into a quadratic equal to zero, and look at its discriminant. | The line… | Number of meeting points | Discriminant | |---|---|---| | cuts the curve | 2 | \(b^2 - 4ac > 0\) | | touches the curve (tangent) | 1 | \(b^2 - 4ac = 0\) | | misses the curve | 0 | \(b^2 - 4ac < 0\) | :::eg Find the set of values of \(k\) for which the line \(y = kx - 1\) intersects the curve \(y = x^2 + 3\) at two distinct points. At intersection the \(y\)-values are equal: \[x^2 + 3 = kx - 1 \quad\Rightarrow\quad x^2 - kx + 4 = 0\] [M1] Two distinct points means two distinct roots, so the discriminant is positive: \[(-k)^2 - 4(1)(4) > 0 \quad\Rightarrow\quad k^2 > 16\] [M1] \(k^2 > 16\) when \(k > 4\) or \(k < -4\) (see inequalities below). [A1] ::: ## Quadratic inequalities To solve \(x^2 - x - 12 > 0\) you need all the values of \(x\) that make the quadratic positive, not just a couple of numbers. The reliable method has three steps. :::steps 1. **Solve the equation** \(x^2 - x - 12 = 0\) to find the critical values. Here \((x - 4)(x + 3) = 0\), so \(x = 4\) or \(x = -3\). 2. **Sketch the graph.** \(a = 1 > 0\), so it is ∪-shaped, crossing the \(x\)-axis at \(-3\) and \(4\). 3. **Read off the answer.** "\(> 0\)" means "where is the graph above the \(x\)-axis?" That is to the left of \(-3\) and to the right of \(4\): \(x < -3\) or \(x > 4\). ::: If the question had been \(x^2 - x - 12 < 0\) (below the axis), the answer would be the part in the middle: \(-3 < x < 4\). :::eg Solve \(2x^2 + 5x - 3 \leq 0\). Factorise: \((2x - 1)(x + 3) = 0\) gives critical values \(x = \tfrac12\) and \(x = -3\). [M1] The graph is ∪-shaped, and "\(\leq 0\)" means on or below the axis, which is between the roots. The end points are included because of the "\(=\)" in \(\leq\): \[-3 \leq x \leq \tfrac{1}{2}\] [A1] ::: :::warn Two inequalities cannot be squashed together the wrong way For "\(x < -3\) or \(x > 4\)" never write \(-3 > x > 4\). That would mean \(x\) is less than \(-3\) **and** greater than \(4\) at the same time, which is impossible. Write two separate inequalities joined by "or". A combined form like \(-3 < x < 4\) is only correct for the region **between** the roots. ::: ## Simultaneous equations: one linear, one quadratic When one equation is linear and the other is quadratic, use **substitution**: rearrange the linear equation to make one letter the subject, then substitute into the quadratic. :::eg Solve the simultaneous equations \(y = x + 1\) and \(x^2 + y^2 = 25\). Substitute \(y = x + 1\) into the second equation: \[x^2 + (x + 1)^2 = 25 \quad\Rightarrow\quad 2x^2 + 2x + 1 - 25 = 0 \quad\Rightarrow\quad x^2 + x - 12 = 0\] [M1] \[(x + 4)(x - 3) = 0 \quad\Rightarrow\quad x = -4 \text{ or } x = 3\] [A1] Now find each \(y\) from the **linear** equation: \(x = -4 \Rightarrow y = -3\), and \(x = 3 \Rightarrow y = 4\). [A1] Solutions: \((-4, -3)\) and \((3, 4)\). Geometrically, these are the two points where the line crosses the circle of radius 5. ::: :::tip Pair your answers Always present the answers as pairs, \((x, y)\). An examiner cannot give the final mark for "\(x = -4, 3\) and \(y = -3, 4\)" if it is unclear which \(y\) goes with which \(x\). ::: ## Disguised quadratics Some equations are quadratics in disguise. If an equation contains a quantity and its square, such as \(x^2\) and \(x^4\), or \(\sqrt{x}\) and \(x\), substitute a new letter. :::eg Solve \(x^4 - 5x^2 + 4 = 0\). Let \(u = x^2\). Then \(x^4 = u^2\), and the equation becomes \[u^2 - 5u + 4 = 0 \quad\Rightarrow\quad (u - 1)(u - 4) = 0 \quad\Rightarrow\quad u = 1 \text{ or } u = 4\] Go back to \(x\): \(x^2 = 1\) gives \(x = \pm 1\), and \(x^2 = 4\) gives \(x = \pm 2\). There are four solutions: \(x = -2, -1, 1, 2\). ::: :::eg Solve \(2x - 7\sqrt{x} + 3 = 0\). Let \(u = \sqrt{x}\), so \(x = u^2\): \[2u^2 - 7u + 3 = 0 \quad\Rightarrow\quad (2u - 1)(u - 3) = 0 \quad\Rightarrow\quad u = \tfrac{1}{2} \text{ or } u = 3\] Then \(x = u^2\), so \(x = \tfrac{1}{4}\) or \(x = 9\). Because \(\sqrt{x}\) can never be negative, any negative value of \(u\) would have to be rejected. Here both are positive, so both answers stand. ::: :::board All boards teach the same quadratics content in their first Pure paper (Cambridge P1, Edexcel IAL P1, and Year 1 Pure for AQA, OCR and Edexcel in the UK). The UK boards also expect you to use the discriminant inside **proof** questions ("prove that the equation has no real roots for all values of \(k\)"). Cambridge mostly tests it through line-and-curve intersections and the range of a function. ::: :::try Start easy, finish at exam standard Q: Solve \(x^2 + 7x + 10 = 0\) by factorising. A: Two numbers that multiply to 10 and add to 7 are 2 and 5. \((x + 2)(x + 5) = 0\), so \(x = -2\) or \(x = -5\). Q: Solve \(3x^2 - 10x - 8 = 0\) by factorising. A: \(ac = -24\). Two numbers that multiply to \(-24\) and add to \(-10\) are \(-12\) and \(2\). \(3x^2 - 12x + 2x - 8 = 3x(x - 4) + 2(x - 4) = (3x + 2)(x - 4)\), so \(x = -\tfrac{2}{3}\) or \(x = 4\). Q: Express \(x^2 - 8x + 3\) in the form \((x + p)^2 + q\) and state the coordinates of the minimum point of \(y = x^2 - 8x + 3\). A: Half of \(-8\) is \(-4\): \(x^2 - 8x + 3 = (x - 4)^2 - 16 + 3 = (x - 4)^2 - 13\). The minimum point is \((4, -13)\). Q: Solve \(5x^2 + 2x - 1 = 0\), giving your answers correct to 3 significant figures. A: \(x = \dfrac{-2 \pm \sqrt{4 + 20}}{10} = \dfrac{-2 \pm \sqrt{24}}{10}\), so \(x = 0.290\) or \(x = -0.690\). Q: Find the set of values of \(k\) for which \(kx^2 + 4x + k = 0\) has no real roots. A: No real roots means \(b^2 - 4ac < 0\): \(16 - 4k^2 < 0\), so \(k^2 > 4\), giving \(k < -2\) or \(k > 2\). Q: Solve the inequality \(x^2 + 2x - 15 < 0\). A: \((x + 5)(x - 3) = 0\) gives critical values \(-5\) and \(3\). The graph is ∪-shaped and we want the part below the axis: \(-5 < x < 3\). Q: Solve the simultaneous equations \(y = 2x - 1\) and \(y = x^2 - 4x + 4\). A: \(x^2 - 4x + 4 = 2x - 1 \Rightarrow x^2 - 6x + 5 = 0 \Rightarrow (x - 1)(x - 5) = 0\). [M1] \(x = 1 \Rightarrow y = 1\) and \(x = 5 \Rightarrow y = 9\). Solutions \((1, 1)\) and \((5, 9)\). [A1 A1] Q: (Exam style) \(f(x) = -x^2 + 6x - 5\). (a) Express \(f(x)\) in the form \(a - (x - b)^2\). (b) State the maximum value of \(f(x)\) and the value of \(x\) at which it occurs. (c) Find the set of values of \(k\) for which the line \(y = k\) meets the curve \(y = f(x)\) at two distinct points. A: (a) \(-x^2 + 6x - 5 = -(x^2 - 6x) - 5 = -\big[(x - 3)^2 - 9\big] - 5 = 4 - (x - 3)^2\). [M1 A1] (b) A square is never negative, so the largest value is \(4\), when \(x = 3\). [B1] (c) The horizontal line \(y = k\) cuts the ∩-shaped curve twice when it is below the maximum: \(k < 4\). [B1] Q: Solve \(x - 6\sqrt{x} + 8 = 0\). A: Let \(u = \sqrt{x}\): \(u^2 - 6u + 8 = 0 \Rightarrow (u - 2)(u - 4) = 0 \Rightarrow u = 2\) or \(4\). So \(x = 4\) or \(x = 16\). ::: :::quiz ? How many real roots does \(2x^2 + 3x + 5 = 0\) have? - Two - One + None > The discriminant is \(3^2 - 4(2)(5) = 9 - 40 = -31\). It is negative, so there are no real roots. ? Which is \(x^2 - 10x + 4\) written in completed square form? + \((x - 5)^2 - 21\) - \((x - 5)^2 + 4\) - \((x - 10)^2 - 96\) - \((x + 5)^2 - 21\) > Half of \(-10\) is \(-5\), so \(x^2 - 10x = (x - 5)^2 - 25\). Then \(-25 + 4 = -21\). ? What are the coordinates of the vertex of \(y = 3(x - 2)^2 + 7\)? - \((-2, 7)\) + \((2, 7)\) - \((2, -7)\) - \((3, 7)\) > In \(a(x + p)^2 + q\) form the vertex is \((-p, q)\). Here the bracket is \((x - 2)\), so \(x = 2\), and \(q = 7\). ? Which set of values satisfies \(x^2 < 9\)? + \(-3 < x < 3\) - \(x < 3\) - \(x < -3\) or \(x > 3\) - \(x < \pm 3\) > The graph of \(y = x^2 - 9\) is below the axis between its roots \(-3\) and \(3\). "\(x < 3\)" alone would wrongly include values like \(-10\). ::: :::recap - A quadratic has the form \(ax^2 + bx + c\) with \(a \neq 0\). Its graph is a parabola: ∪-shaped if \(a > 0\), ∩-shaped if \(a < 0\). - Three ways to solve \(ax^2 + bx + c = 0\): factorising (fastest when it works), completing the square (also gives the vertex), and the formula \(x = \dfrac{-b \pm \sqrt{b^2 - 4ac}}{2a}\) (always works). - In completed square form \(a(x + p)^2 + q\), the vertex is \((-p, q)\). - The discriminant \(b^2 - 4ac\) gives the number of real roots: positive means 2, zero means 1 repeated root, negative means none. - For a line and a curve: set them equal, form a quadratic, and use the discriminant (2 points, tangent, or no meeting). - For inequalities: find critical values, sketch, then read the region from the graph. - Substitute a new letter for disguised quadratics such as \(x^4 - 5x^2 + 4 = 0\). ::: Next: [Functions](#math.p1.functions) builds on everything here, including the range of a quadratic.
files.content/math-3b.md: @group Probability and Statistics @chapter math.s2.poisson @title The Poisson distribution @level a2 @paper CAIE P6 (S2) · Edexcel IAL S2 · UK Further Maths Statistics @time 5–7 hours @summary The Poisson distribution models the number of random events in a fixed interval of time or space, such as calls per hour or flaws per metre. You will learn its conditions, formula, mean and variance, how to rescale it, and how it approximates the binomial and is approximated by the normal distribution. :::why How many calls will a rescue centre receive between 2 am and 3 am? How many flaws will a 50 m cable have? How many goals will a team score? Each of these is a count of events that happen at random but with a steady average rate. Staffing, spare parts and guarantees all depend on knowing how likely each count is. The Poisson distribution is the standard model for this kind of problem, and it is one of the main ideas in Cambridge Paper 6. ::: **Before you start**, you should know the binomial distribution from [Discrete random variables](#math.s1.drv) and the normal distribution from [The normal distribution](#math.s1.normal). You will also use the number \(e \approx 2.718\) from [Logarithms and exponentials](#math.p3.logs). ## Counting random events The binomial distribution counts successes in a fixed number of trials, so its count can never exceed \(n\). Many real counts have no trials and no upper limit: emails arriving in an hour, typing errors on a page, atoms decaying in a second. The count could be \(0, 1, 2, 3, \dots\) and, in principle, anything larger. The Poisson distribution models counts like these. :::def Poisson distribution The distribution of a random variable \(X\) that counts events in a fixed interval of time or space when the events occur singly, at random, independently of each other and at a constant average rate. We write \(X \sim \mathrm{Po}(\lambda)\), where \(\lambda\) is the mean number of events in the interval. ::: The three conditions need a closer look, because exam questions ask you to state them and to say when they fail. 1. **Singly.** Two events cannot happen at exactly the same moment or place. Cars that arrive in convoys break this rule. 2. **Independently and at random.** One event does not make another more or less likely. Road accidents in fog often fail this, because one crash causes the next. 3. **Constant average rate.** The mean number of events is the same for every interval of the same size. Calls to a pizza shop fail this, because Friday evening is far busier than Monday afternoon. :::exam Conditions in context "State a condition for a Poisson model" wants the condition written in the context of the question, for example "the calls arrive independently of each other". A bare "it is random" is too vague. For "explain why the model may not be suitable", say which condition fails and why. ::: ## The formula, the mean and the variance :::key The Poisson distribution If \(X \sim \mathrm{Po}(\lambda)\), then \[P(X = r) = \frac{e^{-\lambda}\,\lambda^{r}}{r!}, \qquad r = 0, 1, 2, 3, \dots\] \[E(X) = \lambda \qquad\text{and}\qquad \mathrm{Var}(X) = \lambda\] ::: Here \(r!\) means \(r \times (r-1) \times \dots \times 1\), and \(0! = 1\). The probability of no events is \(P(X = 0) = e^{-\lambda}\). All the probabilities add to 1 because \(1 + \lambda + \frac{\lambda^2}{2!} + \cdots = e^{\lambda}\). The mean and the variance are equal. That is unusual and useful: if data have a mean and a variance that are very different, a Poisson model is doubtful. :::html ::: :::tip Building probabilities step by step Each probability comes from the one before: \(P(X = r + 1) = \dfrac{\lambda}{r + 1}\,P(X = r)\). For \(\lambda = 4\): \(P(0) = e^{-4} = 0.0183\), then \(P(1) = 4 \times 0.0183 = 0.0733\), then \(P(2) = \frac{4}{2} \times 0.0733 = 0.1465\). Keep full calculator accuracy and round only at the end. ::: Poisson counts have no upper limit, so "at least" and "more than" need the complement. | Words in the question | Meaning | Calculate | |---|---|---| | at most 3, no more than 3 | \(X \le 3\) | \(P(0) + P(1) + P(2) + P(3)\) | | fewer than 3 | \(X \le 2\) | \(P(0) + P(1) + P(2)\) | | at least 3 | \(X \ge 3\) | \(1 - P(X \le 2)\) | | more than 3 | \(X \ge 4\) | \(1 - P(X \le 3)\) | :::eg Emails arrive at random, with a mean of 4 per hour. Find the probability that in a given hour (a) exactly 3 arrive, (b) at most 2 arrive, (c) at least 6 arrive. Let \(X\) be the number of emails in an hour. Then \(X \sim \mathrm{Po}(4)\). (a) \(P(X = 3) = \dfrac{e^{-4}\,4^{3}}{3!} = \dfrac{32}{3}e^{-4} = 0.195\) (b) \(P(X \le 2) = e^{-4}\left(1 + 4 + \dfrac{4^{2}}{2}\right) = 13e^{-4} = 0.238\) (c) "At least 6" is the opposite of "at most 5", so \[P(X \ge 6) = 1 - e^{-4}\left(1 + 4 + 8 + \tfrac{32}{3} + \tfrac{32}{3} + \tfrac{128}{15}\right) = 1 - 0.7851 = 0.215\] ::: ## Changing the interval The mean \(\lambda\) belongs to one particular interval. Because the rate is constant, a longer or shorter interval has a proportionally larger or smaller mean. :::key Scaling the mean If events occur at a constant average rate of \(k\) per unit of time (or length, or area), the number of events in an interval of size \(t\) has distribution \(\mathrm{Po}(kt)\). ::: Always write down the new distribution before you calculate. Counts in separate intervals add, and so do their means: if the number of emails in one hour is \(\mathrm{Po}(4)\), the number in two hours is \(\mathrm{Po}(8)\). [Linear combinations of random variables](#math.s2.linear) proves this. :::warn Scale the mean, not the probability If \(P(\text{no flaws in 10 m}) = 0.449\), then \(P(\text{no flaws in 20 m})\) is **not** \(2 \times 0.449\). Double the mean to \(\lambda = 1.6\) and recalculate: \(e^{-1.6} = 0.202\). As a check, both 10 m halves must be flawless, and \(0.449^{2} = 0.202\). ::: :::eg Flaws occur at random in a cable at an average rate of 0.8 per 10 m. Find the probability that (a) a 25 m length has no flaws, (b) a 5 m length has at least 2 flaws. (a) In 25 m the mean is \(0.8 \times 2.5 = 2.0\), so \(X \sim \mathrm{Po}(2)\) and \[P(X = 0) = e^{-2} = 0.135\] (b) In 5 m the mean is \(0.8 \times 0.5 = 0.4\), so \(Y \sim \mathrm{Po}(0.4)\) and \[P(Y \ge 2) = 1 - P(Y = 0) - P(Y = 1) = 1 - e^{-0.4}(1 + 0.4) = 1 - 0.9384 = 0.0616\] ::: ## Poisson as an approximation to the binomial A binomial \(B(n, p)\) with large \(n\) and small \(p\) counts rare events among many trials, which is the Poisson situation. Its mean is \(np\) and its variance is \(npq\). When \(p\) is small, \(q = 1 - p\) is close to 1, so the variance is close to the mean, just as for a Poisson variable. That is why \(\mathrm{Po}(np)\) fits. | | Binomial \(B(n, p)\) | Poisson \(\mathrm{Po}(\lambda)\) | |---|---|---| | What is counted | successes in \(n\) trials | events in an interval | | Possible values | \(0, 1, \dots, n\) | \(0, 1, 2, \dots\) with no limit | | Mean and variance | \(np\) and \(npq\) | both equal to \(\lambda\) | | Parameters | two: \(n\) and \(p\) | one: \(\lambda\) | :::key Poisson approximation to the binomial If \(X \sim B(n, p)\) with \(n > 50\) and \(np < 5\), then \(X\) is approximately \(\mathrm{Po}(np)\). ::: :::eg In a factory 2% of light bulbs are faulty, independently of each other. A random sample of 150 bulbs is tested. (a) Explain why a Poisson distribution is a suitable approximation. (b) Use it to find the probability that at most 2 bulbs are faulty. (c) Find the exact probability and comment. (a) Let \(X\) be the number of faulty bulbs, so \(X \sim B(150, 0.02)\). Here \(n = 150 > 50\) and \(np = 3 < 5\). [B1] So \(X\) is approximately \(\mathrm{Po}(3)\). [B1] (b) \(P(X \le 2) \approx e^{-3}\left(1 + 3 + \dfrac{9}{2}\right) = 8.5e^{-3}\) [M1] \(= 0.423\) [A1] (c) Exactly, \(P(X \le 2) = 0.98^{150} + 150(0.02)(0.98)^{149} + \binom{150}{2}(0.02)^{2}(0.98)^{148} = 0.421\). [B1] The two answers differ by only 0.002, so the approximation is very good. [B1] ::: ## The normal approximation to the Poisson Look again at the third panel of the figure. When \(\lambda\) is large the Poisson distribution is nearly symmetric and bell-shaped, so a normal curve with the same mean and variance fits it. :::key Normal approximation to the Poisson If \(X \sim \mathrm{Po}(\lambda)\) with \(\lambda > 15\), then \(X\) is approximately \(N(\lambda, \lambda)\). The mean is \(\lambda\), the variance is \(\lambda\) and the standard deviation is \(\sqrt{\lambda}\). ::: A Poisson variable takes whole numbers only, while a normal variable is continuous. In the figure below, the bar for \(r = 20\) is centred on 20 and stretches from 19.5 to 20.5. To include the whole bar we start the normal area at 19.5. This adjustment is called the continuity correction. :::def Continuity correction The adjustment of 0.5 made when a discrete variable (taking whole numbers) is approximated by a continuous one, so that each whole number is represented by the interval from 0.5 below to 0.5 above it. ::: :::html ::: Let \(Y\) be the normal variable. | Poisson probability | Normal calculation | |---|---| | \(P(X = 20)\) | \(P(19.5 < Y < 20.5)\) | | \(P(X \le 20)\) | \(P(Y < 20.5)\) | | \(P(X < 20)\) | \(P(Y < 19.5)\) | | \(P(X \ge 20)\) | \(P(Y > 19.5)\) | | \(P(X > 20)\) | \(P(Y > 20.5)\) | :::tip A reliable routine First rewrite the inequality so it contains "\(\le\)" or "\(\ge\)" and a whole number (so \(X < 20\) becomes \(X \le 19\)). Then add 0.5 to a "\(\le\)" value and subtract 0.5 from a "\(\ge\)" value. A quick sketch of the bars confirms the choice. ::: :::eg \(X \sim \mathrm{Po}(24)\). Use a normal approximation to find \(P(X \ge 30)\). Since \(\lambda = 24 > 15\), use \(Y \sim N(24, 24)\), so \(\sigma = \sqrt{24} = 4.899\). \[P(X \ge 30) \approx P(Y > 29.5)\] Standardise: \(z = \dfrac{29.5 - 24}{\sqrt{24}} = 1.123\), so \[P(Y > 29.5) = 1 - \Phi(1.123) = 0.131\] The exact Poisson answer is 0.132, so the approximation is good. ::: :::warn Variance, not standard deviation For \(N(\lambda, \lambda)\) the second number is the **variance**. Divide by \(\sqrt{\lambda}\), not by \(\lambda\), when you standardise. Forgetting the continuity correction costs a mark in every exam question on this topic. ::: :::eg Cars pass a speed camera at random, at a constant average rate of 3.2 per minute. (a) State two conditions needed for a Poisson model. (b) Find the probability that exactly 2 cars pass in a given minute. (c) Find the probability that fewer than 3 cars pass in a 30-second period. (d) Use a suitable approximation to find the probability that more than 20 cars pass in a 5-minute period. (a) Cars pass singly (never two at exactly the same instant) and independently of each other. [B1 B1] (b) \(X \sim \mathrm{Po}(3.2)\), so \(P(X = 2) = \dfrac{e^{-3.2}\,3.2^{2}}{2!} = 0.209\). [M1 A1] (c) In 30 seconds the mean is 1.6, so \(Y \sim \mathrm{Po}(1.6)\). [B1] \[P(Y < 3) = P(Y \le 2) = e^{-1.6}\left(1 + 1.6 + \frac{1.6^{2}}{2}\right) = 0.783\] [M1 A1] (d) In 5 minutes the mean is 16, so \(W \sim \mathrm{Po}(16)\). Since \(16 > 15\), \(W\) is approximately \(N(16, 16)\). [B1] "More than 20" means \(W \ge 21\), so \(P(W > 20) \approx P(N > 20.5)\). [M1] \[z = \frac{20.5 - 16}{\sqrt{16}} = 1.125, \qquad 1 - \Phi(1.125) = 0.130\] [M1 A1] ::: :::board **Cambridge 9709** examines the Poisson distribution only in Paper 6 (Probability and Statistics 2) and states the conditions \(n > 50\), \(np < 5\) and \(\lambda > 15\). **Edexcel IAL** covers it in Statistics 2 with the same two approximations, but describes the conditions loosely ("\(n\) large, \(p\) small", "\(\lambda\) large"), so follow the wording of the question. **AQA, OCR and Edexcel A Level Mathematics** in the UK do not include the Poisson distribution; it appears in their A Level Further Mathematics statistics options. ::: :::try Start easy, finish at exam standard Q: \(X \sim \mathrm{Po}(1.5)\). Find (a) \(P(X = 2)\), (b) \(P(X \ge 1)\). A: (a) \(P(X = 2) = \dfrac{e^{-1.5} \times 1.5^{2}}{2} = 0.251\). (b) \(P(X \ge 1) = 1 - P(X = 0) = 1 - e^{-1.5} = 0.777\). Q: Say whether a Poisson model is reasonable in each case. If not, state which condition fails or why the variable is not Poisson. (a) The number of texts you receive in each hour of a whole day. (b) The number of sixes in 12 rolls of a die. (c) The number of accidents per day on a motorway, when one crash in fog is usually followed by several more. A: (a) Not reasonable: the rate is not constant (many more texts in the evening than at 4 am), and conversations make texts dependent. (b) Not Poisson: there are a fixed number of trials (12), so the count cannot exceed 12. It is binomial, \(B(12, \tfrac16)\). (c) Not reasonable: accidents are not independent, because one crash makes another more likely. Q: Typing errors occur at random, at a mean rate of 2 per page. Find the probability of (a) no errors on one page, (b) at least one error in 3 pages, (c) exactly 4 errors in 2 pages. A: (a) \(X \sim \mathrm{Po}(2)\): \(P(X = 0) = e^{-2} = 0.135\). (b) In 3 pages the mean is 6: \(P(Y \ge 1) = 1 - e^{-6} = 0.998\). (c) In 2 pages the mean is 4: \(P(W = 4) = \dfrac{e^{-4}\,4^{4}}{4!} = 0.195\). Q: \(X \sim \mathrm{Po}(\lambda)\) and \(P(X = 0) = 0.2\). Find \(\lambda\) and hence \(P(X = 1)\). A: \(e^{-\lambda} = 0.2\), so \(\lambda = \ln 5 = 1.609\). Then \(P(X = 1) = \lambda e^{-\lambda} = 1.609 \times 0.2 = 0.322\). Q: \(Y \sim \mathrm{Po}(\lambda)\) and \(P(Y = 3) = 2P(Y = 2)\). Find \(\lambda\) and \(P(Y \le 4)\). A: \(\dfrac{P(Y = 3)}{P(Y = 2)} = \dfrac{\lambda}{3}\), so \(\dfrac{\lambda}{3} = 2\) and \(\lambda = 6\). [M1 A1] \(P(Y \le 4) = e^{-6}\left(1 + 6 + 18 + 36 + 54\right) = 115e^{-6} = 0.285\). [M1 A1] Q: \(X \sim B(80, 0.03)\). Show that a Poisson approximation is suitable and use it to find \(P(X \ge 3)\). A: \(n = 80 > 50\) and \(np = 2.4 < 5\), so \(X\) is approximately \(\mathrm{Po}(2.4)\). \(P(X \ge 3) = 1 - e^{-2.4}\left(1 + 2.4 + \dfrac{2.4^{2}}{2}\right) = 1 - 0.5697 = 0.430\). Q: \(X \sim \mathrm{Po}(20)\). Use a normal approximation to find \(P(X < 15)\). A: \(X\) is approximately \(Y \sim N(20, 20)\). \(P(X < 15) = P(X \le 14) \approx P(Y < 14.5)\). [M1] \(z = \dfrac{14.5 - 20}{\sqrt{20}} = -1.230\), so the probability is \(\Phi(-1.230) = 0.109\). [M1 A1] Q: (Exam style) A bakery sells a speciality loaf at random, at a mean rate of 4 loaves per day. (a) The bakery bakes 7 loaves each day. Find the probability that it runs out, meaning demand is more than 7. (b) The bakery wants the probability of running out to be less than 1%. What is the smallest number of loaves it should bake each day? (c) Baking 7 loaves a day, find the probability that it runs out on exactly 2 of the next 5 days. A: (a) \(X \sim \mathrm{Po}(4)\). \(P(X > 7) = 1 - P(X \le 7) = 1 - 0.9489 = 0.0511\). [M1 A1] (b) We need \(P(X > n) < 0.01\), that is \(P(X \le n) > 0.99\). [M1] \(P(X \le 8) = 0.9786\), which is too small, but \(P(X \le 9) = 0.9919\). The bakery should bake 9 loaves. [A1] (c) The days are independent, so the number of run-out days is \(B(5, 0.0511)\). [M1] \(P(\text{exactly 2}) = \binom{5}{2}(0.0511)^{2}(0.9489)^{3} = 0.0223\). [A1] ::: :::quiz Quick check ? Which of these is **not** a condition for a Poisson model? - Events occur independently of each other - Events occur at a constant average rate + There is a fixed number of trials - Events occur singly > A fixed number of trials belongs to the binomial distribution. A Poisson count has no upper limit. ? Cars pass a point at a mean rate of 6 per minute. The number passing in 20 seconds has the distribution - \(\mathrm{Po}(6)\) + \(\mathrm{Po}(2)\) - \(\mathrm{Po}(18)\) - \(\mathrm{Po}(0.33)\) > 20 seconds is one third of a minute, so the mean is \(6 \times \tfrac13 = 2\). ? \(X \sim \mathrm{Po}(25)\). Which expression gives the normal approximation to \(P(X \ge 30)\)? + \(P(Y > 29.5)\) with \(Y \sim N(25, 25)\) - \(P(Y > 30.5)\) with \(Y \sim N(25, 25)\) - \(P(Y > 29.5)\) with \(Y \sim N(25, 5)\) - \(P(Y > 30)\) with \(Y \sim N(25, 25)\) > "30 or more" starts at the lower edge of the bar for 30, which is 29.5. The variance is 25, so the second number in \(N(25, 25)\) is correct. ? \(X \sim B(200, 0.01)\). Which approximation is suitable? + \(\mathrm{Po}(2)\) - \(\mathrm{Po}(200)\) - \(N(200, 0.01)\) - \(\mathrm{Po}(0.01)\) > Here \(n = 200 > 50\) and \(np = 2 < 5\), so use \(\mathrm{Po}(np) = \mathrm{Po}(2)\). ::: :::recap - A Poisson variable counts events in a fixed interval when events occur singly, independently and at a constant average rate. Write \(X \sim \mathrm{Po}(\lambda)\). - \(P(X = r) = \dfrac{e^{-\lambda}\lambda^{r}}{r!}\) for \(r = 0, 1, 2, \dots\), with \(E(X) = \mathrm{Var}(X) = \lambda\). - "At least" and "more than" use the complement: \(P(X \ge 3) = 1 - P(X \le 2)\). - Scale the mean, never the probability: rate \(k\) per unit gives \(\mathrm{Po}(kt)\) over an interval of size \(t\). - If \(X \sim B(n, p)\) with \(n > 50\) and \(np < 5\), then \(X \approx \mathrm{Po}(np)\). - If \(X \sim \mathrm{Po}(\lambda)\) with \(\lambda > 15\), then \(X \approx N(\lambda, \lambda)\). Use the continuity correction of 0.5. - In exam answers, state conditions in context and show the substituted formula before the calculator value. ::: Next: [Linear combinations of random variables](#math.s2.linear) shows how to add independent random variables, including Poisson ones.

@group Pure Mathematics 1 @chapter math.p1.functions @title Functions @level as @paper CAIE P1 · Edexcel IAL P1/P2 · UK Pure Years 1–2 @time 6–8 hours @summary A function is a rule that turns each input into exactly one output. You will learn domain and range, one-one and many-one functions, composite and inverse functions, how restricting a domain makes an inverse possible, and how changes to an equation move, stretch and reflect a graph. :::why Every formula in science and business is a function: put in a time, get out a distance; put in a price, get out a profit. The language of functions (input, output, domain, range, inverse) lets you say exactly what a formula can and cannot do. It also gives you graph transformations, which let you sketch new curves from ones you already know, and it is the language that calculus is written in. Paper 1 regularly includes a multi-part functions question that combines a completed square, a range, an inverse and a composite function. ::: **Before you start**, you should be comfortable with [Quadratics](#math.p1.quadratics), especially completing the square, and with graphs from [Coordinates and straight lines](#math.f.graphs). ## What is a function? A function is a machine. You feed in a number, the machine follows a fixed rule, and out comes a new number. The square-root button on a calculator is a function: feed in 25 and you always get 5, never two different answers. That "one answer only" property is the heart of the definition. :::def Function A rule that gives exactly one output for each allowed input. ::: There are two ways to write the same function. Both of these mean "double the input, then add 3": \[f(x) = 2x + 3 \qquad\text{or}\qquad f : x \mapsto 2x + 3\] Read \(f(4)\) as "f of 4". It is the output when the input is 4, so \(f(4) = 2(4) + 3 = 11\). The second form reads "f maps \(x\) to \(2x + 3\)". Cambridge uses both forms. :::def Domain The set of all allowed input values of a function. ::: :::def Range The set of all output values that the function actually produces. ::: The symbol \(\mathbb{R}\) stands for the real numbers (every number on the number line), and \(x \in \mathbb{R}\) means "\(x\) is any real number". If a question gives no domain, use the largest set of real numbers for which the rule works. At this level only two things stop a rule working: dividing by zero and taking the square root of a negative number. | Function | Largest domain | Reason | |---|---|---| | \(\dfrac{1}{x - 3}\) | \(x \neq 3\) | cannot divide by 0 | | \(\sqrt{x - 2}\) | \(x \geq 2\) | cannot take the root of a negative | | \(\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{x - 2}}\) | \(x > 2\) | the root must be positive, because it is also a denominator | To find the range, ask "which \(y\)-values does the graph reach?" A sketch or a completed square usually answers it. :::tip Write the range with f(x) or y Write \(f(x) \geq -3\) or \(y \geq -3\). Never write \(x \geq -3\): \(x\) is the input, and the range is about outputs. ::: :::eg A function is defined by \(f(x) = x^2 - 4x + 1\) for \(0 \leq x \leq 5\). Find the range of \(f\). Complete the square: \(f(x) = (x - 2)^2 - 3\). The graph is ∪-shaped with its lowest point at \(x = 2\), which lies inside the domain, so the least value is \(-3\). Now check both ends of the domain: \(f(0) = 1\) and \(f(5) = 25 - 20 + 1 = 6\). The graph falls from \(1\) to \(-3\), then rises to \(6\), so the greatest value is the larger end value, \(6\). The range is \(-3 \leq f(x) \leq 6\). **Common error:** writing \(1 \leq f(x) \leq 6\) from the end values alone. That misses the dip to \(-3\) at the vertex. ::: ## One-one and many-one functions Compare \(f(x) = x^3\) and \(g(x) = x^2\). Every output of \(x^3\) comes from one input only. But \(g(2) = 4\) and \(g(-2) = 4\): two different inputs give the same output. :::def One-one function A function in which each output comes from exactly one input. ::: :::def Many-one function A function in which at least one output comes from two or more different inputs. ::: The **horizontal line test** tells you which kind you have. Draw horizontal lines across the graph. If any line cuts the graph more than once, the function is many-one. If every line cuts it at most once, it is one-one. :::html ::: A mapping where one input gives two outputs (such as \(y = \pm\sqrt{x}\)) is not a function at all. This matters because **only one-one functions have inverses**. ## Composite functions Sometimes you run one machine and feed its output into a second. The result is a **composite function**. Write \(fg(x)\) for \(f(g(x))\): apply \(g\) first, then \(f\). Work from the right. :::eg \(f(x) = 2x + 1\) and \(g(x) = x^2 - 3\), for \(x \in \mathbb{R}\). Find \(fg(x)\) and \(gf(x)\), and solve \(gf(x) = 6\). Start with \(fg(x)\): put \(g(x)\) into \(f\). \[\begin{aligned} fg(x) &= f\big(g(x)\big) = f(x^2 - 3) \\ &= 2(x^2 - 3) + 1 \\ &= 2x^2 - 5 \end{aligned}\] Now \(gf(x)\): put \(f(x)\) into \(g\). \[\begin{aligned} gf(x) &= g\big(f(x)\big) = g(2x + 1) \\ &= (2x + 1)^2 - 3 \\ &= 4x^2 + 4x - 2 \end{aligned}\] The two answers differ, so order matters. To solve \(gf(x) = 6\): \[\begin{aligned} 4x^2 + 4x - 2 &= 6 \\ 4x^2 + 4x - 8 &= 0 \\ x^2 + x - 2 &= 0 \\ (x + 2)(x - 1) &= 0 \end{aligned}\] Hence \(x = -2\) or \(x = 1\). **Check:** \(f(1) = 3\) and \(g(3) = 9 - 3 = 6\). It works. ::: Writing \(f^2(x)\) means \(ff(x)\), "do \(f\) twice". For \(fg\) to exist, every output of \(g\) must be an allowed input for \(f\). With \(f(x) = \sqrt{x}\) and \(g(x) = x - 5\) for \(x \geq 5\), the outputs of \(g\) are all at least 0, so \(fg(x) = \sqrt{x - 5}\) is fine. If \(g\) were defined for all real \(x\), some outputs would be negative and \(fg\) would break down. :::warn Read composites from the right \(fg(x)\) is not "\(f\) times \(g\)", and it does not mean "\(f\) first". It means \(f(g(x))\), so \(g\) acts first. Mixing up \(fg\) and \(gf\) is a very common way to lose marks. ::: ## Inverse functions An **inverse function** undoes what the original did. If \(f\) turns 3 into 7, then \(f^{-1}\) turns 7 back into 3. A kettle that heats water is undone by letting it cool; subtracting 5 undoes adding 5. :::def Inverse function For a one-one function \(f\), the inverse function \(f^{-1}\) reverses \(f\): if \(f(a) = b\) then \(f^{-1}(b) = a\). The domain of \(f^{-1}\) is the range of \(f\), and the range of \(f^{-1}\) is the domain of \(f\). ::: So \(f^{-1}f(x) = x\) and \(ff^{-1}(x) = x\). To find an inverse: :::steps 1. Write \(y = f(x)\). 2. Rearrange to make \(x\) the subject. 3. Replace \(y\) by \(x\) in your answer, and write it as \(f^{-1}(x)\). 4. State the domain of \(f^{-1}\): it is the range of \(f\). ::: :::eg \(f(x) = \dfrac{2x + 1}{x - 3}\) for \(x \neq 3\). Find \(f^{-1}(x)\), and state its domain. Write \(y = \dfrac{2x + 1}{x - 3}\) and clear the fraction. Then collect the \(x\) terms on one side and factorise: \[\begin{aligned} y(x - 3) &= 2x + 1 \\ xy - 3y &= 2x + 1 \\ xy - 2x &= 3y + 1 \\ x(y - 2) &= 3y + 1 \\ x &= \frac{3y + 1}{y - 2} \end{aligned}\] So \(f^{-1}(x) = \dfrac{3x + 1}{x - 2}\). For the domain, find the range of \(f\). Since \(2x + 1 = 2(x - 3) + 7\), we can write \(f(x) = 2 + \dfrac{7}{x - 3}\). The fraction is never zero, so \(f(x)\) never equals 2. The range is \(f(x) \neq 2\), so the domain of \(f^{-1}\) is \(x \neq 2\). This matches the denominator of \(f^{-1}(x)\). **Check:** \(f(4) = 9\) and \(f^{-1}(9) = \dfrac{28}{7} = 4\). We return to the start. ::: :::warn f⁻¹ is not 1/f The "\(-1\)" in \(f^{-1}(x)\) labels the inverse function. It does **not** mean \(\dfrac{1}{f(x)}\). For \(f(x) = 2x\), the inverse is \(f^{-1}(x) = \tfrac{x}{2}\), while \(\dfrac{1}{f(x)} = \dfrac{1}{2x}\). ::: ### The graph of an inverse Because \(f\) takes \(a\) to \(b\) and \(f^{-1}\) takes \(b\) back to \(a\), every point \((a, b)\) on the graph of \(f\) matches a point \((b, a)\) on the graph of \(f^{-1}\). Swapping coordinates is a **reflection in the line \(y = x\)**. Domain and range swap as well. :::html ::: If a question asks you to solve \(f(x) = f^{-1}(x)\) and \(f\) is an increasing function, the two graphs meet on the line \(y = x\), so it is enough to solve \(f(x) = x\). ## Restricting a domain The function \(f(x) = x^2 - 4x + 7\) for \(x \in \mathbb{R}\) is many-one: the parabola is symmetrical, so two inputs share each output. But we are free to choose the domain. If we cut the parabola in half at its line of symmetry, each half is one-one and has an inverse. The line of symmetry comes from the completed square: \[f(x) = (x - 2)^2 + 3\] The vertex is \((2, 3)\). Restricting to \(x \geq 2\) keeps the right-hand half, whose range is \(f(x) \geq 3\). To find the inverse, rearrange \(y = (x - 2)^2 + 3\) to get \((x - 2)^2 = y - 3\), so \(x - 2 = \pm\sqrt{y - 3}\). Which sign? The original domain is \(x \geq 2\), so \(x - 2\) is positive and we take the plus sign: \[f^{-1}(x) = 2 + \sqrt{x - 3}, \qquad x \geq 3\] Had the domain been \(x \leq 2\), we would take the minus sign, giving \(f^{-1}(x) = 2 - \sqrt{x - 3}\). :::exam Domains in inverse questions "Find the smallest value of \(k\) for which \(f\) is one-one when \(x \geq k\)" asks for the \(x\)-coordinate of the vertex. Marks for "state the domain of \(f^{-1}\)" are easy to lose: it is always the **range** of \(f\), written with \(x\), for example \(x \geq 3\). ::: :::eg (Exam style) The function \(f\) is defined by \(f(x) = 3x^2 - 12x + 5\) for \(x \geq k\). (a) Express \(f(x)\) in the form \(a(x - p)^2 + q\). (b) State the smallest value of \(k\) for which \(f\) is one-one. (c) For this value of \(k\), find \(f^{-1}(x)\) and state its domain. **(a)** Take out a factor of 3 from the first two terms, then complete the square inside: \[\begin{aligned} 3x^2 - 12x + 5 &= 3(x^2 - 4x) + 5 \\ &= 3\big[(x - 2)^2 - 4\big] + 5 \end{aligned}\] [M1] \[= 3(x - 2)^2 - 7\] [A1] **(b)** The line of symmetry is \(x = 2\), so the smallest value is \(k = 2\). [B1] **(c)** Let \(y = 3(x - 2)^2 - 7\). Then \(\dfrac{y + 7}{3} = (x - 2)^2\). [M1] Because \(x \geq 2\), take the positive root: \(x = 2 + \sqrt{\dfrac{y + 7}{3}}\), so \[f^{-1}(x) = 2 + \sqrt{\frac{x + 7}{3}}\] [A1] The domain of \(f^{-1}\) is the range of \(f\). The least value of \(f\) is \(-7\), so the domain is \(x \geq -7\). [B1] ::: ## Transformations of graphs If you know the graph of \(y = f(x)\), you can sketch many related graphs without plotting points. Each change to the equation moves, stretches or reflects the picture in a predictable way. | Equation | Transformation of \(y = f(x)\) | |---|---| | \(y = f(x) + a\) | translation \(\begin{pmatrix}0\\a\end{pmatrix}\): up \(a\)
\((x, y) \to (x,\, y + a)\) | | \(y = f(x + a)\) | translation \(\begin{pmatrix}-a\\0\end{pmatrix}\): left \(a\)
\((x, y) \to (x - a,\, y)\) | | \(y = af(x)\) | stretch parallel to the \(y\)-axis, scale factor \(a\)
\((x, y) \to (x,\, ay)\) | | \(y = f(ax)\) | stretch parallel to the \(x\)-axis, scale factor \(\tfrac{1}{a}\)
\((x, y) \to (\tfrac{x}{a},\, y)\) | | \(y = -f(x)\) | reflection in the \(x\)-axis
\((x, y) \to (x,\, -y)\) | | \(y = f(-x)\) | reflection in the \(y\)-axis
\((x, y) \to (-x,\, y)\) | Why does \(f(x + 2)\) move the graph **left**? Suppose \(f(3) = 5\), so \((3, 5)\) lies on \(y = f(x)\). On the new graph, the input that gives output 5 is the one with \(x + 2 = 3\), that is \(x = 1\). The point has moved from \((3, 5)\) to \((1, 5)\), two units to the left. The same reasoning shows that \(f(2x)\) reaches every output when \(x\) is only half as big, so the graph is squashed towards the \(y\)-axis. :::key The inside/outside rule Changes **outside** the bracket act on \(y\) and do what you expect: \(+a\) lifts, \(\times a\) stretches vertically. Changes **inside** the bracket act on \(x\) and do the opposite: \(x + a\) moves left, \(ax\) squashes horizontally by \(\tfrac{1}{a}\). ::: Try the sliders. The first curve is \(y = x^2\) and the second is the transformed copy. Move \(c\) and \(d\) to slide the copy sideways and up or down. Move \(a\) to stretch it, and push \(a\) below zero to flip it over. :::html
::: When transformations are combined, work in the order you would calculate. For \(y = 3f(x) + 1\), start with \(f(x)\), multiply by 3, then add 1: stretch first, then translate. For a bracket such as \(f(2x - 4)\), first factorise it as \(f\big(2(x - 2)\big)\). Then squash by \(\tfrac12\) parallel to the \(x\)-axis, and translate 2 to the right. :::warn Order matters \(3f(x) + 1\) and \(3\big(f(x) + 1\big) = 3f(x) + 3\) are different graphs. Always stretch before you translate vertically. A full description of a transformation needs its type and its details: a translation needs a vector, a stretch needs a direction and a scale factor, and a reflection needs a line. ::: :::eg (Exam style) The curve \(y = f(x)\) has a minimum point at \((2, -3)\). Write down the coordinates of the minimum point on each curve: (a) \(y = f(x + 1) - 4\), (b) \(y = 2f(x)\), (c) \(y = f(3x)\), (d) \(y = -f(x)\). (e) Describe fully the two transformations that map \(y = f(x)\) onto \(y = 3f(x - 2) + 1\), and give the image of the minimum point. **(a)** Left 1 and down 4: \((2 - 1,\; -3 - 4) = (1, -7)\). [B1] **(b)** The \(y\)-coordinate doubles: \((2, -6)\). [B1] **(c)** The \(x\)-coordinate is divided by 3: \(\left(\tfrac{2}{3}, -3\right)\). [B1] **(d)** The graph is reflected in the \(x\)-axis: \((2, 3)\), and it is now a **maximum** point. [B1] **(e)** A stretch parallel to the \(y\)-axis with scale factor 3, [B1] followed by a translation of \(\begin{pmatrix}2\\1\end{pmatrix}\). [B1] The minimum point moves \((2, -3) \to (2, -9) \to (4, -8)\). [B1] ::: :::board Cambridge puts all of this in Paper 1 (AS). The UK boards (AQA, OCR, Pearson Edexcel) split it: graph transformations are in Year 1, but domain and range, composite and inverse functions, and modulus functions are A Level (Year 2) content. Edexcel IAL covers the same ideas across P1 and P2. Notation differs slightly: Cambridge often writes \(f : x \mapsto 2x + 3\), the UK boards usually write \(f(x) = 2x + 3\), and every board accepts both. Modulus functions such as \(y = |f(x)|\) are in Cambridge Paper 3; see [Algebra: modulus, polynomials and partial fractions](#math.p3.algebra). ::: :::try Start easy, finish at exam standard Q: Let \(f(x) = 3x - 5\). Find \(f(4)\), \(f(-2)\) and the value of \(x\) for which \(f(x) = 10\). A: \(f(4) = 12 - 5 = 7\) and \(f(-2) = -6 - 5 = -11\). Solving \(3x - 5 = 10\) gives \(3x = 15\), so \(x = 5\). Q: The function \(g\) is defined by \(g(x) = 2x^2 - 8x + 3\) for \(x \geq 3\). Find the range of \(g\). A: Complete the square: \(g(x) = 2(x - 2)^2 - 5\), with its vertex at \(x = 2\). That is **not** in the domain \(x \geq 3\). For \(x \geq 3\) the graph only rises, so the least value is \(g(3) = 18 - 24 + 3 = -3\). The range is \(g(x) \geq -3\). Q: \(f(x) = x + 4\) and \(g(x) = 3x^2\) for \(x \in \mathbb{R}\). Find \(fg(x)\) and \(gf(x)\), and solve \(fg(x) = gf(x)\). A: \(fg(x) = 3x^2 + 4\) and \(gf(x) = 3(x + 4)^2 = 3x^2 + 24x + 48\). Setting them equal, the \(3x^2\) terms cancel: \(4 = 24x + 48\), so \(24x = -44\) and \(x = -\tfrac{11}{6}\). Q: Find the inverse of \(f(x) = \dfrac{5}{x - 2}\) for \(x \neq 2\), and state the domain of \(f^{-1}\). A: Let \(y = \dfrac{5}{x - 2}\). Then \(x - 2 = \dfrac{5}{y}\), so \(x = 2 + \dfrac{5}{y}\) and \(f^{-1}(x) = 2 + \dfrac{5}{x}\). The fraction \(\dfrac{5}{x - 2}\) is never zero, so the range of \(f\) is \(f(x) \neq 0\). The domain of \(f^{-1}\) is therefore \(x \neq 0\). Q: \(f(x) = x^2 - 6x + 10\) for \(x \geq k\). (a) Write \(f(x)\) in completed square form. (b) State the smallest \(k\) for which \(f\) is one-one. (c) For this \(k\), find \(f^{-1}(x)\) and its domain. A: (a) \(f(x) = (x - 3)^2 + 1\). (b) The vertex is at \(x = 3\), so \(k = 3\). (c) \(y - 1 = (x - 3)^2\), and since \(x \geq 3\) we take the positive root: \(f^{-1}(x) = 3 + \sqrt{x - 1}\). The range of \(f\) is \(f(x) \geq 1\), so the domain of \(f^{-1}\) is \(x \geq 1\). Q: State the single transformation that maps \(y = f(x)\) onto (a) \(y = f(x - 3)\), (b) \(y = 2f(x)\), (c) \(y = f\!\left(\tfrac{1}{2}x\right)\), (d) \(y = f(-x)\). A: (a) A translation of \(\begin{pmatrix}3\\0\end{pmatrix}\), that is 3 units to the right. (b) A stretch parallel to the \(y\)-axis with scale factor 2. (c) A stretch parallel to the \(x\)-axis with scale factor 2, because the scale factor is \(1 \div \tfrac12\). (d) A reflection in the \(y\)-axis. Q: (Exam style) (a) Express \(x^2 - 6x + 4\) in the form \((x - p)^2 + q\). (b) Describe the translation that maps the curve \(y = x^2\) onto the curve \(y = x^2 - 6x + 4\). (c) Write down the equation of the line of symmetry of \(y = x^2 - 6x + 4\). A: (a) Half of \(-6\) is \(-3\), so \(x^2 - 6x = (x - 3)^2 - 9\) and \(x^2 - 6x + 4 = (x - 3)^2 - 5\). [M1 A1] (b) Comparing with \(y = f(x - 3) - 5\) where \(f(x) = x^2\): a translation of \(\begin{pmatrix}3\\-5\end{pmatrix}\), that is 3 right and 5 down. [B1] (c) The vertex is at \((3, -5)\), so the line of symmetry is \(x = 3\). [B1] Q: (Exam style) \(f(x) = 3x - 2\) and \(g(x) = x^2 + 1\) for \(x \in \mathbb{R}\). (a) Find \(gf(x)\). (b) Solve \(gf(x) = 10\). (c) Find \(f^{-1}(x)\) and solve \(f(x) = f^{-1}(x)\). A: (a) \(gf(x) = (3x - 2)^2 + 1 = 9x^2 - 12x + 5\). [M1 A1] (b) \((3x - 2)^2 + 1 = 10\), so \((3x - 2)^2 = 9\) and \(3x - 2 = \pm 3\). Hence \(x = \tfrac{5}{3}\) or \(x = -\tfrac{1}{3}\). [M1 A1] (c) From \(y = 3x - 2\) we get \(x = \dfrac{y + 2}{3}\), so \(f^{-1}(x) = \dfrac{x + 2}{3}\). [B1] Solving \(3x - 2 = \dfrac{x + 2}{3}\): \(9x - 6 = x + 2\), so \(8x = 8\) and \(x = 1\). [M1 A1] (Because \(f\) is increasing, solving \(f(x) = x\) gives the same answer: \(3x - 2 = x\), \(x = 1\).) ::: :::quiz ? The function \(f(x) = x^2\) is defined for all real \(x\). Which statement is true? - \(f\) is one-one and has an inverse. + \(f\) is many-one, so it has no inverse as it stands. - The range of \(f\) is all real numbers. - \(f\) is not a function because \(f(2) = f(-2)\). > Both 2 and \(-2\) give the output 4, so \(f\) is many-one. That is allowed for a function (each input still has one output), but a many-one function has no inverse. Its range is \(f(x) \geq 0\). ? \(f(x) = 2x + 1\) and \(g(x) = x - 4\). What is \(fg(x)\)? + \(2x - 7\) - \(2x - 3\) - \(2x^2 - 7x - 4\) - \(2x - 8\) > \(fg(x) = f(g(x)) = 2(x - 4) + 1 = 2x - 7\). The answer \(2x - 3\) is \(gf(x)\), found by applying the functions in the wrong order. ? How does the graph of \(y = f(x + 2)\) compare with the graph of \(y = f(x)\)? - It moves 2 units to the right. + It moves 2 units to the left. - It moves 2 units up. - It is stretched by scale factor 2 parallel to the \(x\)-axis. > A change inside the bracket acts on \(x\) and does the opposite of what you expect. The point \((3, 5)\) on \(y = f(x)\) becomes \((1, 5)\) on \(y = f(x + 2)\). ? \(f(x) = (x - 2)^2 + 1\) has domain \(x \geq 2\). What is the domain of \(f^{-1}\)? - \(x \geq 2\) + \(x \geq 1\) - \(x \geq 0\) - all real numbers > The domain of \(f^{-1}\) is the range of \(f\). The least value of \(f\) is 1, so the domain of \(f^{-1}\) is \(x \geq 1\). The value 2 is the domain of \(f\), which becomes the range of \(f^{-1}\). ::: :::recap - A function gives exactly one output for each input. The domain is the set of allowed inputs and the range is the set of outputs produced. Write the range with \(f(x)\) or \(y\). - A function is one-one if each output comes from one input (horizontal line test). Only one-one functions have inverses. - \(fg(x) = f(g(x))\): apply \(g\) first. In general \(fg \neq gf\). - To find \(f^{-1}\): write \(y = f(x)\), make \(x\) the subject, then swap letters. Its domain is the range of \(f\), and its graph is the reflection of \(f\) in \(y = x\). - To make a quadratic one-one, restrict its domain to one side of the vertex, which you find by completing the square. Choose the \(\pm\) in the inverse to match the original domain. - Outside the bracket, \(f(x) + a\) and \(af(x)\) act on \(y\) as expected. Inside, \(f(x + a)\) moves left by \(a\) and \(f(ax)\) stretches horizontally by \(\tfrac{1}{a}\). \(-f(x)\) reflects in the \(x\)-axis and \(f(-x)\) in the \(y\)-axis. - For combined transformations, work in the order you would calculate: stretch first, then translate. ::: Next: [Coordinate geometry](#math.p1.coord) uses equations to describe straight lines and circles, and you will meet transformed circles again there.

@group The road to exam day @chapter road.overview @title The preparation road at a glance @level guide @paper All subjects · all boards @time 20 minutes to read @summary Six phases take you from your first day of study to results day. This page shows what each phase is for, how long it takes on three different timelines, the milestones you must not miss, and how to know when you are ready to move on. :::why Two years, or even one, is a long time, and long projects fail in a predictable way: weeks drift past, the hard topics get pushed back, and past papers start far too late. A road with clear phases turns one big, frightening goal into small weekly jobs. It also tells you what to do next on any given day, which is half the battle when you study alone. ::: ## The six phases Every successful exam preparation, whatever the subject or board, passes through the same six phases. They are not strict boxes. Learning and practice run side by side, and past-paper work starts before the last topic is finished. But the order matters: you cannot practise what you have not learned, and timed papers only help once you know most of the content. :::html ::: | Phase | What you do | Why it matters | How long | |---|---|---|---| | 1. [Fix your foundations](#road.foundations) | Check and repair the GCSE/IGCSE skills each subject assumes: algebra, units, graphs, essay writing | Every A Level topic is built on them, and small gaps slow down everything later | 2–6 weeks | | 2. [Learn the content](#road.learn) | Work through the syllabus topic by topic: read actively, make notes, follow worked examples | You cannot practise or revise what you never understood | About half of your total time | | 3. [Practise and test yourself](#road.practice) | Retrieval practice, spaced review, flashcards, topic questions, an error log | Understanding fades within days unless you test it; testing makes it stick | Alongside phase 2, then 3–6 weeks of its own | | 4. [Past papers](#road.pastpapers) | Real papers under timed conditions, marked honestly with the official mark scheme | Teaches the exam's style, its timing and the wording that earns marks | 8–12 weeks | | 5. [Final revision](#road.final) | Condense notes, target weak topics, sit full mock exams | Turns what you know into marks you can rely on under pressure | The last 6–8 weeks | | 6. [Exam day](#road.examday) | Prepare the logistics, manage your time in the paper, then deal with results, reviews and resits | Avoids losing marks to nerves, admin or a missing plan B | The exam series and results day | ## Three tracks: how long each phase takes How long you spend in each phase depends on how much time you have. The three most common situations are below. Find yours, then use the [study planner](#road.planner) to turn it into dated weeks. | | 2-year school route | 12-month intensive | 5–6-month resit or crash plan | |---|---|---|---| | Who it suits | Students in Years 12–13 at a school or college | Private candidates studying full-time, often straight after IGCSE | Students resitting, or who already know much of the content | | Typical dates | September of Year 12 → May/June of Year 13 | June → June, or October → October/November of the next year | June → October/November, or December → May/June | | 1. Foundations | 3–4 weeks (the summer before, plus September) | 3–4 weeks | 1 week: a diagnostic test only | | 2. Learn | September of Year 12 to about February of Year 13 | 26–30 weeks | 4–8 weeks, weak topics only | | 3. Practise | Every week, plus about 4 weeks of consolidation | Every week, plus about 3 weeks | Every week: the main activity | | 4. Past papers | Topic questions from Year 12; full papers January–April of Year 13 | 8–10 weeks | 8–10 weeks | | 5. Final revision | 8 weeks (April–May of Year 13) | 6–8 weeks | 3–4 weeks | | 6. Exam day | May/June; results in August | Your chosen series | Your chosen series | | Study outside lessons | 10–15 hours a week | 30–36 hours a week | 8–12 hours a week per subject | :::board Staged, linear and modular Cambridge International lets you take the AS papers at the end of Year 12 and the rest of the A Level a year later (**staged assessment**). An AS result can be carried forward for up to 13 months. If your school works this way, you run phases 4–6 twice: a short version for AS in Year 12, then the full version in Year 13. AQA and OCR A Levels are **linear**: every paper is sat in May/June at the end of the course. Edexcel International A Levels (IAL) are **modular**, with exams in January, May/June and October, so you can sit some units early and spread the load. ::: ## Milestones you must not miss | When | Milestone | Details | |---|---|---| | Before you start | Choose your subjects and board, and download the syllabus for **your** exam year | [Choosing your subjects](#start.choose), [Exam boards](#start.boards) | | First month (private candidates) | Find an exam centre; ask about entry deadlines, fees and practical papers | In Turkey: the British Council (Istanbul, Ankara) and Pearson-approved schools. See [Studying as a private candidate](#road.private) | | Every 6–8 weeks | A timed test on everything learned so far | Record the score in your progress tracker | | Autumn of your final year | University applications | UCAS deadlines for 2027 entry: 15 October 2026 (Oxford, Cambridge and most medicine, dentistry and veterinary courses), 13 January 2027 (most other courses). See [University applications](#road.university) | | Several months before the exams | Exam entries close | Schools enter you; private candidates enter through their centre. Late entries cost extra | | 2–4 months before the first paper | Mock exams | A full set of papers in exam conditions | | Start of phase 5 | Past-paper target | At least 5 full papers per component done and marked; 8–12 by exam day | | August (for June exams) | Results day | Cambridge results for the June 2026 series came out on 11 August 2026 | ## How many hours a week? Cambridge designs each A Level around **360 guided learning hours** of teaching (about 180 for an AS Level). That is class time with a teacher; practice and revision come on top. As a rough guide: - **At school:** lessons plus 3–5 hours of your own study per subject per week, so 10–15 hours a week for three subjects. Raise this to 20 or more in the final 8 weeks. - **Private candidate, full-time:** 10–12 hours per subject per week, so 30–36 hours for three subjects. Treat it like a job: a fixed start time, fixed breaks, and one day a week off. - **Resitting one or two subjects:** 8–12 hours per subject per week. :::tip Hours are not the goal Two hours of testing yourself beat five hours of rereading. Track your hours to make sure the time goes in, but judge your progress by your scores on questions you have not seen before. ::: ## Are you ready to move on? Use these checks at the end of each phase. If you fail one, do not panic: spend another week or two on that phase, then check again. | Phase | You are ready to move on when… | |---|---| | 1. Foundations | You score at least 8 out of 10 on each foundation self-check without looking anything up | | 2. Learn | For every syllabus learning outcome, you can explain the idea aloud and answer a basic question without notes | | 3. Practise | You score 70% or more on mixed topic questions a week after learning them, and the same mistakes have stopped appearing in your error log | | 4. Past papers | Your last three full papers, timed and honestly marked, reach your target grade | | 5. Final revision | Every topic in your tracker is green, and you can write out the key formulas and definitions from memory | :::warn The commonest way to fall behind: living in phase 2 Many students spend months rereading notes and making them prettier, then reach the exam having answered almost no questions. Rereading feels productive because everything looks familiar, but recognising an idea is not the same as being able to use it. From the first week, end every study session with questions you answer without looking. ::: :::exam Start from the syllabus, finish with the mark scheme Two documents define what you need: the **syllabus** (what can be asked) and the **mark schemes** (what earns marks). Download the syllabus for your exam year before you study anything. Read your first mark scheme early, during phase 2, so you know what examiners look for from the start. ::: :::tip Already part-way through? You do not have to start at phase 1. If your exams are four months away, do one past paper per subject this week, mark it, and study the results. Then jump to the phase that fixes your biggest problem, and use the 5–6-month track for timing. ::: ## Where to go next Start by [building your personal study plan](#road.planner), then follow the phases in order, beginning with [Phase 1: Fix your foundations](#road.foundations). Along the way, read [Study methods that actually work](#road.methods), [Exam technique](#road.technique) and [Motivation, sleep and stress](#road.wellbeing). :::recap - Six phases: fix foundations, learn, practise, past papers, final revision, exam day. They overlap, but the order matters. - Pick your track: the 2-year school route, the 12-month intensive, or the 5–6-month resit or crash plan. - Download the syllabus for your exam year first, and read a mark scheme early. - Private candidates: find an exam centre and check its entry deadlines in the first month. - Cambridge designs an A Level around 360 guided learning hours of teaching; your own practice comes on top. - Judge progress by scores on unseen questions, not by hours or pages of notes. - Move on from a phase only when you pass its "ready" check. ::: Next: [Build your personal study plan](#road.planner). @chapter road.planner @title Build your personal study plan @level tool @paper All subjects · all boards @time 30 minutes @summary Turn the six phases into a dated, week-by-week plan for your own exam date and subjects. Then learn how to read the plan, adapt it when life gets in the way, and fill in a weekly timetable, with three complete example plans. A good plan answers two questions: **is my goal realistic?** and **what should I do this week?** Enter your exam date and your subjects below. The planner counts the weeks you have and spreads them across the [six phases](#road.overview), so you can see when each phase should start and finish. :::html
::: :::tip Which date should I enter? Use the date of your **first** paper, not the last, because final revision has to be finished by then. If the timetable is not published yet, take the earliest date in your board's window for that exam series. Planning for a week too early is harmless; planning for a week too late is not. ::: ## Build or check a plan by hand The planner does the arithmetic, but you should understand it so that you can check the result, or redo it with a pen and a calendar. :::steps 1. Count the whole weeks from next Monday to your first paper. 2. Keep about one week in ten free as a **buffer** for illness, holidays and family events. 3. Working back from the exam, mark the last 6–8 weeks as final revision (phase 5) and the 4–6 weeks before that as full past papers (phase 4). 4. Mark the first 2–4 weeks as foundations (phase 1). 5. The weeks left in the middle are for learning (phase 2), with practice (phase 3) built into every week. Share them between your subjects' topics. 6. Add the fixed dates: entry deadline, mocks, holidays and UCAS deadlines. ::: Then do a **reality check**. Each chapter of this guide shows a study time at the top (for example, 6–8 hours for [Quadratics](#math.p1.quadratics)). Add about half as much again for practice, multiply by the number of topics, and compare the total with the hours your learning weeks give you. If it does not fit, you have three honest choices: study more hours a week, take fewer subjects in this series, or move to a later series. Never solve the problem by cutting phases 4 and 5, because that is where grades are made. ## How to read your plan - **Phase dates are targets, not walls.** Phases overlap. Start past-paper questions on each topic as soon as you finish it, long before phase 4 officially begins. - **The learning weeks are the tightest.** If your plan gives you fewer than about 10 weeks per subject to learn the content, you are on an intensive track, and your weekly hours matter more than anything else. - **Phase 5 has a minimum.** Even a short plan needs at least 3–4 weeks of final revision. ## Adapting the plan Every plan goes wrong at some point. What matters is how you respond. | Situation | What to do | |---|---| | 1–2 weeks behind | Use a buffer week, or add 3–5 hours a week for a month. Do not push every later phase back | | 3 or more weeks behind | Decide now: more hours, one subject moved to the next series, or an AS Level only this time (a Cambridge AS Level is a qualification in its own right) | | Ahead of schedule | Do more mixed practice and past-paper questions; do not race ahead to new content | | A topic takes twice as long as planned | Normal for hard topics. Borrow time from a buffer week, never from practice | | Ill or away for a week | Restart with a weekly review; do not try to "catch up" by working through the night | Run the planner again once a month: it shows whether you are on track while there is still time to act. :::warn A plan with no spare time breaks in week three If every hour of every week is filled, the first cold or family wedding pushes everything back, and the plan starts to feel like a list of failures. Leave buffer weeks, keep one day a week free, and plan only the next week in detail. ::: ## Three example plans ### A. School student: Year 12 from September 2026, exams in June 2028 | Term | Main phases | Targets and milestones | |---|---|---| | Autumn 2026 (Year 12) | 1 in September, then 2 and 3 | Foundation self-checks in the first 3 weeks; weekly reviews from October; first unit tests in November | | Spring 2027 | 2 and 3, plus past-paper questions by topic | Most AS content finished by Easter | | Summer 2027 | AS exams in May/June if your school uses staged assessment; otherwise school exams | Start the A Level content in June; in the holidays, research universities and draft your personal statement | | Autumn 2027 (Year 13) | 2 and 3 for the A Level content | UCAS: mid-October deadline for Oxford, Cambridge and medicine, January for most courses; admissions tests | | Spring 2028 | Content finished by February; mocks; then 4 | From February, 1–2 timed papers per subject per week; at least 5 per component by Easter | | Summer 2028 | 5 (the 8 weeks before your first paper), then 6 | Exams in May/June; results in August 2028 | ### B. Private candidate: October 2026 to June 2027, Mathematics, Physics and Chemistry A full-time candidate studying about 36 hours a week for Cambridge 9709, 9702 and 9701 in the May/June 2027 series. Week 1 starts on Monday 5 October 2026, and the plan assumes a first paper in early May. | Weeks | Dates | Phase | Mathematics 9709 | Physics 9702 | Chemistry 9701 | |---|---|---|---|---|---| | 1–2 | 5–18 Oct | 1 | Algebra, powers, graphs | Units, standard form, rearranging | Formulas, equations, basic moles | | 3–8 | 19 Oct – 29 Nov | 2 + 3 | Pure 1 | AS topics 1–6 | AS topics 1–8 | | 9–12 | 30 Nov – 27 Dec | 2 + 3 | Pure 3, first half | AS topics 7–11 | AS topics 9–16 | | 13 | 28 Dec – 3 Jan | Buffer | Rest and catch up | Rest and catch up | Rest and catch up | | 14–17 | 4–31 Jan 2027 | 2 + 3 | Pure 3, second half | A Level topics 12–18 | AS 17–22, A Level 23–26 | | 18–21 | 1–28 Feb | 2 + 3 | Probability & Statistics 1, Mechanics | A Level topics 19–25 | A Level topics 27–37 | | 22–25 | 1–28 Mar | 4 | Two timed papers a week | Timed papers; Paper 5 planning practice | Timed papers; Paper 5 planning practice | | 26–30 | 29 Mar – 2 May | 5 | Final revision; full mocks in weeks 26 and 29 | As Maths | As Maths | | 31 on | From 3 May | 6 | Exams | Exams | Exams | :::warn This plan is intensive Thirty weeks of 36 hours gives about 360 hours per subject: the same as Cambridge's guided learning hours, but without a teacher. It suits students with strong IGCSE grades in all three subjects who can study full-time. If you are more than two weeks behind in week 8, move your weakest subject to the October/November 2027 series. Cambridge science candidates also sit a practical exam (Paper 3), so check early that your centre can run it, and book some laboratory practice before March. ::: ### C. Resit student: sitting again in November Emre sat A Level Chemistry in June 2027 and knows that Paper 4 went badly. He needs an A for a university application next year, so he starts preparing for the October/November 2027 series the week after his last June paper. Waiting for results day in August would cost him eight weeks. He plans 10–12 hours a week. | Weeks | When | Phase | Focus | |---|---|---|---| | 1 | Late June | 1: diagnosis | One paper of each component done cold and marked; every topic sorted into red, amber or green; ask the centre for the November entry deadline | | 2–7 | July to mid-August | 2 + 3 | Relearn two red topics a week; daily flashcards; topic questions after each one | | Results day | August | – | Confirm the grade; ask the centre about a copy of the marked script; make sure the November entry is in | | 8–13 | Mid-August to late September | 4 | One or two timed papers a week, marked the same day; every lost mark redone a week later | | 14–17 | October | 5 | Amber topics, condensed notes, two full mocks | | 18 on | October/November | 6 | The exams; results in January | ## A weekly timetable template Copy this pattern into a notebook or calendar and adapt it to your subjects. Each day mixes new learning with practice on earlier topics, and every week ends with a review. | Day | Private candidate, full-time (about 36 hours) | School student (about 9 hours, plus homework) | |---|---|---| | Monday | 09:00–12:00 Maths, new topic · 13:30–16:30 Physics, new topic · 20 min flashcards | 1 hour: redo today's lesson examples without looking · 20 min flashcards | | Tuesday | Chemistry, new topic · Maths, questions on Monday's topic · flashcards | 1 hour Chemistry questions · 20 min flashcards | | Wednesday | Physics, questions · Chemistry, questions · flashcards | 1 hour Physics questions · 20 min flashcards | | Thursday | Maths, new topic · Physics, new topic · flashcards | 1 hour Maths questions · 20 min error log | | Friday | Chemistry, new topic · mixed questions from all three · flashcards | Free evening | | Saturday | 09:00–12:00 one timed test or past-paper section · 30 min marking it and updating the error log | 2–3 hours: one timed section, marked; catch up | | Sunday | 45 min weekly review and plan; the rest of the day free | 45 min weekly review and plan; homework | :::exam Plan around the exam timetable When the timetable is published, mark every paper on your plan. Note which paper comes first in each subject and any days with two papers. Then arrange your last two weeks in the same order, so the paper you sit first gets the first final mock. ::: :::recap - Enter the date of your **first** paper; if the timetable is not out yet, use the earliest date of the exam series window. - Work back from the exam: final revision, then past papers, then learning. Keep about one week in ten as a buffer. - Reality-check the learning weeks: each chapter's study time plus half again for practice, times the number of topics. - If you fall 3 or more weeks behind, decide early: more hours, a later series for one subject, or AS only. - Never shorten phases 4 and 5 to rescue phase 2. - Review every Sunday and re-run the planner once a month. ::: Next: [Phase 1: Fix your foundations](#road.foundations). @chapter road.foundations @title Phase 1: Fix your foundations @level guide @paper All subjects · all boards @time 2–6 weeks (this phase) @summary Every A Level assumes skills from GCSE or IGCSE. This phase checks those skills with a short self-test and repairs the gaps before they slow you down. It also covers the academic English that second-language learners need. :::why Most students who struggle at A Level do not struggle with the new ideas. They struggle because an old skill is shaky: rearranging a formula, handling a negative number, writing a clear paragraph. Every new topic then takes twice as long, and the student concludes "I'm not good at this subject" when the real problem is a two-hour gap from three years ago. A few weeks spent on foundations now saves months later. ::: ## What each A Level assumes Cambridge writes its AS and A Level syllabuses for students who have studied the subject at IGCSE or GCSE (or an equivalent course). You do not need a top grade, but the core skills must be quick and reliable, because at A Level they are tools inside bigger problems, not the problem itself. ### Mathematics, and the maths inside the sciences | Skill | You should be able to… | Repair it here | |---|---|---| | Number | Work with fractions, negative numbers, percentages and ratios without a calculator | [Numbers, fractions and percentages](#math.f.numbers) | | Algebra | Expand and factorise; solve linear and simultaneous equations; rearrange formulas | [Algebra from scratch](#math.f.algebra) | | Powers | Use the laws of indices, simplify surds, work in standard form | [Powers, roots, surds and standard form](#math.f.powers) | | Graphs | Find a gradient, use \(y = mx + c\), plot points and read values from a graph | [Coordinates and straight lines](#math.f.graphs) | | Geometry | Use Pythagoras' theorem, sine, cosine and tangent, angle facts, areas and volumes | [Geometry and basic trigonometry](#math.f.geometry) | ### Physics, Chemistry and Biology The sciences use five maths skills constantly, so check these even if Mathematics is not one of your subjects. - **Units and prefixes:** converting mm to m, kJ to J, \(\mathrm{cm^3}\) to \(\mathrm{dm^3}\), and knowing that \(1\,\mathrm{dm^3} = 1000\,\mathrm{cm^3}\). - **Rearranging:** making any letter the subject of a formula such as \(pV = nRT\) or \(v^2 = u^2 + 2as\). - **Standard form:** writing \(0.000\,045\,6\) as \(4.56 \times 10^{-5}\) and entering it correctly on a calculator. - **Significant figures:** giving an answer to the same number of significant figures as the data, usually 2 or 3. - **Graphs:** choosing scales, drawing a line of best fit, and finding a gradient from a large triangle.
