Each science also has its own starting knowledge: atoms, ions and equations in Chemistry; forces, energy and circuits in Physics; cells, organs and basic genetics in Biology. Check and repair these with [Physics from zero](#phys.f.basics), [Chemistry from zero](#chem.f.basics) and [Biology from zero](#bio.f.basics). ### Business, Economics and other essay subjects Essay subjects assume you can read a long case study quickly, pick out the useful facts and numbers, calculate a percentage change, and write a clear paragraph that makes one point and explains it. No prior Business or Economics course is needed, but if these skills feel slow, start with [Business from zero](#bus.f.basics) and [Writing top-band business answers](#bus.writing). ## The ten-minute self-check Do these without a calculator or notes. Give yourself one mark for each fully correct answer. Score 8 or more and you can start phase 2; otherwise, repair the skills you missed first, using the links above. :::try Foundation self-check (Mathematics and sciences) Q: Work out \(\tfrac{2}{3} + \tfrac{3}{4}\). A: Use a common denominator of 12: \(\tfrac{8}{12} + \tfrac{9}{12} = \tfrac{17}{12}\), which is \(1\tfrac{5}{12}\). Q: Expand and simplify \((2x - 3)(x + 4)\). A: \(2x^2 + 8x - 3x - 12 = 2x^2 + 5x - 12\). Q: Factorise \(x^2 - 7x + 12\). A: Two numbers that multiply to 12 and add to \(-7\) are \(-3\) and \(-4\), so \((x - 3)(x - 4)\). Q: Make \(u\) the subject of \(v^2 = u^2 + 2as\). A: \(u^2 = v^2 - 2as\), so \(u = \pm\sqrt{v^2 - 2as}\). Q: Solve the simultaneous equations \(2x + y = 7\) and \(x - y = 2\). A: Adding them gives \(3x = 9\), so \(x = 3\). Then \(y = 7 - 2(3) = 1\). Q: Simplify \(\dfrac{x^5 \times x^{-2}}{x^2}\). A: Add the powers when multiplying and subtract when dividing: \(x^{5 - 2 - 2} = x^1 = x\). Q: Write \(0.000\,045\,6\) in standard form, and give \(0.004\,562\) to 2 significant figures. A: \(4.56 \times 10^{-5}\) and \(0.0046\). Q: Convert 250 mm to metres, 3.5 kW to watts, and \(250\,\mathrm{cm^3}\) to \(\mathrm{dm^3}\). A: \(0.25\,\mathrm{m}\), \(3500\,\mathrm{W}\) and \(0.25\,\mathrm{dm^3}\) (because \(1\,\mathrm{dm^3} = 1000\,\mathrm{cm^3}\)). Q: Find the gradient and the \(y\)-intercept of the line \(2y - 6x = 8\). A: Rearrange to \(y = 3x + 4\): the gradient is 3 and the line crosses the \(y\)-axis at \((0, 4)\). Q: A price rises from $40 to $46. Find the percentage increase. A: The increase is $6, and \(\tfrac{6}{40} \times 100 = 15\%\). ::: For essay subjects, the check is a list of "I can" statements. Be honest: tick one only if you could do it today, under time pressure. - I can read a one-page article in English in under five minutes and summarise it in three sentences. - I can write a paragraph that makes one point, explains why, and gives an example. - I can calculate a percentage change and say what it means in words. - I can read a simple table or chart and describe the trend with numbers. - I can define ten basic terms in my subject (for Business: profit, revenue, costs, market, stakeholder and so on) in one sentence each. ## Academic English for second-language learners Every paper is set and marked in English, and many students who know the science well lose marks to language. The good news: exam English is a small, learnable language of its own. - **Learn the command words.** "Describe" (say what happens) and "explain" (say why it happens) earn different marks. See [Command words decoded](#road.commands). - **Keep a vocabulary notebook.** Four columns: the English term, the word in your own language, the definition in English, and an example sentence. Learn definitions as fixed phrases, exactly as the syllabus words them. - **Write short, complete sentences.** Examiners reward correct science and clear reasoning, not elegant style. One idea per sentence is safer than one long sentence with three ideas. - **Read in English every day.** Fifteen minutes of your textbook or a good subject website builds reading speed, which matters in long case-study and data questions. - **Use the [glossary](#tools.glossary)** in this guide: every key term from every chapter is collected there. | English term | Turkish | Definition in English | |---|---|---| | gradient | eğim | the change in \(y\) divided by the change in \(x\) | | dynamic equilibrium | dinamik denge | forward and reverse reactions happen at equal rates, so concentrations stay constant | | demand | talep | the quantity buyers are willing and able to buy at each price | | evaluate | değerlendirmek | judge the strengths and weaknesses, then reach a conclusion | :::warn "I got an A at IGCSE, so I can skip this" Skills fade, especially over a long summer, and A Level needs them to be fast as well as correct. Do the self-check anyway: it takes ten minutes, and it either confirms you are ready or finds a gap while it is still cheap to fix. ::: :::exam Foundation skills carry marks in every paper A correct method with a slip in rearranging, a wrong power of ten or a missing unit can still lose the final accuracy mark. In Cambridge Mathematics, a non-exact answer not given to 3 significant figures (unless the question asks otherwise) can also cost marks. Examiners usually accept small spelling mistakes, but not when the misspelt word could be another technical term, such as ethane and ethene, or mitosis and meiosis. ::: ## How long should phase 1 take? | Your self-check result | Plan | |---|---| | 8–10, and quick | About 2 weeks: repair anything you missed and read the "from zero" chapter for each science, then start phase 2 | | 6–7 | 3–4 weeks: work through the foundation chapters for every skill you missed, then redo the self-check | | 5 or fewer, or no IGCSE in the subject | 5–6 weeks: work through all the foundation chapters for that subject in order | | Any score, if English is your second language | Add 15 minutes of subject reading in English every day, all the way to the exam | :::tip Fix the core now, the rest just in time You do not need to repair everything before you start learning. Fix the core skills now (algebra, rearranging, units, paragraph writing), then repair smaller gaps as topics need them. Every chapter in this guide begins with a "Before you start" line that links to exactly what it assumes. ::: :::recap - Most A Level difficulty comes from shaky GCSE/IGCSE skills, not from the new ideas. - Maths skills to check: number, algebra, powers and standard form, graphs, geometry and trigonometry. - Science skills to check: units and prefixes, rearranging, standard form, significant figures, graphs. - Essay subjects need fast reading, clear paragraphs and confident use of data. - Score 8 out of 10 on the self-check before moving on; repair what you missed with the foundation chapters. - Second-language learners: learn the command words, keep a four-column vocabulary notebook and read in English daily. - Phase 1 takes 2–6 weeks, depending on your score. ::: Next: [Phase 2: Learn the content](#road.learn). @chapter road.learn @title Phase 2: Learn the content @level guide @paper All subjects · all boards @time About half of your preparation time @summary How to work through the syllabus so that the ideas stay: studying each chapter actively, turning the syllabus into a checklist, making notes that help, choosing a textbook, keeping a steady pace, and getting unstuck. :::why Phase 2 is the longest part of the road, and the easiest to get wrong. Reading a chapter is not the same as learning it. You have learned a topic when you can explain it and use it without looking, a week later. Everything in this phase is designed to get you to that point with as little wasted time as possible. ::: ## How to study one chapter actively Passive study (reading, highlighting, copying) feels comfortable because the material looks familiar while it is in front of you. Active study makes your brain produce the ideas itself, which is harder in the moment and far more effective. Use this routine for every chapter in this guide or your textbook. :::steps 1. **Preview (5 minutes).** Read the summary, the headings and the key-term cards. Ask yourself what the topic is for. 2. **Study one section at a time.** At the end of each section, look away and explain it aloud or on paper in your own words. 3. **Work through each worked example with the solution covered.** Attempt each step before you reveal it. 4. **Answer the practice questions without notes**, then check them against the full answers and mark honestly. 5. **Write your notes from memory**, then compare them with the chapter and fill the gaps in a different colour. 6. **Finish with the quick check**, and make flashcards from the key terms and formulas. ::: Work in focused blocks of 25–50 minutes with a short break between them, and keep your phone in another room. The timer below helps. :::html
::: ## Turn the syllabus into a checklist The syllabus for your exam year is the official list of everything that can be examined. Download it free from your board's website. In the subject content section, each topic is broken into numbered **learning outcomes**, short statements of what you must be able to do. Copy them into a tracker, in a notebook or a spreadsheet, and colour each one as you go. | Learning outcome (Quadratics, Cambridge Paper 1, in our words) | Learned | Practised | Exam-ready | |---|---|---|---| | Complete the square and use it to find the vertex | Yes | Yes | Green | | Use the discriminant to decide how many real roots there are | Yes | Yes | Amber | | Solve quadratic inequalities | Yes | No | Red | | Solve one linear and one quadratic equation simultaneously | No | No | Red | - **Red:** not learned yet, or you cannot do it even with notes. - **Amber:** you can do it with notes, or slowly. - **Green:** you can do it without notes, under time pressure, at least a week after learning it. The tracker becomes the backbone of your whole preparation. In phase 5 it tells you exactly which topics need work. ## Making notes that help Good notes are short, written partly from memory, and built for testing yourself later. Three formats work well. Use whichever suits the topic. | Method | How it works | Best for | |---|---|---| | Cornell notes | A page split into a cue column, a notes column and a summary strip | First notes on a topic: definitions, explanations, methods | | Concept map | The main idea in the centre, with branches and labelled links | Connections: organic reactions, the cardiovascular system, macroeconomic policy | | One-page summary | One sheet per topic: key terms, formulas, one diagram, one worked example, common mistakes | The end of a topic, and final revision | :::html ::: :::warn Notes are not the goal Beautiful notes with colours and perfect handwriting take hours and teach little. If you are copying sentences from the textbook, stop. Close the book, write what you remember, then check. Notes are a tool for testing yourself, not a product. ::: ## Choosing a textbook One good textbook per subject, this guide and the past papers are enough. Collecting more resources feels productive, but it is usually a way of avoiding practice. - **Cambridge:** look for books that carry Cambridge's endorsement mark on the cover. Cambridge lists endorsed resources on its website, from publishers such as Cambridge University Press and Hodder Education. - **Edexcel IAL:** Pearson publishes its own student books for the IAL specifications. - **AQA and OCR:** each board approves or endorses textbooks from several publishers for its own specifications. - **Check the syllabus years.** A book written for an older syllabus can miss new topics or include ones that were removed. Compare its contents with the current syllabus before you buy, especially second-hand. ## Pacing: how fast should you go? Your plan from the [study planner](#road.planner) gives you a number of learning weeks. Divide the topics by the weeks to get your weekly target. For Cambridge, the number of topics in the syllabus is: | Subject (Cambridge) | Topics or sections | Topics per week with 20 learning weeks | |---|---|---| | Mathematics 9709 (Pure 1, Pure 3, Mechanics, Probability & Statistics 1) | 8 + 9 + 5 + 5 = 27 | about 1.4 | | Physics 9702 | 25 (1–11 AS, 12–25 A Level) | about 1.3 | | Chemistry 9701 | 37 (1–22 AS, 23–37 A Level) | about 1.9 | | Biology 9700 | 19 (1–11 AS, 12–19 A Level) | about 1 | Topics differ in size, so treat these as averages. Study all your subjects every week rather than one subject per month: switching between subjects is tiring at first, but it gives each topic time to settle and keeps every subject fresh. If a topic takes more than one and a half times its budget, mark it amber, move on, and come back to it in your buffer week. ## Flashcards as you go Make flashcards on the day you finish each chapter, while you still know what matters. Aim for 5–15 cards per chapter: - **one fact per card**, written as a question: "What is the discriminant of \(ax^2 + bx + c\)?" - **definitions** word for word on the back, exactly as the syllabus uses them; - **"why" questions** as well as "what" questions: "Why does the rate of reaction increase with temperature?" Paper cards in a box or a free flashcard app both work. How and when to review them is in [Phase 3](#road.practice). ## The weekly review Once a week, for 30–45 minutes, step back from new content. :::steps 1. Test yourself for 15 minutes, without notes, on this week's topics and one older topic. 2. Update the colours in your tracker. 3. Read your error log: is any mistake appearing again and again? 4. Compare where you are with your plan, and write next week's topics into your timetable. ::: ## When you are stuck Being stuck is a normal part of learning, not a sign that you cannot do the subject. Work down this list. 1. **Slow down.** Reread the section, then copy out the worked example line by line, asking why each step follows from the one before. 2. **Go back one step.** Most stuck points are really an earlier gap. Follow the "Before you start" link at the top of the chapter. 3. **Find a different explanation:** your textbook, a video, or a friend who explains it in other words. 4. **Ask a precise question.** "I don't understand moles" is hard to answer; "I don't see why we divide by 2 in line 3" is easy. Teachers, study groups and online forums all respond better to precise questions. 5. **Set a time limit.** After 30 minutes stuck, mark the topic red, move on, and return in two days. Sleep often does the work for you. :::tip Explain it to a younger student If you can explain a topic simply to someone two years younger, without notes, you understand it. If you get stuck halfway, you have found exactly the part to study again. ::: :::exam Learn definitions word for word Definitions are quick marks, and mark schemes look for precise key words. "Acceleration is the rate of change of velocity" scores; "acceleration is how fast something speeds up" does not. Put every definition from the syllabus and from this guide's key-term cards onto flashcards, and practise writing them out exactly. ::: :::recap - Learning means being able to explain and use an idea without looking, a week later. - Study each chapter actively: preview, explain each section, attempt worked examples before reading them, answer questions without notes. - Turn the syllabus learning outcomes into a red/amber/green tracker. - Use Cornell notes, concept maps or one-page summaries; write notes from memory. - Use one endorsed textbook per subject that matches your syllabus years. - Pace yourself: divide topics by learning weeks, and study every subject every week. - Make flashcards on the day you finish a chapter, and review your week every weekend. ::: Next: [Phase 3: Practise and test yourself](#road.practice). @chapter road.practice @title Phase 3: Practise and test yourself @level guide @paper All subjects · all boards @time Alongside phase 2, then 3–6 weeks @summary Practice turns understanding into marks. This phase uses retrieval practice, spaced repetition, flashcards and mixed questions, with an error log that makes sure each mistake happens only once. :::why You can understand a topic perfectly on Monday and be unable to answer a question on it by Friday. Forgetting is normal, and it happens to everyone. The cure is not more reading: it is testing yourself, spread out over time. This phase runs alongside phase 2 from the first week, and becomes your main activity once all the content is learned. ::: ## Retrieval practice: test, don't reread :::def Retrieval practice Learning by recalling information from memory, for example by answering questions or writing down everything you remember, instead of reading the material again. ::: Every time you pull an idea out of memory, the memory becomes stronger and easier to find next time. Rereading does not do this, because the answer is already in front of you. A large 2013 review of ten common study techniques rated practice testing and spaced practice as the two most useful, and rereading and highlighting among the least useful. Ways to practise retrieval: - **Blank page:** write everything you remember about a topic on a blank sheet, then check it against your notes and add what you missed in a different colour. - **Flashcards**, answered aloud or on paper before you turn the card over. - **Quizzes:** the quick check at the end of each chapter, and the mixed [practice quizzes](#practice.quiz). - **Exam-style questions**, from your textbook, this guide and past papers. ## Spaced repetition: when to review :::def Spaced repetition Reviewing material at increasing intervals (for example after 1, 3, 7, 14 and 30 days), so that each review happens just as the memory starts to fade. ::: :::html ::: Review a topic about **1, 3, 7, 14 and 30 days** after you first learn it, then once a month until the exam. For example, for a topic learned on Monday 12 October 2026: | Review | Day | Date | What to do (5–15 minutes) | |---|---|---|---| | 1st | 1 | Tuesday 13 October | Blank page, then check | | 2nd | 3 | Thursday 15 October | Flashcards for the topic | | 3rd | 7 | Monday 19 October | 3–4 exam-style questions | | 4th | 14 | Monday 26 October | Quiz or mixed questions | | 5th | 30 | Wednesday 11 November | A past-paper question, timed | Every review is a test, never a reread. If a review goes badly, restart the cycle for that topic from day 1. Write the review dates in your diary on the day you learn the topic, so you never have to remember them. ## Flashcards that work The **Leitner system** organises paper flashcards in five boxes. Box 1 is reviewed every day, box 2 every 3 days, box 3 every week, box 4 every 2 weeks and box 5 every month. A card you answer correctly moves up one box; a card you get wrong goes back to box 1. Flashcard apps such as Anki do the same scheduling automatically. - **Answer before you flip.** Say or write the full answer first. A vague "I knew that" counts as wrong. - **Be strict.** Half right is wrong for a definition, because the mark scheme wants the key words. - **Mix card types:** definitions, formulas, "why" questions, and blank diagrams to label. ## Interleaving: mix your topics :::def Interleaving Practising a mixture of different topics or question types in one session, so that you must decide which method each question needs, instead of practising one method many times in a row. ::: | | Blocked practice | Interleaved practice | |---|---|---| | What it looks like | 20 questions on completing the square | 12 questions mixing quadratics, functions, series and trigonometry | | How it feels | Smooth and fast | Slower and harder | | What it trains | Repeating a method you already know is needed | Choosing the right method, which is what the exam demands | | When to use it | The first practice on a new topic | Everything after that | Exam questions never tell you which chapter they come from. Once you have learned three or four topics, make most of your practice interleaved. ## Topic questions After each topic, climb this ladder: textbook exercises, then the practice questions in this guide, then **past-paper questions on that topic**. Collections of Cambridge questions sorted by topic ("topical past papers") are widely available, and they let you practise a topic in exam style long before you sit full papers. Aim for at least 10–15 exam-style questions on each topic, more for big topics, before you call it green. ## The error log The error log is the most valuable document you will make. Every mark you lose goes into it, with the reason and a rule to stop it happening again. | Date | Question | Topic | Marks lost | What went wrong | Type | Rule for next time | Redo on | |---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---| | 12 Oct | Maths practice Q4 | Quadratics | 2 | Used \(-b = -4\) when \(b = -4\) | Careless slip | Write \(a\), \(b\), \(c\) with their signs before substituting | 19 Oct | | 14 Oct | Physics topic test Q2 | Kinematics | 2 | Did not convert \(\mathrm{km\,h^{-1}}\) to \(\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\) | Method | Convert every quantity to SI units first | 21 Oct | | 15 Oct | Chemistry worksheet Q5 | Moles | 3 | Ignored the 1 : 2 ratio in the equation | Knowledge | Always use the mole ratio from the balanced equation | 22 Oct | | 20 Oct | Business 12-mark question | Motivation | 4 | No judgement at the end | Exam technique | End with a justified conclusion that answers the question | 27 Oct | Use five types: **knowledge** (you did not know it), **method** (you knew the topic but chose or applied the wrong method), **reading** (you misread the question), **careless slip**, and **exam technique** (timing, missing working, no evaluation). Once a week, read the whole log and count the types. If most are knowledge errors, go back to phase 2 for those topics. If most are careless slips, slow down and check every answer. Then redo each logged question on its redo date, without looking at your old answer. ## Calculation subjects and essay subjects :::cols :::col Calculations (Maths, Physics, Chemistry) - Do many questions: volume matters. - Write full working, as in the exam: method marks need visible steps. - Check units and significant figures at the end of every answer. - Redo wrong questions from a blank page, not by reading the solution. - Time yourself from early on: about 1.5 minutes per mark in Cambridge Maths. ::: :::col Essays (Business, Economics, long-answer Biology) - Plan every answer for 3–5 minutes before writing. - Build each paragraph: knowledge, application, analysis, evaluation. - Write timed answers, then mark them against the mark scheme's levels. - Collect strong chains of reasoning ("this leads to… which means…"). - See [Writing top-band business answers](#bus.writing). ::: ::: ## Measuring readiness Test each topic with mixed questions a week or more after learning it, and record your score. | Score | Meaning | What to do | |---|---|---| | 80% or more | Exam-ready | Mark it green; review it once a month | | 60–79% | Nearly there | Mark it amber; work through its error-log entries and do more topic questions | | Below 60% | Not secure yet | Mark it red; go back to the chapter (phase 2) | You are ready to give past papers most of your time when your average across mixed sets is 70% or more, no topic is red, and the same mistakes have stopped appearing in your error log. :::tip Start every session with retrieval Spend the first 10 minutes of each study session on questions or flashcards from older topics, before any new work. It warms you up, and it builds your spaced reviews into every day without extra planning. ::: :::warn Looking at the answer too soon When a question gets hard, it is tempting to look at the solution after a minute. Struggle for at least 5–10 minutes first: the effort of trying is what makes the method stick. If you do look, close the solution and redo the whole question from a blank page. ::: :::exam Practise in exam format from the start Write practice answers exactly as you would in the exam: full working, units, sentences rather than notes, and diagrams labelled. Habits formed in practice are the ones you will use under pressure, so make them exam habits from the first week. ::: :::recap - Retrieval practice (testing yourself) beats rereading; use blank pages, flashcards, quizzes and exam-style questions. - Review each topic about 1, 3, 7, 14 and 30 days after learning it, then monthly; every review is a test. - Use a Leitner box or a flashcard app, and be strict with yourself. - Interleave: once you know a few topics, mix them in every practice set. - Keep an error log with a type and a rule for every lost mark, and redo each question a week later. - Green at 80% or more on mixed questions a week after learning; move on to past papers at a 70% average with no red topics. ::: Next: [Phase 4: Past papers and mark schemes](#road.pastpapers). @chapter road.pastpapers @title Phase 4: Past papers and mark schemes @level guide @paper All subjects · all boards @time 8–12 weeks @summary Where to find official past papers, mark schemes, examiner reports and grade thresholds; how many papers to do and in what order; how to sit them under timed conditions and mark them honestly; and the redo cycle that turns each lost mark into a gained one. :::why Past papers are the closest thing to the real exam that exists. They show you the style of the questions, how long you really need, and the exact ideas that earn marks. Students who do many past papers, mark them honestly and learn from every mistake usually outscore students who simply know more content. ::: ## Where to find them Use the official sources first. Each board publishes four kinds of document for each exam series: **question papers**, **mark schemes**, **examiner reports** (what candidates did well and badly) and **grade thresholds** or grade boundaries (the raw marks needed for each grade). | Board | Where to look | Notes | |---|---|---| | Cambridge International | The syllabus page on [cambridgeinternational.org](https://www.cambridgeinternational.org) | Cambridge publishes some past papers on its website. The full archive is on the School Support Hub, which registered schools use; private candidates can ask their exam centre | | Pearson Edexcel (IAL) | Your subject's page on [qualifications.pearson.com](https://qualifications.pearson.com) | Papers, mark schemes and examiner reports under the exam materials; grade boundaries on their own page | | AQA | [aqa.org.uk](https://www.aqa.org.uk) | Past papers and mark schemes for each specification | | OCR | [ocr.org.uk](https://www.ocr.org.uk) | Past papers in the assessment section of each qualification | With every board, the newest series is sometimes available only to teachers for a while. Many other websites copy the official files. If you use one, make sure each paper comes with its matching mark scheme. ### Reading Cambridge file names Cambridge files have names like **9709_s25_qp_12**. Once you can read them, finding the right paper takes seconds. | Part | Meaning | |---|---| | 9709 | The syllabus code (Mathematics) | | s25 | The series and year: s = May/June, w = October/November, m = February/March; 25 = 2025 | | qp, ms, er, gt | Question paper, mark scheme, examiner report, grade thresholds | | 12 | Paper 1, variant 2 | Cambridge sets several versions (**variants**) of most papers in each series for different time zones. That is why there are so many papers to practise with: a few recent years give you 20 or more versions of some components. ## How many, and in what order? Aim for **8–12 full papers per component** by exam day, plus topic questions, and more for components you find hard. Use them in this order: 1. **Older papers** (about 6–10 years old): cut into topic questions during phase 3. 2. **Middle years:** full timed papers in phase 4. 3. **The two or three most recent series:** saved for full mocks in phase 5. Before you start, read the "changes to the syllabus" page at the front of your syllabus. Papers written before a syllabus change can include topics that are no longer examined, and miss new ones. Skip those questions, or replace them with questions from this guide. ## Sitting a paper under timed conditions :::steps 1. Choose the same time of day as the real exam, a quiet desk, and only the permitted equipment: pens, pencil, ruler, an allowed calculator, and the formula list or data booklet your board provides (for Cambridge Mathematics, the list called MF19). 2. Put your phone in another room and set a timer for the real length of the paper. 3. Read the front cover as if it were the real exam. 4. Work to time. Cambridge Mathematics Paper 1 has 75 marks in 1 hour 50 minutes, so allow about 1.5 minutes per mark. 5. When time runs out, draw a line. You may finish in a different colour to see what more time would give, but count only the marks above the line. ::: ## Marking honestly Mark the paper the same day, or the next, with the official mark scheme. Be strict: if your answer does not clearly contain the point the mark scheme describes, do not give yourself the mark. Generous self-marking only hides the problems you need to fix. Mathematics mark schemes use a short code. Learn it, because it tells you exactly how marks are earned: | Code | Meaning | |---|---| | M1 | A method mark, for a correct method applied to the problem | | A1 | An accuracy mark: only possible if the related M mark is earned | | B1 | An independent mark for a correct answer or statement | | FT | Follow through: credit for correct work that uses your own earlier wrong answer | | CAO | Correct answer only | | OE | Or equivalent: another correct form of the answer is accepted | | AWRT | Answer which rounds to the value given | | AG | Answer given in the question: every step must be shown | Science mark schemes list the acceptable answers for each mark point, and essay mark schemes describe **levels**: what an answer must show to reach each band of marks. Then turn your raw mark into a grade with the grade thresholds for that series and variant. Thresholds change from series to series because some papers are harder than others, so always use the matching one. Aim to be comfortably above your target grade, not just on it. :::exam Why the method mark matters An A mark depends on its M mark. A correct final answer from a wrong or invisible method can score nothing, while a wrong final answer from a correct method can still score most of the marks. In "show that" questions, the answer is printed (the mark scheme labels it AG), so all the marks are for the steps. Always write your working where the examiner can follow it. ::: ## Read the examiner report For every paper you sit, read the examiner report's comments on it. Examiners describe the common errors, the misunderstandings they saw most often, and what the best answers did. Ten minutes with the report often explains a lost mark better than the mark scheme does. Copy anything that applies to you into your error log. ## Topic by topic, or full papers? | | Topic-by-topic questions | Full papers | |---|---|---| | When | Phase 3 and the start of phase 4 | Most of phase 4, and all of phase 5 | | What it trains | Depth in one topic; finding gaps quickly | Timing, stamina, switching between topics, choosing methods | | The risk | The topic heading tells you which method to use | One paper cannot cover every topic | Use both. Start phase 4 with one full paper per component per week, plus topic sets for your weakest areas. Build up to two or three full papers a week in the last month of the phase. ## The redo cycle :::steps 1. **Sit** the paper, timed. 2. **Mark** it honestly, the same day. 3. **Log** every lost mark in your error log, with its type and a rule for next time. 4. **Relearn:** for a knowledge gap, go back to the chapter; for a method gap, do three to five similar questions. 5. **Redo** every question that lost marks, from a blank page, a week later. 6. **Track** your scores for each component, with the grade thresholds next to them, so you can see the trend. ::: :::warn Do not memorise mark-scheme wording without understanding it Mark schemes are written for examiners, not as model answers. Phrases learned by heart without understanding end up in the wrong context, where they earn nothing. Questions are reworded every year, and the mark is for the idea used correctly. Learn why each point earns its mark, then practise explaining it in your own words while keeping the key technical terms. ::: :::tip Keep the newest papers for later Do not use the two or three most recent series before phase 5. They are the best guide to your own exam, so save them for full mocks under real conditions. ::: :::recap - Use official sources: Cambridge (public website and the School Support Hub through your centre), Pearson, AQA and OCR, with mark schemes, examiner reports and grade thresholds. - Read Cambridge file names: syllabus, series and year, document type, paper and variant (9709_s25_qp_12). - Aim for 8–12 full papers per component: old papers as topic questions, middle years timed, newest saved for mocks. - Sit papers in real conditions and to time: about 1.5 minutes per mark in Cambridge Maths Paper 1. - Mark strictly; learn M, A, B, FT and AG; compare your mark with the thresholds for that exact paper. - Read the examiner report for every paper, and follow the redo cycle: sit, mark, log, relearn, redo, track. - Understand mark-scheme points; never memorise their wording blindly. ::: Next: [Phase 5: Final revision](#road.final). @chapter road.final @title Phase 5: Final revision @level guide @paper All subjects · all boards @time The last 6–8 weeks @summary A week-by-week plan for the last eight weeks before your first paper, with daily timetables, how to run your own mocks, how to condense your notes, formula practice, sleep, and the habits to avoid. :::why The last eight weeks decide more grades than any other part of the course. By now you know most of the content; this phase makes it reliable under pressure. Done well, it is calm and organised: you know exactly what to do each day, and each week you can see the gaps closing. ::: ## The last eight weeks, week by week Count the weeks back from your **first** paper. If you have only six weeks, combine weeks 8 and 7, and weeks 6 and 5. | Weeks to go | Main focus | Full papers per subject | Also this week | |---|---|---|---| | 8 | Audit: update your tracker, list every red and amber topic, plan the eight weeks | 1, as a baseline | Get the final exam timetable and mark every paper on your plan | | 7 | Red topics, first half: relearn, then practise | 1 | Condensed notes for each red topic | | 6 | Red topics, second half | 1–2 | Start daily formula and definition drills | | 5 | Mock week: a full set of papers in exam conditions | A full set | Mark everything; update the error log | | 4 | Fix the mock: relearn every topic that lost marks, then amber topics | 2 | Finish a one-page summary for every topic | | 3 | Timed papers from recent series | 2–3 | The redo cycle after every paper | | 2 | Final mocks with the newest papers, in the order of your exams | 2–3 | Shift your sleep to fit the exam start times | | 1 | Light review: summaries, flashcards, error-log rules; nothing new | Parts of papers only | Logistics: route, equipment, ID, statement of entry | ## The last two weeks - **Follow the timetable.** The subject you sit first gets the first mocks and the most review time in the final days. - **Sit papers at exam times.** If your papers start in the morning, do your mocks in the morning, so your brain is used to working hard at that hour. - **Read your rules daily.** Read the "rule for next time" column of your error log every day. It is a personal list of the traps you fall into. - **Make one sheet per paper:** the formulas, definitions and mistakes that matter most for that paper. Read it the evening before. - **Plan the gaps between papers.** With three days between two papers, for example: one timed paper on day 1, weak topics on day 2, light review on day 3. ## Daily timetable templates On a full revision day (study leave, weekends, or every day for a private candidate): | Time | Activity | |---|---| | 08:30–09:00 | Flashcards and error-log rules | | 09:00–10:50 | A timed paper (subject A) | | 10:50–11:10 | Break, away from your desk | | 11:10–12:30 | Mark the paper and log every lost mark | | 12:30–13:30 | Lunch, away from screens | | 13:30–15:00 | Relearn the topics the morning's paper exposed | | 15:00–15:20 | Break and some movement | | 15:20–16:50 | Subject B: topic questions on a weak topic | | 16:50–19:00 | Exercise, free time, dinner | | 19:00–20:00 | Subject C: condensed notes and flashcards | | From 20:00 | Free time; screens off an hour before bed | That is about 7.5 hours of real work. More than this, day after day, usually means less is learned per hour. On a school day, add about two hours after lessons: | Time | Activity | |---|---| | 17:00–17:45 | Topic questions on a red or amber topic | | 18:00–18:45 | One timed section of a past paper | | 19:45–20:30 | Mark it, update the error log, 20 minutes of flashcards | ## Running your own mocks If your school runs mock exams, treat them as the real thing. If you study alone, run your own: - the same length, the same time of day and the same rules as the real exam; - a clear table, no notes, phone in another room, and if possible someone in the room acting as the invigilator; - the whole set of papers over a few days, in the same order as your real timetable; - marking within 24 hours, followed by the redo cycle from [Phase 4](#road.pastpapers). A disappointing mock is useful: it shows you the problems while there is still time to fix them. Treat the score as information, not as a judgement of you. ## Condensing your notes Condensing works because every step forces you to choose what matters and to recall it. 1. **Chapter notes** from phase 2. 2. **One page per topic:** write it from memory first, then check and fill the gaps. 3. **One page per paper:** only the formulas, definitions and traps for that paper. 4. **A final card per paper** to read on the evening before. ## Formulas, definitions and data Get a clean copy of what your board provides in the exam: for Cambridge, the formula list MF19 for Mathematics, the data and formulae pages printed in each Physics paper, and the Data Booklet for Chemistry. Learn what is on it, and where, so you never waste time searching. Then **memorise everything else.** Each day in the last three weeks, write out every formula and definition for one paper on a blank page in five minutes, check it, and correct it. Our sheets help: [Maths](#tools.f.math), [Physics](#tools.f.phys), [Chemistry](#tools.f.chem), [Biology](#tools.f.bio) and [Business, economics and accounting](#tools.f.bus). ## Sleep, food and exercise Your brain stores the day's learning while you sleep, so sleep is part of revision, not time taken away from it. Most teenagers need 8–10 hours a night. An all-nighter before a paper makes you slower and more error-prone the next day. Two weeks before the exams, move your bedtime and wake-up time so that you are alert at the time your papers start. A daily walk or other exercise helps you sleep and manage stress, and avoiding caffeine after mid-afternoon protects your sleep. There is more in [Motivation, sleep and stress](#road.wellbeing). ## What not to do | Don't | Do instead | |---|---| | Start new textbooks, courses or apps | Stick to your notes, this guide and past papers | | Reread your notes for hours | Test yourself: papers, flashcards, blank pages | | Revise only your favourite topics | Work from your red and amber list | | Sit papers without marking them | Mark every paper within 24 hours | | Use the newest papers too early | Save them for the last three weeks | | Stay up late to "finish" a topic | Keep the same bedtime every night | | Compare hours with friends or on social media | Compare your scores with your own scores last week | :::tip Revise by question, not by chapter In the final weeks, start from questions rather than from your notes. Do a question; if you cannot, open the chapter, fix that one gap, and try a similar question. Your time goes exactly where your marks are being lost. ::: :::warn The last-week panic switch In the final week, many students abandon their plan and start rereading everything from the beginning. It feels safe but achieves little, and it leaves no time for the subject you sit first. Trust the plan you made when you were calm: light review, error-log rules, sleep. ::: :::exam Turn your mock into a timing plan After each mock, note how long each question took. Then write a timing plan for each paper: for Cambridge Mathematics Paper 1 (75 marks in 1 hour 50 minutes), about 1.5 minutes per mark, so roughly 45 minutes for the first 30 marks. Practise the plan in your final mocks so that pacing feels automatic on the day. ::: :::recap - Count back from your first paper; use the 8-week table, merging weeks if you have only six. - Weeks 8–6 for red topics, week 5 a full mock, week 4 fixing the mock, weeks 3–2 timed papers and final mocks, week 1 light review. - Sit papers at real exam times, mark within 24 hours, and read your error-log rules daily. - Condense: chapter notes, one page per topic, one page per paper, one card per paper. - Know what is on your formula list or data booklet, and memorise everything else. - Sleep 8–10 hours; shift your bedtime to the exam timetable two weeks ahead. - No new resources, no all-nighters, no last-week panic. ::: Next: [Phase 6: Exam day, results and resits](#road.examday). @chapter road.examday @title Phase 6: Exam day, results and resits @level guide @paper All subjects · all boards @time Read it a week before your first paper @summary Checklists for the night before and the morning of each exam; how to read the paper, manage your time and keep going when you are stuck; and what happens next: results day, enquiries about results, resits, UCAS Clearing and a plan B. :::why By exam day the learning is done, but marks can still be lost to things that have nothing to do with knowledge: a forgotten calculator, a misread question, fifteen minutes stuck on one part. This chapter removes those risks. It then walks you through what happens after the last paper, including what to do if results day does not go to plan. ::: ## The night before - **Check the details** on your **statement of entry**, the document from your centre that lists your candidate number and each paper's date and start time. Confirm the time and the room, and set two alarms. - **Pack your bag:** - photo ID (a passport or national ID card): private candidates will not be allowed in without it; - your statement of entry; - a permitted calculator with fresh batteries; - at least three black pens, two pencils, an eraser, a sharpener and a ruler, plus a protractor and compasses for Mathematics; - a clear pencil case and a clear water bottle, if your centre allows them. - **Check your calculator is allowed.** Rules differ by board and subject. For example, Cambridge Mathematics does not allow graphic calculators or calculators that can do algebra. - **Read your one-page sheet** for the paper, then stop. Do not start anything new. - **Plan your route**, with time to spare for traffic, and go to bed at your normal time. :::warn Pens, pencils and correction fluid Cambridge papers ask for black or dark blue pen, and do not allow erasable pens or correction fluid. Use pencil only for diagrams and graphs, and for multiple-choice answer sheets, which are marked by machine and need a soft pencil. If you make a mistake in pen, cross it out with a single neat line and write the correction next to it. ::: ## The morning - Eat breakfast and drink some water, even if you are nervous. - Arrive at least 30 minutes early. Private candidates should check the arrival time their centre gives. - Take a last look at your one-page sheet, then put it away before you enter the room. - Leave your phone, smartwatch and any other device at home or hand them in as instructed. Having one with you in the exam room can count as malpractice, even if it is switched off. - Go to the toilet before the exam starts. ## In the exam ### Reading the paper 1. Write your name, centre number and candidate number exactly as they appear on your statement of entry. 2. Read the front cover: the number of questions, the total marks, and whether you must answer every question or choose some. 3. If you have time, look through the whole paper for a minute so that nothing surprises you later. 4. Read each question twice. Underline the command word and the key data. 5. Look at the marks for each part and the space given for the answer. Both tell you how much the examiner expects. ### Timing: minutes per mark Divide the time by the total marks to get your pace. For example, Cambridge Mathematics Paper 1 has 75 marks in 1 hour 50 minutes, which is about 1.5 minutes per mark, so a 6-mark question deserves about 9 minutes. | Cambridge paper | Marks | Time | Minutes per mark | |---|---|---|---| | Mathematics Paper 1 or 3 | 75 | 1 h 50 min | about 1.5 | | Mathematics Paper 2, 4, 5 or 6 | 50 | 1 h 15 min | 1.5 | | Physics, Chemistry or Biology Paper 1 (multiple choice) | 40 | 1 h 15 min | just under 2 per question | | Physics, Chemistry or Biology Paper 2 (AS structured) | 60 | 1 h 15 min | 1.25 | | Physics, Chemistry or Biology Paper 4 (A Level structured) | 100 | 2 h | 1.2 | | Business Paper 2 | 60 | 1 h 30 min | 1.5 | | Economics Paper 2 | 60 | 2 h | 2 | To keep 10 minutes for checking in Mathematics Paper 1, work at about 1.3 minutes per mark. Edexcel IAL, AQA and OCR papers have different lengths, so work out your own pace from the front cover of a past paper. :::exam Let the marks guide you The marks for each part tell you what the examiner wants. A 2-mark "explain" question usually needs two separate points, or one point and its reason. A 1-mark "state" question needs a short answer, not a paragraph. For calculations, a part worth 4 or 5 marks needs several clear steps of working, because most of those marks are method marks. ::: ### When you are stuck - **Move on** once you have spent about twice the time the marks deserve. Circle the question number and come back at the end. - **Write what you know.** A formula, a labelled diagram or the first line of working can earn method marks. - **Use answers given in the question.** If you cannot show that \(x = 4\) in part (a), use \(x = 4\) in part (b) anyway: the later marks are still available. - **Never leave a multiple-choice question blank.** No marks are taken away for wrong answers, so eliminate what you can and choose. - **If panic starts,** put your pen down, breathe slowly for thirty seconds, and read the next question. One hard question is only a few marks. - **Need more space?** Use the extra page at the back of the booklet, and write the question number clearly. ### The last ten minutes Check that you answered what was asked ("exact", "in terms of \(\pi\)", "to 3 significant figures"), that every answer has a unit where one is needed, that no part is left blank, and that your multiple-choice answer sheet is complete. ## After each paper Leave the room and do not go through the answers with friends: it only creates worry about marks you can no longer change. Eat, rest, then spend thirty minutes planning for your next paper. If something affected your performance, such as illness, a family emergency or a disturbance in the room, tell your exams officer the same day. Your centre may be able to apply for **special consideration**, but only within a short time after the exam. ## Results day - **When:** Cambridge results for the May/June series come out in August (the June 2026 results were released on 11 August 2026), and results for the October/November series in January. Each Edexcel IAL series has its own results day; check Pearson's key dates. - **How:** your centre gives you your results, and some centres also give you a login to see them online. - **University places:** if you applied through UCAS, check UCAS Hub on results day to see whether your place is confirmed. Before the exams, ask your centre whether it will send your results to UCAS. Read your results calmly, and decide what to do before you phone anyone. ## Enquiries about results If a grade is lower than you expected, your centre can ask the board to check it. Cambridge calls these **enquiries about results**; Pearson, AQA and OCR call them post-results services or reviews of results. The usual options are: - a **clerical re-check** that all the marks were counted and added correctly; - a **review of marking**, with a faster priority service when a university place depends on the result; - a **copy of your marked script**, which shows exactly where you lost marks. This is very useful if you plan to resit. Every service has a fee and a strict deadline, and it must be requested through your centre, including by private candidates. A review looks for marking errors; it is not a second marking, and **marks can go down as well as up**. It is usually worth it only if you believe you are close to a grade boundary. ## Resits | Board | When you can resit | How it works | |---|---|---| | Cambridge International | October/November (results in January), or the next May/June | You normally sit all the papers of the AS or A Level again; ask your centre whether anything can be carried forward, such as an AS result within 13 months | | Pearson Edexcel IAL | January, May/June or October | Modular: you can resit only the units you choose, and your best result for each unit counts | | AQA and OCR (UK A Levels) | May/June only | Linear: you sit all the papers again, a year later | Resit when a university offer or a career depends on the grade, and when you know exactly what went wrong. If your university has already accepted you, the time is usually better spent preparing for the course. If you decide to resit, read the [study planner](#road.planner) example for a resit student, and start straight away. :::tip Write your plan B before results day In July, while you are calm, write down what you will do if you miss your offer by one grade, and by two. On results day you will then follow a plan instead of making big decisions in a panic. ::: ## UCAS Clearing and plan B If you miss the conditions of your offer, do not assume the worst. Universities sometimes accept students who just miss their grades, so check UCAS Hub first, and phone the admissions office if your status is unclear (have your UCAS Personal ID ready). If you have no place, **Clearing** lets you apply for university courses that still have places. You phone universities, and if one makes you an offer, you add it as your Clearing choice in UCAS Hub. Clearing is busiest on A Level results day and in the days after. Other good plan B routes include: - a course with a **foundation year**, which has lower entry requirements; - a **gap year** with resits, then a new application with real grades instead of predicted ones; - universities in Turkey or other countries that accept A Level results; - apprenticeships and work-based routes. There is more on applications in [University applications and admissions tests](#road.university). :::warn Do not grab the first Clearing offer An offer on the phone can feel like relief, but you will spend three or four years on that course. Ask about the course content, the city and the costs, compare two or three options, and talk it through with someone you trust before you accept. ::: :::recap - Night before: statement of entry, photo ID, permitted calculator, black pens, pencils, eraser and ruler; normal bedtime. - Morning: breakfast, arrive at least 30 minutes early, no phone or smartwatch in the room. - Pace yourself by minutes per mark: about 1.5 in Cambridge Maths Paper 1 (75 marks in 1 hour 50 minutes). - Stuck? Move on, write what you know, use given answers, never leave a multiple-choice question blank. - Report illness or disruption to your exams officer the same day. - Cambridge June results come out in August, November results in January. Enquiries about results have fees and short deadlines, and marks can go down. - Resits: Cambridge in November or June, Edexcel IAL in January, June or October (best unit result counts), AQA and OCR in June only. - Write a plan B before results day; Clearing, foundation years and gap years are all good routes. ::: You have reached the end of the road. Go back to [The preparation road at a glance](#road.overview) at any time to check where you are, or read [Studying as a private candidate](#road.private) if you are preparing without a school.
files.content/math-4.md: @group Mechanics @chapter math.m.forces @title Forces and equilibrium @level as @paper CAIE P4 · Edexcel IAL M1 · UK Mechanics @time 5–7 hours @summary Mechanics begins with forces. You will learn to name the forces on an object, draw a force diagram, resolve forces into components, find a resultant, and use equilibrium, friction and Newton's third law on flat surfaces and slopes. :::why Every bridge, crane, climbing rope and roof is designed so that the forces on it balance. If they do not, something moves, usually in the wrong direction. Mechanics is the mathematics of forces and motion. It is a short, high-scoring paper (Cambridge Paper 4) once you can draw a good force diagram, and this chapter teaches the skills that every later mechanics chapter uses: spotting forces, splitting them into components and writing equations. ::: **Before you start**, you need right-angled triangle trigonometry from [Geometry and basic trigonometry](#math.f.geometry) and confident algebra from [Algebra from scratch](#math.f.algebra). Slopes use \(\sin\) and \(\cos\) of angles, as in [Trigonometry](#math.p1.trig). ## Forces and the mechanics model A **force** is a push or a pull. Forces are measured in **newtons** (N). They have both a size and a direction, so they are vectors: a force of 10 N means nothing until you say which way it acts. :::def Force A push or a pull on an object. It is a vector quantity, measured in newtons (N). A resultant force on an object changes its velocity. ::: :::def Resultant force The single force that has the same effect as all the forces on an object together. It is the vector sum of the forces. ::: Real objects are complicated, so mechanics replaces them with simple **models**. The words in an exam question tell you what to ignore. | Word in the question | What it means for your model | |---|---| | particle | All the mass is at one point. Ignore size, shape and spin. | | light (string, rod, pulley) | The mass is zero. A light string has the same tension at both ends. | | inextensible string | It does not stretch, so connected objects move together. | | smooth | No friction. The contact force is perpendicular to the surface. | | rough | Friction may act. | | uniform (rod, plank) | The mass is spread evenly, so the weight acts at the midpoint. | | smooth pulley or peg | A string slides over it freely, so the tension is the same on both sides. | ## The forces you will meet | Force | Usual symbol | Direction | Where it comes from | |---|---|---|---| | Weight | \(W = mg\) | Vertically down | Gravity pulling on mass \(m\) | | Normal reaction | \(R\) | Perpendicular to the surface, away from it | A surface pushing back | | Friction | \(F\) | Along the surface, against sliding | A rough surface | | Tension | \(T\) | Along the string, pulling the object | A taut string or rope | | Thrust | \(T\) | Along a rod, pushing the object | A compressed rod | | Driving force | \(D\) | In the direction of motion | An engine, or a person pushing | | Resistance | \(F\) or a number | Against the motion | Air, water, friction in the machinery | **Mass** \(m\) (in kg) measures how much matter an object has. **Weight** is the force of gravity on it, \(W = mg\). Cambridge tells you to "take \(g = 10\)", so a 5 kg mass has weight \(5 \times 10 = 50\) N. Edexcel and the UK boards use \(g = 9.8\), so the same mass weighs 49 N. Use whichever value the paper gives. :::def Normal reaction The component of the contact force between two surfaces that acts at right angles ("normal") to the surfaces, pushing the object away from the surface. ::: ## Force diagrams A **force diagram** shows every force on one object. Nearly every mechanics mark depends on drawing it carefully, so do it first, every time. :::html ::: :::steps 1. Draw the object as a box or a dot. For a particle, draw every force starting at the same point. 2. Draw the weight \(W = mg\) straight down. 3. Look at everything touching the object. For each surface draw a normal reaction \(R\), and a friction force \(F\) if the surface is rough. For each string draw a tension \(T\) pulling away from the object along the string. 4. Add any given forces (a push, a pull, a driving force) and any resistance. 5. Label every force with its size or a letter, and mark the direction you will take as positive. ::: :::warn Do not invent forces There is no "force of motion" and no "force of the throw" once a ball has left your hand. An object needs a force to change its velocity, not to keep moving. Every force on your diagram must come from something you can name: gravity, a surface, a string, an engine. ::: ## Resolving forces A force at an angle can be replaced by two perpendicular forces, called its **components**, which together have exactly the same effect. Finding them is called **resolving**. :::key Resolving a force A force \(F\) at angle \(\theta\) to a given direction has components - \(F\cos\theta\) **along** that direction, and - \(F\sin\theta\) **perpendicular** to it. The angle must be measured from the direction you are resolving along. If you are given the angle to the other direction, swap \(\cos\) and \(\sin\). ::: :::eg A force of 20 N acts at \(30^\circ\) above the horizontal. Find its horizontal and vertical components. Horizontal: \(20\cos 30^\circ = 17.3\) N. Vertical: \(20\sin 30^\circ = 10.0\) N. **Check:** \(\sqrt{17.3^2 + 10^2} = 20\), as it should be. ::: :::tip Choose your two directions wisely You can resolve in any two perpendicular directions. Choose them so that as many unknown forces as possible lie along one of them. On a slope, resolve along and perpendicular to the slope. With strings, use horizontal and vertical. ::: ## Resultant of several forces To find the resultant: choose \(x\) and \(y\) directions, add up all the \(x\)-components, add up all the \(y\)-components, then combine the two totals with Pythagoras and \(\tan\). :::eg Two forces act on a particle at \(O\). \(P = 12\) N acts along the positive \(x\)-axis. \(Q = 10\) N acts at \(60^\circ\) above the negative \(x\)-axis. Find the magnitude and direction of the resultant. Components of \(Q\): \(x\)-component \(-10\cos 60^\circ = -5\), and \(y\)-component \(10\sin 60^\circ = 8.66\). Totals: \(X = 12 - 5 = 7\) N and \(Y = 8.66\) N. \[\text{magnitude} = \sqrt{7^2 + 8.66^2} = \sqrt{124} = 11.1 \text{ N}\] \[\tan\alpha = \frac{8.66}{7} \quad\Rightarrow\quad \alpha = 51.1^\circ\] The resultant is 11.1 N, at \(51.1^\circ\) above the positive \(x\)-axis. ::: ## Equilibrium :::def Equilibrium A particle is in equilibrium when the resultant force on it is zero. It is then either at rest or moving in a straight line at constant speed (Newton's first law). ::: Equilibrium gives two equations, one for each of two perpendicular directions: the components in each direction add to zero. In words: forces up = forces down, and forces left = forces right. :::eg A particle of mass 5 kg hangs in equilibrium from two light strings. One string makes \(30^\circ\) with the horizontal and the other makes \(60^\circ\) with the horizontal, on opposite sides. Find the tension in each string. Take \(g = 10\). The weight is \(5 \times 10 = 50\) N. Let \(T_1\) be the tension in the \(30^\circ\) string and \(T_2\) the tension in the \(60^\circ\) string. Horizontally, left equals right: \[T_1\cos 30^\circ = T_2\cos 60^\circ \quad\Rightarrow\quad T_2 = \sqrt{3}\,T_1\] Vertically, up equals down: \[T_1\sin 30^\circ + T_2\sin 60^\circ = 50\] Substitute \(T_2 = \sqrt3\,T_1\): \[\tfrac12 T_1 + \sqrt3\cdot\tfrac{\sqrt3}{2}T_1 = \tfrac12 T_1 + \tfrac32 T_1 = 2T_1 = 50\] So \(T_1 = 25\) N and \(T_2 = 25\sqrt3 = 43.3\) N. **Sense check:** the steeper string carries more of the weight, so its tension is larger. ::: ## Friction When two rough surfaces are pushed together, a **friction** force acts along the surfaces and resists sliding. :::def Friction A contact force that acts along the surfaces, opposing sliding (or the tendency to slide). It is zero for a smooth contact. ::: Friction can only be as big as the situation needs, up to a maximum that depends on how hard the surfaces are pressed together: :::key The friction law \[F \leq \mu R\] where \(R\) is the normal reaction and \(\mu\) is the **coefficient of friction** between the two surfaces. When the object is **about to slip** (limiting equilibrium) or is **sliding**, \(F = \mu R\), and friction acts against the motion (or the direction it would move). ::: :::def Limiting friction The maximum value of friction, \(\mu R\), reached when an object is on the point of slipping. ::: The **contact force** between two surfaces is the resultant of \(R\) and \(F\). Its magnitude is \(\sqrt{R^2 + F^2}\). :::warn Friction is not always \(\mu R\) Take a 10 kg box on a floor with \(\mu = 0.4\) (so \(R = 100\) N and the maximum friction is 40 N). If you push it with only 30 N, nothing moves, and the friction is **30 N**, not 40 N. Friction matches the push until the push exceeds \(\mu R\). Write \(F = \mu R\) only when the question says "limiting equilibrium", "about to slip" or "sliding". ::: :::eg A crate of mass 10 kg lies on rough horizontal ground with coefficient of friction 0.4. A rope at \(30^\circ\) above the horizontal pulls it. Find the tension in the rope when the crate is about to slide. Take \(g = 10\). The rope lifts the crate slightly, so \(R\) is less than the weight. Vertically: \(R + T\sin 30^\circ = 100\), so \(R = 100 - 0.5T\). Horizontally: \(T\cos 30^\circ = F\). The crate is about to slide, so \(F = 0.4R\). \[T\cos 30^\circ = 0.4(100 - 0.5T) \quad\Rightarrow\quad T(\cos 30^\circ + 0.2) = 40\] \[T = \frac{40}{1.0660} = 37.5 \text{ N}\] Then \(R = 100 - 0.5(37.5) = 81.2\) N. ::: ## Inclined planes On a slope, resolve **along** the slope and **perpendicular** to it. Gravity does not point along either direction, so the weight must be split. :::html ::: :::key Weight on a slope inclined at angle \(\theta\) - Component of weight **down** the slope: \(mg\sin\theta\) - Component of weight **into** the slope: \(mg\cos\theta\) - With no other forces perpendicular to the slope, \(R = mg\cos\theta\). - A block just about to slide down a rough slope, with no other forces, has \(\mu = \tan\theta\). ::: :::eg (Exam style) A block of mass 5 kg rests on a rough plane inclined at angle \(\theta\) to the horizontal, where \(\sin\theta = 0.6\) and \(\cos\theta = 0.8\). The coefficient of friction between the block and the plane is 0.5. A force of magnitude \(P\) N acts on the block up the plane, parallel to a line of greatest slope. Find the set of values of \(P\) for which the block stays in equilibrium. Take \(g = 10\). Perpendicular to the plane: \(R = 50\cos\theta = 50 \times 0.8 = 40\) N. [M1 A1] Maximum friction: \(F_{\max} = 0.5 \times 40 = 20\) N. [B1] The weight component down the plane is \(50\sin\theta = 30\) N. [B1] **Least \(P\):** the block is about to slide down, so friction acts up the plane. Resolving along the plane: \(P + 20 = 30\), so \(P = 10\). [M1 A1] **Greatest \(P\):** the block is about to slide up, so friction acts down the plane. Resolving along the plane: \(P = 30 + 20 = 50\). [M1 A1] The block is in equilibrium for \(10 \leq P \leq 50\). [A1] ::: ## Newton's third law :::def Newton's third law If object A exerts a force on object B, then B exerts an equal and opposite force on A. The two forces are the same type of force and act on **different** objects. ::: Think of two ice-skaters who push off from each other: each feels the same size of force, in opposite directions. A common error concerns a book on a table. The weight of the book and the normal reaction on the book are equal and opposite, but they are **not** a third-law pair, because both act on the book. The partner of the book's weight is the book's pull on the Earth. The partner of the table's push on the book is the book's push on the table. In problems, the law tells you that a string pulling two particles has the same tension on both, and that two blocks in contact push on each other with equal and opposite forces. :::board Cambridge 9709 Paper 4 and Edexcel IAL Mechanics 1 treat this topic in the same way and use the same model words. The differences are small. Cambridge says "take \(g = 10\)" and expects 3 significant figures. Edexcel IAL and the UK boards use \(g = 9.8\) and expect 2 or 3 significant figures. Edexcel IAL also gives forces as vectors in \(\mathbf{i}\) and \(\mathbf{j}\) notation, such as \((3\mathbf{i} - 2\mathbf{j})\) N, which you add component by component. In the UK A Level Mathematics specifications (Edexcel, AQA, OCR), friction and \(F \leq \mu R\) are second-year content. ::: :::exam Forces questions: where the marks are Draw the force diagram before writing any equation, and mark the positive direction. Examiners give a method mark for each correct resolving equation, so write one equation for each direction. Give the full working for \(R\) before using \(F = \mu R\). State "limiting equilibrium" when you use \(F = \mu R\), and give answers to 3 significant figures. ::: :::try Start easy, finish at exam standard Q: A force of 50 N acts at \(40^\circ\) above the horizontal. Find its horizontal and vertical components. A: Horizontal: \(50\cos 40^\circ = 38.3\) N. Vertical: \(50\sin 40^\circ = 32.1\) N. Q: A particle of mass 2.5 kg hangs at rest from a light vertical string. Find the tension. Take \(g = 10\). A: Equilibrium: the tension balances the weight, \(T = 2.5 \times 10 = 25\) N. Q: A box of mass 8 kg rests on a rough horizontal floor with coefficient of friction 0.25. A horizontal force of 15 N is applied to the box. Take \(g = 10\). (a) Show that the box does not move. (b) Find the friction force. (c) Find the magnitude of the contact force between the box and the floor. A: (a) \(R = 80\) N, so the maximum friction is \(0.25 \times 80 = 20\) N. The push of 15 N is less than 20 N, so the box does not move. (b) The box is in equilibrium, so \(F = 15\) N (not 20 N). (c) Contact force \(= \sqrt{R^2 + F^2} = \sqrt{80^2 + 15^2} = 81.4\) N. Q: A particle of mass 6 kg rests on a smooth plane inclined at \(30^\circ\) to the horizontal. It is held by a light string parallel to the plane. Find the tension in the string and the normal reaction. Take \(g = 10\). A: Along the plane: \(T = 60\sin 30^\circ = 30\) N. Perpendicular to the plane: \(R = 60\cos 30^\circ = 52.0\) N. Q: A block rests in limiting equilibrium on a rough plane inclined at \(20^\circ\) to the horizontal. No other force acts on it. Find the coefficient of friction. A: Along the plane: \(F = mg\sin 20^\circ\). Perpendicular: \(R = mg\cos 20^\circ\). Limiting: \(F = \mu R\), so \(\mu = \tan 20^\circ = 0.364\). Q: Forces of 6 N and 8 N act on a particle at right angles to each other. A third force \(F\) keeps the particle in equilibrium. Find the magnitude of \(F\) and the angle between \(F\) and the 8 N force. A: The resultant of the 6 N and 8 N forces is \(\sqrt{36 + 64} = 10\) N, at \(\tan^{-1}(6/8) = 36.9^\circ\) to the 8 N force. \(F\) must be equal and opposite, so \(F = 10\) N, and the angle between \(F\) and the 8 N force is \(180^\circ - 36.9^\circ = 143.1^\circ\). Q: (Exam style) A block of mass 4 kg is held in equilibrium on a smooth plane inclined at \(30^\circ\) to the horizontal by a horizontal force of magnitude \(P\) N. Find \(P\) and the normal reaction \(R\). Take \(g = 10\). A: Resolve along the plane: \(P\cos 30^\circ = 40\sin 30^\circ\). [M1] \(P = 40\tan 30^\circ = 23.1\) N. [A1] Resolve perpendicular to the plane: \(R = 40\cos 30^\circ + P\sin 30^\circ\). [M1] \(R = 34.64 + 11.55 = 46.2\) N. [A1] Q: (Exam style) A block of mass 3 kg is on a rough plane inclined at \(30^\circ\) to the horizontal, with coefficient of friction 0.2. A horizontal force \(P\) N pushes the block up the plane and the block is about to slide up. Find \(P\). Take \(g = 10\). A: Perpendicular to the plane: \(R = 30\cos 30^\circ + P\sin 30^\circ\). [M1 A1] Along the plane (friction acts down the plane): \(P\cos 30^\circ = 30\sin 30^\circ + 0.2R\). [M1 A1] Substitute: \(P\cos 30^\circ = 15 + 0.2(25.98 + 0.5P)\), so \(P(0.8660 - 0.1) = 15 + 5.196\). [M1] \(P = \dfrac{20.196}{0.7660} = 26.4\) N. [A1] ::: :::quiz ? A 6 kg box rests on a rough horizontal floor with \(\mu = 0.5\). A horizontal force of 20 N is applied and the box does not move. Take \(g = 10\). What is the friction force? - 30 N + 20 N - 10 N - 0 N > The maximum friction is \(0.5 \times 60 = 30\) N, but friction is only as large as needed. The box is in equilibrium, so friction equals the 20 N push. ? A block of mass \(m\) is on a smooth slope inclined at \(\theta\) to the horizontal. What is the component of its weight down the slope? - \(mg\cos\theta\) + \(mg\sin\theta\) - \(mg\tan\theta\) - \(mg\) > The component along the slope uses \(\sin\theta\), and the component into the slope uses \(\cos\theta\). Check with \(\theta = 0^\circ\): a flat surface has no component down it, and \(\sin 0^\circ = 0\). ? A book rests on a table. Which pair of forces is a Newton's third law pair? - The weight of the book and the table's push on the book + The Earth's pull on the book and the book's pull on the Earth - The weight of the book and the book's push on the table > A third-law pair acts on two different objects and is the same type of force. The first option is two forces on the book that balance. The third option mixes gravity with a contact force. ? A particle is in equilibrium under three forces. Which statement must be true? + The resultant force is zero. - The particle is at rest. - The three forces have equal magnitudes. - Each force is perpendicular to the other two. > Equilibrium means zero resultant force. The particle could be at rest or moving at constant velocity, and the forces can have any magnitudes that balance. ::: :::recap - A force is a vector, measured in newtons. Weight is \(W = mg\); take \(g = 10\) (Cambridge) or \(g = 9.8\) (Edexcel and UK boards). - Always draw a force diagram: weight, then a normal reaction and friction at each surface, then tensions and any given forces. - A force \(F\) at angle \(\theta\) to a direction has components \(F\cos\theta\) along it and \(F\sin\theta\) perpendicular to it. - The resultant comes from adding components in two perpendicular directions, then using Pythagoras and \(\tan\). - Equilibrium means the resultant is zero: the components add to zero in each of two perpendicular directions. - Friction obeys \(F \leq \mu R\), with \(F = \mu R\) only when the object is about to slip or is sliding. - On a slope, the weight splits into \(mg\sin\theta\) down the slope and \(mg\cos\theta\) into it. - Newton's third law: the two forces of a pair are equal, opposite, of the same type, and act on different objects. ::: Next: [Kinematics: describing motion](#math.m.kinematics) describes how an object moves, and [Newton's laws and connected particles](#math.m.newton) links forces to that motion.

Zero to A*

Learn A Level Mathematics, Physics, Chemistry, Biology, Engineering and Business from the very first idea, with worked examples marked the way examiners mark them. Then follow a step-by-step road all the way to exam day.

@group Skills that raise grades @chapter road.methods @title Study methods that actually work @level guide @paper All boards · all subjects @time 45 minutes to read, then use all year @summary Research shows that some popular study habits, such as rereading and highlighting, do very little. This chapter shows you the methods that do work (testing yourself, spacing and mixing your practice) and how to build them into a normal week. :::why Two students can study for the same hours and get very different grades. Usually the difference is method, not talent. Rereading feels productive but builds familiarity, not memory. Testing yourself feels harder, and that difficulty is what makes knowledge stay. Change how you study and every hour from now on is worth more. ::: **Before you start**, read [The preparation road at a glance](#road.overview) so you know where these methods fit. They are the engine of [Phase 2: Learn the content](#road.learn) and [Phase 3: Practise and test yourself](#road.practice). ## What the research says In 2013 the psychologist John Dunlosky and four colleagues reviewed the research on ten popular learning techniques and rated how useful each one is for real students. | Rating | Technique | What it means | |---|---|---| | **High** | Practice testing | Recalling or answering questions without looking | | **High** | Distributed practice | Spreading study of a topic over days or weeks | | Moderate | Elaborative interrogation | Asking yourself "why is this true?" | | Moderate | Self-explanation | Explaining each step of a solution to yourself | | Moderate | Interleaved practice | Mixing problem types in one session | | Low | Summarising | Writing shorter versions of a text | | Low | Highlighting | Marking key words while reading | | Low | Keyword mnemonics | Linking new words to memorable images | | Low | Imagery for text | Picturing what you read | | Low | Rereading | Reading the same notes again | "Low" does not mean useless; it means a small benefit for the time it takes. Yet rereading and highlighting are the most popular study habits of all. They feel good because familiar words make your brain mistake "I recognise this" for "I know this", an **illusion of competence**. The exam gives you a blank space, not the page, so producing knowledge from memory is what you must practise. ## Retrieval practice: test yourself first :::def Retrieval practice Learning by recalling information from memory (for example by answering questions or writing everything you remember on a topic) instead of rereading it. Each successful recall makes the memory stronger and easier to find later. ::: Retrieval works even when you get answers wrong, as long as you check and correct them straight away. Good ways to retrieve: - **Blank-page recall ("blurting").** Close your notes and write everything you remember about a topic for 10 minutes. Then fill the gaps from your notes in a different colour. The coloured parts are your revision list. - **Chapter questions.** Do the practice questions at the end of each chapter here without looking back. - **Flashcards** (see below) and **past-paper questions**, which are retrieval in the exact form the exam uses. See [Phase 4: Past papers and mark schemes](#road.pastpapers). :::tip Turn your notes into questions After you finish a section, write three questions it answers in the margin, for example "What does the discriminant tell you?" Next time, cover the notes and answer the questions. Your notes become a self-test instead of something to reread. ::: ## Spacing: little and often beats one long session :::def Spaced practice Spreading study of the same material over several sessions separated by gaps of days or weeks, instead of doing it all at once. Also called distributed practice. ::: Memory fades quickly after you first learn something, and each recall after a gap makes it fade more slowly. A useful rule of thumb is to review a new topic about **1 day, 3 days, 1 week, 2 weeks and 1 month** after first learning it. The exact gaps matter less than the habit of coming back. The opposite is **cramming**: everything in one long session just before a test. It can get you through tomorrow's test, but most of it is gone weeks later, and A Levels examine two years of content at the end. :::warn Rewatching is rereading Watching the same video lesson twice is the video version of rereading. Watch it once, carefully, then close it and test yourself. Rewatch only the part you could not recall. ::: ## Interleaving: mix your practice :::def Interleaving Mixing different topics or types of problem within one practice session (for example differentiation, vectors and probability), so that you must decide which method each question needs. ::: When you do twenty questions on one method in a row (**blocked practice**), you know the method before you read the question. In the exam, nobody tells you, and interleaving trains that choice. Use blocked practice for a brand-new topic, then switch to mixed sets once the basic questions feel easy. ## Making ideas stick: elaboration, examples and pictures **Elaboration** means connecting a new idea to what you already know by asking "why?" and "how?". Why does a higher temperature speed up a reaction? How does that link to activation energy? Every connection is another route your memory can use. **Concrete examples** make abstract ideas easy to picture. "Price elastic demand" is hard to remember; "when one brand of crisps raises its price, many buyers switch brands" is easy. Collect one or two examples of your own for every definition. **Dual coding** means combining words with visuals. Draw blood flow through the heart, a supply and demand diagram or a flowchart of protein synthesis, and label it from memory. Words and pictures give you two routes to the same idea. ## Worked examples, then fade them When you are a beginner, solving problems alone can overload you, so study a **worked example** first. Then remove the support step by step: | Stage | What you do | |---|---| | 1. Study | Read a full worked example. Explain each step to yourself: why this step, why now? | | 2. Complete | Try a similar example where the last steps are hidden. Finish it. | | 3. Solo | Do a similar question with no help, then check against a full solution. | | 4. Mixed | Do the same type of question inside a mixed set, under time pressure. | Once you reach stage 4 easily, stop studying examples for that topic and spend your time on questions. ## The Feynman technique The physicist Richard Feynman was famous for explaining hard ideas in simple words. This technique finds exactly where your understanding breaks. :::steps 1. Choose one concept, for example "moles" or "opportunity cost". 2. Explain it out loud or on paper as if teaching a younger student. Use plain words and an example. 3. Notice where you hesitate, use jargon you cannot explain, or say "it just is". Those are your gaps. 4. Go back to your notes or the chapter and fix those gaps only. 5. Explain it again, more simply. Finish with the exact syllabus definition. ::: :::tip If English is your second language Explain the idea first in your own language to check you understand it. Then explain it again in English, using the precise syllabus terms. Examiners reward the correct technical words, so collect them in a personal word list with a short meaning next to each. ::: ## Spaced-repetition flashcards Flashcards combine retrieval and spacing.
